title: Isaiah

stories.title: 📜 Isaiah 1
summaryBullets: This is the vision concerning Judah and Jerusalem that Isaiah son of Amoz saw during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah. (1:1).
Listen, O heavens, and give ear, O earth, for the LORD has spoken: “I have raised children and brought them up, but they have rebelled against Me. (1:2).
The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger, but Israel does not know; My people do not understand.” (1:3).

Alas, O sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity, a brood of evildoers, children who act corruptly! They have forsaken the LORD; they have despised the Holy One of Israel and turned their backs on Him. (1:4).
Why do you want more beatings? Why do you keep rebelling? Your head has a massive wound, and your whole heart is afflicted. (1:5).
From the sole of your foot to the top of your head, there is no soundness— only wounds and welts and festering sores neither cleansed nor bandaged nor soothed with oil. (1:6).
Your land is desolate; your cities are burned with fire. Foreigners devour your fields before you — a desolation demolished by strangers. (1:7).
And the Daughter of Zion is abandoned like a shelter in a vineyard, like a shack in a cucumber field, like a city besieged. (1:8).
Unless the LORD of Hosts had left us a few survivors, we would have become like Sodom, we would have resembled Gomorrah. (1:9).
Hear the word of the LORD, you rulers of Sodom; listen to the instruction of our God, you people of Gomorrah! (1:10).

“What good to Me is your multitude of sacrifices?” says the LORD. “I am full from the burnt offerings of rams and the fat of well-fed cattle; I take no delight in the blood of bulls and lambs and goats. (1:11).
When you come to appear before Me, who has required this of you— this trampling of My courts? (1:12).
Bring your worthless offerings no more; your incense is detestable to Me. New Moons, Sabbaths, and convocations— I cannot endure iniquity in a solemn assembly. (1:13).
I hate your New Moons and your appointed feasts. They have become a burden to Me; I am weary of bearing them. (1:14).
When you spread out your hands in prayer, I will hide My eyes from you; even though you multiply your prayers, I will not listen. Your hands are covered with blood. (1:15).
Wash and cleanse yourselves. Remove your evil deeds from My sight. Stop doing evil! (1:16).
Learn to do right; seek justice and correct the oppressor. Defend the fatherless and plead the case of the widow.” (1:17).
“Come now, let us reason together,” says the LORD. “Though your sins are like scarlet, they will be as white as snow; though they are as red as crimson, they will become like wool. (1:18).
If you are willing and obedient, you will eat the best of the land. (1:19).
But if you resist and rebel, you will be devoured by the sword.” For the mouth of the LORD has spoken. (1:20).
See how the faithful city has become a harlot! She once was full of justice; righteousness resided within her, but now only murderers! (1:21).
Your silver has become dross; your fine wine is diluted with water. (1:22).
Your rulers are rebels, friends of thieves. They all love bribes and chasing after rewards. They do not defend the fatherless, and the plea of the widow never comes before them. (1:23).
Therefore the Lord GOD of Hosts, the Mighty One of Israel, declares: “Ah, I will be relieved of My foes and avenge Myself on My enemies. (1:24).
I will turn My hand against you; I will thoroughly purge your dross; I will remove all your impurities. (1:25).
I will restore your judges as at first, and your counselors as at the beginning. After that you will be called the City of Righteousness, the Faithful City.” (1:26).
Zion will be redeemed with justice, her repentant ones with righteousness. (1:27).
But rebels and sinners will together be shattered, and those who forsake the LORD will perish. (1:28).
Surely you will be ashamed of the sacred oaks in which you have delighted; you will be embarrassed by the gardens that you have chosen. (1:29).
For you will become like an oak whose leaves are withered, like a garden without water. (1:30).
The strong man will become tinder and his work will be a spark; both will burn together, with no one to quench the flames. (1:31).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 32:1: Heaven and earth called to witness.
Amos 5:21-24: Rejection of feasts and call for justice.
Micah 6:6-8: What the LORD requires: justice, kindness, humility.
Romans 9:27-29: Citation of Isaiah on a remnant (cf. 1:9).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת (YHWH Tseva’ot), Greek (LXX): Κύριος Σαβαώθ, Aramaic: מָרֵי צְבָאוֹת (Marei Tzva’ot)
translationNotes.note: Title emphasizing command over heavenly armies (appears repeatedly 1:9) (1:24).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צִיּוֹן (Tsiyyon), Greek: Σιών (Siōn), Aramaic: צִיּוֹן
translationNotes.note: Poetic name for Jerusalem and its hill (1:8) (1:27).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נִוָּכְחָה (niwwākhchāh) from יָכַח (yakhaḥ, ‘contend/decide’); Greek (LXX): δεῦτε καὶ διαλεχθῶμεν
translationNotes.note: Legal/dispute language in 1:18.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שָׁנִי (shani) / תּוֹלָע (tolāʿ); Greek: κόκκινον / κόκκος
translationNotes.note: Color terms in the cleansing promise (1:18).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֵלִים/אֵלָה (’elim/’elah), גַּנּוֹת (gannōt); Greek: τερέβινθος, κῆποι
translationNotes.note: Sites mentioned in 1:29-30 as objects of shame; terms given without explanation of practices.

stories.keyTakeaway: Isaiah announces charges against Judah, rejects empty offerings, calls for justice, and declares a purging that restores judges while rebels are destroyed.

stories.title: 🏔️ Isaiah 2
summaryBullets: This is the message that was revealed to Isaiah son of Amoz concerning Judah and Jerusalem: (2:1).
In the last days the mountain of the house of the LORD will be established as the chief of the mountains; it will be raised above the hills, and all nations will stream to it. (2:2).

And many peoples will come and say: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD, to the house of the God of Jacob. He will teach us His ways so that we may walk in His paths.” For the law will go forth from Zion, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem. (2:3).

Then He will judge between the nations and arbitrate for many peoples. They will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks. Nation will no longer take up the sword against nation, nor train anymore for war. (2:4).
Come, O house of Jacob, let us walk in the light of the LORD. (2:5).

For You have abandoned Your people, the house of Jacob, because they are filled with influences from the east; they are soothsayers like the Philistines; they strike hands with the children of foreigners. (2:6).
Their land is full of silver and gold, with no limit to their treasures; their land is full of horses, with no limit to their chariots. (2:7).
Their land is full of idols; they bow down to the work of their hands, to what their fingers have made. (2:8).
So mankind is brought low, and man is humbled — do not forgive them! (2:9).
Go into the rocks and hide in the dust from the terror of the LORD and the splendor of His majesty. (2:10).
The proud look of man will be humbled, and the loftiness of men brought low; the LORD alone will be exalted in that day. (2:11).
For the Day of the LORD of Hosts will come against all the proud and lofty, against all that is exalted— it will be humbled— (2:12).
against all the cedars of Lebanon, lofty and lifted up, against all the oaks of Bashan, (2:13).
against all the tall mountains, against all the high hills, (2:14).
against every high tower, against every fortified wall, (2:15).
against every ship of Tarshish, and against every stately vessel. (2:16).
So the pride of man will be brought low, and the loftiness of men will be humbled; the LORD alone will be exalted in that day, (2:17).
and the idols will vanish completely. (2:18).
Men will flee to caves in the rocks and holes in the ground, away from the terror of the LORD and from the splendor of His majesty, when He rises to shake the earth. (2:19).
In that day men will cast away to the moles and bats their idols of silver and gold — the idols they made to worship. (2:20).
They will flee to caverns in the rocks and crevices in the cliffs, away from the terror of the LORD and from the splendor of His majesty, when He rises to shake the earth. (2:21).
Put no more trust in man, who has only the breath in his nostrils. Of what account is he? (2:22).
crossRefs: Micah 4:1-3: Micah records the same oracle, the mountain of the house of the LORD raised above the hills and the nations beating their swords into plowshares.
Joel 3:9-10: The nations are summoned to war and told to do the reverse, beating their plowshares into swords and their pruning hooks into spears.
Genesis 11:1-9: Men build a city and a tower to make a name for themselves, and the LORD comes down and scatters them.
Revelation 6:15-16: Kings, nobles, and slaves hide in the caves and among the rocks and beg the mountains to hide them from the face of the One on the throne.
Deuteronomy 17:16-17: Israel's king is forbidden to acquire many horses, many wives, or great quantities of silver and gold.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יוֹם יְהוָה (yom YHWH), Greek (LXX): ἡμέρα Κυρίου, Aramaic: יוֹם יי
translationNotes.note: Phrase for the time when the LORD arises to terrify the earth (2:12-21).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֲרָבוֹת / אִתִּים (ḥaravot / ittīm), חֲנִיתוֹת / מַזְמֵרוֹת (ḥanitot / mazmerot); Greek: μάχαιραι / ἄροτρα, λόγχαι / δρέπανα
translationNotes.note: Tools/weapons in 2:4.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֳנִיּוֹת תַּרְשִׁישׁ (’oniyot Tarshish); Greek: ναῦς Θαρσείς
translationNotes.note: Maritime symbol of pride/commerce in 2:16.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סוּסִים (susim, horses) - אֱלִילִים (elilim, worthless things)
translationNotes.note: 2:7-8 lists what fills the land in one breath: silver and gold with no end, horses and chariots with no end, and idols. Deuteronomy 17:16-17 names the first two as the exact things a king of Israel must not pile up, horses above all, because getting them meant dealing with Egypt. Elilim, the word for the idols, is a mocking diminutive built to sound like elohim while meaning nothings.

translationNotes.term: Into the holes of the rocks
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בִּמְעָרוֹת צֻרִים (bi-me'aroth tsurim, into caves of rock)
translationNotes.note: The line repeats three times, at 2:10, 2:19 and 2:21, and it is not a figure of speech. The Judean hill country is soft limestone honeycombed with caves, quarried cisterns and rock tombs, and hiding in them is what people actually did when an army came through; 1 Samuel 13:6 has Israel hiding in caves, thickets, cliffs, tombs and pits from the Philistines. 2:20 has them throwing their silver idols into the same holes on the way in.

stories.keyTakeaway: Isaiah describes a future time when God's temple will be exalted and nations will seek his instruction, establishing peace; he then condemns Judah for idolatry and pride, warning that the Lord will humble all human arrogance and destroy their idols.

headings.text: The Mountain of the House of the Lord

stories.title: 🏔️ Isaiah 3
summaryBullets: For behold, the Lord GOD of Hosts is about to remove from Jerusalem and Judah both supply and support: the whole supply of food and water, (3:1).
the mighty man and the warrior, the judge and the prophet, the soothsayer and the elder, (3:2).
the commander of fifty and the dignitary, the counselor, the cunning magician, and the clever enchanter. (3:3).
“I will make mere lads their leaders, and children will rule over them.” (3:4).
The people will oppress one another, man against man, neighbor against neighbor; the young will rise up against the old, and the base against the honorable. (3:5).
A man will seize his brother within his father’s house: “You have a cloak— you be our leader! Take charge of this heap of rubble.” (3:6).
On that day he will cry aloud: “I am not a healer. I have no food or clothing in my house. Do not make me leader of the people!” (3:7).
For Jerusalem has stumbled and Judah has fallen because they spoke and acted against the LORD, defying His glorious presence. (3:8).
The expression on their faces testifies against them, and like Sodom they flaunt their sin; they do not conceal it. Woe to them, for they have brought disaster upon themselves. (3:9).
Tell the righteous it will be well with them, for they will enjoy the fruit of their labor. (3:10).
Woe to the wicked; disaster is upon them! For they will be repaid with what their hands have done. (3:11).
Youths oppress My people, and women rule over them. O My people, your guides mislead you; they turn you from your paths. (3:12).
The LORD arises to contend; He stands to judge the people. (3:13).
The LORD brings this charge against the elders and leaders of His people: “You have devoured the vineyard; the plunder of the poor is in your houses. (3:14).
Why do you crush My people and grind the faces of the poor?” declares the Lord GOD of Hosts. (3:15).
The LORD also says: “Because the daughters of Zion are haughty — walking with heads held high and wanton eyes, prancing and skipping as they go, jingling the bracelets on their ankles — (3:16).
the Lord will bring sores on the heads of the daughters of Zion, and the LORD will make their foreheads bare.” (3:17).
In that day the Lord will take away their finery: their anklets and headbands and crescents; (3:18).
their pendants, bracelets, and veils; (3:19).
their headdresses, ankle chains, and sashes; their perfume bottles and charms; (3:20).
their signet rings and nose rings; (3:21).
their festive robes, capes, cloaks, and purses; (3:22).
and their mirrors, linen garments, tiaras, and shawls. (3:23).
Instead of fragrance there will be a stench; instead of a belt, a rope; instead of styled hair, baldness; instead of fine clothing, sackcloth; instead of beauty, shame. (3:24).
Your men will fall by the sword, and your warriors in battle. (3:25).
And the gates of Zion will lament and mourn; destitute, she will sit on the ground. (3:26).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 24:14-16: Nebuchadnezzar deports Jerusalem's commanders, mighty men, craftsmen, and metalsmiths and leaves only the poorest people of the land.
Exodus 23:6: The law forbids denying justice to the poor in their lawsuits.
Exodus 22:22-24: Israel is warned not to mistreat any widow or orphan, because the LORD will hear their cry and answer with the sword.
Ecclesiastes 10:16: A land is called cursed whose king is a youth and whose princes feast in the morning.
Amos 4:1: The women of Samaria who oppress the poor and crush the needy are called cows of Bashan and summoned for judgment.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׂק (saq); Greek: σάκκος (sakkos)
translationNotes.note: A coarse, dark goat-hair fabric worn against bare skin as a universal sign of mourning, repentance, or distress (1 Kings 21:27; Jonah 3:5; Matthew 11:21). Wearing it publicly broadcast grief or contrition; the discomfort itself was part of the symbolism.

translationNotes.term: The supply and the support removed
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׂר־חֲמִשִּׁים (sar chamishshim, captain of fifty) - חֲכַם חֲרָשִׁים (chakham charashim, skilled craftsman)
translationNotes.note: 3:1-3 removes a society office by office, and every title is a real post. The captain of fifty commands the smallest standing unit in the army, the rank the men sent for Elijah hold at 2 Kings 1:9-14. The charash is the metalworker, and Assyria and Babylon both deported that trade first on purpose: 2 Kings 24:14 has the craftsmen and the smiths taken to Babylon, which left a country unable to make or mend a weapon.

translationNotes.term: Grinding the faces of the poor
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וּפְנֵי עֲנִיִּים תִּטְחָנוּ (u-phne aniyyim titchanu)
translationNotes.note: Tachan is the verb for milling grain, the daily work of crushing kernels between two stones until nothing is left whole. 3:15 puts human faces under that stone. The verse frames it as a court question, what do you mean by crushing my people, and 3:14 has already named the defendants: the elders and princes, with the plunder of the poor in their houses.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׂהֲרֹנִים (saharonim, crescents) - לְחָשִׁים (lechashim, charms) - בָּתֵּי הַנֶּפֶשׁ (batte ha-nephesh, perfume flasks)
translationNotes.note: Twenty-one items, the most detailed inventory of dress anywhere in the Old Testament, and several are not jewellery at all. Saharonim are crescent amulets, moon shapes, the same ornaments hung on the Midianite kings' camels at Judges 8:21. Lechashim comes from the word for whispering and means charms worn to work. Batte ha-nephesh reads houses of the breath and means the little sealed bottles that held scent.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כִּי־תַחַת יֹפִי (ki tachath yophi)
translationNotes.note: 3:24 runs five reversals and the last one is one word in Hebrew, ki, a mark burned into the skin. It is the sign put on a slave. The other four are as physical: stench for perfume, a rope for a sash, shaved scalp for styled hair, sackcloth for a fine robe, and sackcloth was coarse goat hair worn against the skin.

translationNotes.term: She shall sit on the ground
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פְּתָחֶיהָ (pethacheha, her gates) - לָאָרֶץ תֵּשֵׁב (la-arets teshev)
translationNotes.note: The gate was where a city did its legal and commercial business, so 3:26 saying her gates mourn is saying the courts and the markets have stopped. Sitting on the bare ground was the posture of mourning and of a prisoner: Job's friends sit with him seven days (Job 2:13), and Lamentations 2:10 has the elders of Zion sitting on the ground in silence.

stories.keyTakeaway: The Lord will strip Jerusalem and Judah of their leaders, supply, and security, replacing them with incompetent youths; he judges the elders and wealthy for oppressing the poor, and promises to humiliate the proud women of Zion by removing their finery and bringing them to ruin.

headings.text: A Warning to the Daughters of Zion

stories.title: 🏔️ Isaiah 4
summaryBullets: In that day seven women will take hold of one man and say, “We will eat our own bread and provide our own clothes. Just let us be called by your name. Take away our disgrace!” (4:1).
On that day the Branch of the LORD will be beautiful and glorious, and the fruit of the land will be the pride and glory of Israel’s survivors. (4:2).
Whoever remains in Zion and whoever is left in Jerusalem will be called holy— all in Jerusalem who are recorded among the living— (4:3).
when the Lord has washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion and cleansed the bloodstains from the heart of Jerusalem by a spirit of judgment and a spirit of fire. (4:4).
Then the LORD will create over all of Mount Zion and over her assemblies a cloud of smoke by day and a glowing flame of fire by night. For over all the glory there will be a canopy, (4:5).
a shelter to give shade from the heat by day, and a refuge and hiding place from the storm and the rain. (4:6).
crossRefs: Zechariah 3:8: The LORD tells Joshua the high priest that He is about to bring His servant, the Branch.
Jeremiah 23:5: The LORD promises to raise up for David a righteous Branch who will reign as King and do justice in the land.
Exodus 13:21-22: The LORD goes ahead of Israel in a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night, and neither leaves its place.
Numbers 9:15-17: The cloud covers the tabernacle by day and looks like fire at night, and Israel breaks camp only when it lifts.
Exodus 32:32-33: Moses asks to be blotted out of the book the LORD has written, and the LORD answers that He blots out whoever sins against Him.

translationNotes.term: Seven women take hold of one man
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יֵאָסֵף חֶרְפָּתֵנוּ (yeasef cherpatenu)
translationNotes.note: The picture assumes a generation of men killed in war. A husband owed his wife food, clothing, and marital rights (Exodus 21:10); these women give up the first two by name and ask only to be called by his name, meaning legal marriage. An unmarried, childless woman had no standing and no support in old age, and that is the disgrace they want taken away.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צֶמַח (tsemach)
translationNotes.note: Tsemach means what sprouts up out of the ground, a green shoot. The prophets turn it into a fixed title: Jeremiah 23:5 and 33:15 promise David a righteous Branch, and Zechariah 3:8 and 6:12 call the coming figure My servant the Branch. Isaiah 11:1 uses two different words for the same image, choter and netser.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כָּתוּב לַחַיִּים (katuv la-chayyim)
translationNotes.note: Towns kept written registers of their citizens, and a name in the roll was the proof of belonging. Scripture uses that register as a picture: Moses asks to be blotted out of God's book (Exodus 32:32-33), Psalm 69:28 asks that enemies not be enrolled with the righteous, Malachi 3:16 has a scroll of remembrance written, and Daniel 12:1 has deliverance for everyone found written in the book.

translationNotes.term: A cloud by day and fire by night
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עָנָן (anan) - Hebrew: אֵשׁ (esh)
translationNotes.note: This is the exodus pillar. Exodus 13:21-22 has the LORD going before Israel in a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night, and Exodus 40:34-38 has the cloud settling on the tabernacle so that Israel moved only when it lifted. Verse 5 puts that same covering over the whole of Mount Zion rather than over one tent.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֻפָּה (chuppah)
translationNotes.note: A chuppah is the wedding canopy, the covered chamber a bridegroom brought his bride into. The word occurs only three times in the Old Testament: here, in Psalm 19:5 where the sun comes out of his chuppah like a bridegroom, and in Joel 2:16 where the bride is called out of hers. It is still the name of the canopy used at a Jewish wedding.

stories.keyTakeaway: After a time of devastation, seven women will eagerly attach themselves to one man for survival and social standing. The Lord's Branch will restore the land's beauty; the surviving remnant in Jerusalem will be called holy and protected by the Lord's cloud and fire, which will shelter them from heat and storm.

stories.title: 🍇 Isaiah 5
summaryBullets: I will sing for my beloved a song of his vineyard: My beloved had a vineyard on a very fertile hill. (5:1).

He dug it up and cleared the stones and planted the finest vines. He built a watchtower in the middle and dug out a winepress as well. He waited for the vineyard to yield good grapes, but the fruit it produced was sour! (5:2).
“And now, O dwellers of Jerusalem and men of Judah, I exhort you to judge between Me and My vineyard. (5:3).
What more could have been done for My vineyard than I have done for it? Why, when I expected sweet grapes, did it bring forth sour fruit? (5:4).
Now I will tell you what I am about to do to My vineyard: I will take away its hedge, and it will be consumed; I will tear down its wall, and it will be trampled. (5:5).
I will make it a wasteland, neither pruned nor cultivated, and thorns and briers will grow up. I will command the clouds that rain shall not fall on it.” (5:6).

For the vineyard of the LORD of Hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah are the plant of His delight. He looked for justice, but saw bloodshed; for righteousness, but heard a cry of distress. (5:7).
Woe to you who add house to house and join field to field until no place is left and you live alone in the land. (5:8).
I heard the LORD of Hosts declare: “Surely many houses will become desolate, great mansions left unoccupied. (5:9).
For ten acres of vineyard will yield but a bath of wine, and a homer of seed only an ephah of grain.” (5:10).
Woe to those who rise early in the morning in pursuit of strong drink, who linger into the evening, to be inflamed by wine. (5:11).
At their feasts are the lyre and harp, tambourines and flutes and wine. They disregard the actions of the LORD and fail to see the work of His hands. (5:12).
Therefore My people will go into exile for their lack of understanding; their dignitaries are starving and their masses are parched with thirst. (5:13).
Therefore Sheol enlarges its throat and opens wide its enormous jaws, and down go Zion’s nobles and masses, her revelers and carousers! (5:14).
So mankind will be brought low, and each man humbled; the arrogant will lower their eyes. (5:15).
But the LORD of Hosts will be exalted by His justice, and the holy God will show Himself holy in righteousness. (5:16).
Lambs will graze as in their own pastures, and strangers will feed in the ruins of the wealthy. (5:17).
Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of deceit and pull sin along with cart ropes, (5:18).
to those who say, “Let Him hurry and hasten His work so that we may see it! Let the plan of the Holy One of Israel come so that we may know it!” (5:19).
Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who turn darkness to light and light to darkness, who replace bitter with sweet and sweet with bitter. (5:20).
Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes and clever in their own sight. (5:21).
Woe to those who are heroes in drinking wine and champions in mixing strong drink, (5:22).
who acquit the guilty for a bribe and deprive the innocent of justice. (5:23).

Therefore, as a tongue of fire consumes the straw, and as dry grass shrivels in the flame, so their roots will decay and their blossoms will blow away like dust; for they have rejected the instruction of the LORD of Hosts and despised the word of the Holy One of Israel. (5:24).

Therefore the anger of the LORD burns against His people; His hand is raised against them to strike them down. The mountains quake, and the corpses lie like refuse in the streets. Despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised. (5:25).
He lifts a banner for the distant nations and whistles for those at the ends of the earth. Behold— how speedily and swiftly they come! (5:26).
None of them grows weary or stumbles; no one slumbers or sleeps. No belt is loose and no sandal strap is broken. (5:27).
Their arrows are sharpened, and all their bows are strung. The hooves of their horses are like flint; their chariot wheels are like a whirlwind. (5:28).
Their roaring is like that of a lion; they roar like young lions. They growl and seize their prey; they carry it away, and no one can rescue it. (5:29).
In that day they will roar over it, like the roaring of the sea. If one looks over the land, he will see darkness and distress; even the light will be obscured by clouds. (5:30).
crossRefs: Psalm 80:8-16: Israel as a vine brought from Egypt.
Isaiah 27:2-6: A later vineyard song with different outcome.
Amos 6:1-7: Woe against the complacent and indulgent.
Micah 2:1-2: Seizing fields and houses condemned.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּאֻשִׁים (be’ushim); Greek (LXX): ἀκάνθαι/ὄμφακες (var. renderings)
translationNotes.note: Term for the bad yield in 5:2-4.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִשְׁפָּט/מִשְׂפָּח (mishpat/mispach), צְדָקָה/צְעָקָה (tsedaqah/tse‘aqah)
translationNotes.note: Paronomasia in 5:7 contrasting what was sought and what was found.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הוֹי (hoy), Greek (LXX): οὐαί, Aramaic: וַי
translationNotes.note: Interjection introducing denunciations (5:8-22).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נֵס (nes); Greek (LXX): σημεῖον/σημαία
translationNotes.note: Raised to summon distant nations (5:26).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בַּת (bath), חֹמֶר (ḥomer), אֵיפָה (eifah), צֶמֶד (tsemed, ‘yoke’-area); Greek: βάθος, κόρος, εφά
translationNotes.note: Units in 5:10 for yield and planting.
The standard Old Testament dry measure for grain, about 22 quarts or 5.8 gallons (22 liters). Ruth carries home an ephah of barley after a day's gleaning (Ruth 2:17).
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֵיפָה (ephah)

translationNotes.note: The liquid equivalent of an ephah, about 5.8 gallons (22 liters). Solomon's 'molten sea' in the temple held 2,000 baths (1 Kings 7:26).
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בַּת (bath)

translationNotes.note: The Old Testament realm of the dead; a shadowy underworld where both righteous and wicked descend (Genesis 37:35; Psalm 16:10). Not necessarily a place of torment; more a state of cessation and silence. The Septuagint and New Testament render it with the Greek word hades.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁאוֹל (sheol)
Hebrew: מִגְדָּל (migdal), tower - יֶקֶב (yeqev), winepress
translationNotes.note: Isaiah 5:1-2 lists the real work of planting a vineyard on a hillside, in order. The stones are cleared and stacked as terrace walls to hold the soil on the slope. A stone tower goes up in the middle so a watchman can sleep out there through the vintage and keep off thieves and animals. The press is not a machine but a shallow basin cut into the bedrock, where the grapes are trodden, with a channel running to a lower catch basin. Presses of exactly this kind are still cut into the rock across the Judean hills.

translationNotes.term: a ten-acre vineyard yielding one bath
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צֶמֶד (tsemed), a yoke of land - חֹמֶר (chomer), homer
translationNotes.note: Isaiah 5:10 states the failure as a farmer would: ten yoke of vineyard, meaning the ground a pair of oxen could plow in ten days, produces one bath of wine, roughly six gallons. A homer of seed returns an ephah, and an ephah is one tenth of a homer, so the sowing returns ten percent. Both figures describe land that costs more to work than it gives back.

stories.keyTakeaway: Isaiah sings the vineyard song identifying Israel as the vineyard, pronounces six woes, and depicts nations summoned as swift instruments against the land.

stories.title: 🔥 Isaiah 6
summaryBullets: In the year that King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord seated on a throne, high and exalted; and the train of His robe filled the temple. (6:1).
Above Him stood seraphim, each having six wings: With two wings they covered their faces, with two they covered their feet, and with two they were flying. (6:2).
And they were calling out to one another: “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Hosts; all the earth is full of His glory.” (6:3).
At the sound of their voices the doorposts and thresholds shook, and the temple was filled with smoke. (6:4).
Then I said: “Woe is me, for I am ruined, because I am a man of unclean lips dwelling among a people of unclean lips; for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of Hosts.” (6:5).
Then one of the seraphim flew to me, and in his hand was a glowing coal that he had taken with tongs from the altar. (6:6).
And with it he touched my mouth and said: “Now that this has touched your lips, your iniquity is removed and your sin is atoned for.” (6:7).
Then I heard the voice of the Lord saying: “Whom shall I send? Who will go for Us?” And I said: “Here am I. Send me!” (6:8).
And He replied: “Go and tell this people, ‘Be ever hearing, but never understanding; be ever seeing, but never perceiving.’ (6:9).

Make the hearts of this people calloused; deafen their ears and close their eyes. Otherwise they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their hearts, and turn and be healed.” (6:10).
Then I asked: “How long, O Lord?” And He replied: “Until the cities lie ruined and without inhabitant, until the houses are left unoccupied and the land is desolate and ravaged, (6:11).
until the LORD has driven men far away and the land is utterly forsaken. (6:12).
And though a tenth remains in the land, it will be burned again. As the terebinth and oak leave stumps when felled, so the holy seed will be a stump in the land.” (6:13).
crossRefs: 2 Chronicles 26:16-23: King Uzziah’s death noted.
Exodus 19:18: Sinai covered with smoke (theophany imagery).
Revelation 4:8: “Holy, holy, holy” echoed by living creatures.
John 12:41: Later reference to Isaiah’s vision.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׂרָפִים (serafim, ‘burning ones’), Greek (LXX): σεραφίμ, Aramaic: שרפים
translationNotes.note: Winged beings in the temple vision (6:2-6).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קָדוֹשׁ קָדוֹשׁ קָדוֹשׁ (qadosh qadosh qadosh); Greek (LXX): ἅγιος ἅγιος ἅγιος
translationNotes.note: Threefold acclamation in 6:3.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הִנְנִי שְׁלָחֵנִי (hineni, shelacheni); Greek (LXX): ἰδού εἰμι· ἀπόστειλόν με
translationNotes.note: Isaiah’s response to the call (6:8).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew verbs: הַשְׁמֵן (hashmen, ‘make fat’), הַכְבֵּד (hachbed, ‘make heavy’), הַשְׁע (hashaʿ, ‘shut/ smear’); Greek (LXX): πώρωσον, βάρυνον, κάμμυσον
translationNotes.note: Commission wording in 6:9-10.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: זֶרַע קֹדֶשׁ (zeraʿ qodesh); Greek (LXX): σπέρμα ἅγιον
translationNotes.note: Designation for the stump remnant (6:13).

translationNotes.term: in the year King Uzziah died
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֻזִּיָּהוּ (Uzziyahu)
translationNotes.note: Isaiah dates his vision by a death, and it is a pointed one. Uzziah reigned over Judah for fifty-two years and made it strong, then went into the temple to burn incense himself, which only the priests could do; leprosy broke out on his forehead and he lived apart until he died (2 Chronicles 26:16-21). So the year that a king who forced his way into the sanctuary died is the year Isaiah is taken into the throne room of God and says he is undone.

stories.keyTakeaway: Isaiah sees the LORD enthroned, is purified by a coal, receives a commission of hardening, and is told devastation will come with only a stump remaining.

stories.title: 👶 Isaiah 7
summaryBullets: Now in the days that Ahaz son of Jotham, the son of Uzziah, was king of Judah, Rezin king of Aram marched up to wage war against Jerusalem. He was accompanied by Pekah son of Remaliah the king of Israel, but he could not overpower the city. (7:1).
When it was reported to the house of David that Aram was in league with Ephraim, the hearts of Ahaz and his people trembled like trees in the forest shaken by the wind. (7:2).
Then the LORD said to Isaiah, “Go out with your son Shear-jashub to meet Ahaz at the end of the aqueduct that feeds the upper pool, on the road to the Launderer’s Field, (7:3).
and say to him: Calm down and be quiet. Do not be afraid or disheartened over these two smoldering stubs of firewood— over the fierce anger of Rezin and Aram and of the son of Remaliah. (7:4).
For Aram, along with Ephraim and the son of Remaliah, has plotted your ruin, saying: (7:5).
‘Let us invade Judah, terrorize it, and divide it among ourselves. Then we can install the son of Tabeal over it as king.’ (7:6).
But this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘It will not arise; it will not happen. (7:7).
For the head of Aram is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin. Within sixty-five years Ephraim will be shattered as a people. (7:8).
The head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria is the son of Remaliah. If you do not stand firm in your faith, then you will not stand at all.’” (7:9).
Again the LORD spoke to Ahaz, saying, (7:10).
“Ask for a sign from the LORD your God, whether from the depths of Sheol or the heights of heaven.” (7:11).
But Ahaz replied, “I will not ask; I will not test the LORD.” (7:12).
Then Isaiah said, “Hear now, O house of David! Is it not enough to try the patience of men? Will you try the patience of my God as well? (7:13).
Therefore the Lord Himself will give you a sign: Behold, the virgin will be with child and give birth to a son, and will call Him Immanuel. (7:14).
By the time He knows enough to reject evil and choose good, He will be eating curds and honey. (7:15).
For before the boy knows enough to reject evil and choose good, the land of the two kings you dread will be laid waste. (7:16).
The LORD will bring on you and on your people and on the house of your father a time unlike any since the day Ephraim separated from Judah— He will bring the king of Assyria.” (7:17).
On that day the LORD will whistle to the flies at the farthest streams of the Nile and to the bees in the land of Assyria. (7:18).
And they will all come and settle in the steep ravines and clefts of the rocks, in all the thornbushes and watering holes. (7:19).
On that day the Lord will use a razor hired from beyond the Euphrates— the king of Assyria— to shave your head and the hair of your legs, and to remove your beard as well. (7:20).
On that day a man will raise a young cow and two sheep, (7:21).
and from the abundance of milk they give, he will eat curds; for all who remain in the land will eat curds and honey. (7:22).
And on that day, in every place that had a thousand vines worth a thousand shekels of silver, only briers and thorns will be found. (7:23).
Men will go there with bow and arrow, for the land will be covered with briers and thorns. (7:24).
For fear of the briers and thorns, you will no longer traverse the hills once tilled by the hoe; they will become places for oxen to graze and sheep to trample. (7:25).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 16:5-9: Rezin and Pekah besiege Ahaz, who strips the temple and the palace treasury to hire Tiglath-pileser of Assyria against them.
2 Chronicles 28:5-8: Aram and Israel inflict heavy losses on Ahaz, killing 120,000 men of Judah in one day and carrying off 200,000 captives.
Matthew 1:22-23: Matthew cites the sign given here, the virgin who will be with child and bear a son called Immanuel, God with us.
Deuteronomy 6:16: Israel is commanded not to test the LORD as they tested Him at Massah, the rule Ahaz hides behind when he refuses a sign.
2 Kings 15:29-30: Tiglath-pileser captures Ijon, Hazor, Gilead, and Galilee and deports the people, and Hoshea kills Pekah.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עִמָּנוּ אֵל (‘Immanu-El, ‘God with us’), Greek (LXX): Ἐμμανουήλ, Aramaic: עמנואל
translationNotes.note: Name announced as the sign in 7:14 and echoed in 8:8-10.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עַלְמָה (‘almah, ‘young woman’), Greek (LXX): παρθένος (parthenos), Aramaic: עַלִימְתָא
translationNotes.note: Word used in (7:14); Hebrew denotes a young woman of marriageable age; Greek renders with ‘virgin.’

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁאָר יָשׁוּב (She’ar-yashuv, ‘a remnant shall return’)
translationNotes.note: Isaiah’s son accompanying him in 7:3.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֹׁמְרוֹן (Shomron)
translationNotes.note: The central highland region between Judea and Galilee; capital of the northern kingdom of Israel from 880 BC until Assyrian deportation in 722 BC. The mixed-population descendants who remained ('Samaritans') were despised by Judeans as ethnically and religiously impure. Jesus' choice to travel through Samaria (John 4) and to make a Samaritan the hero of His parable (Luke 10) deliberately upends that prejudice.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁאוֹל (sheol)
translationNotes.note: The Old Testament realm of the dead; a shadowy underworld where both righteous and wicked descend (Genesis 37:35; Psalm 16:10). Not necessarily a place of torment; more a state of cessation and silence. The Septuagint and New Testament render it with the Greek word hades.

translationNotes.term: Rezin and the son of Remaliah
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲרָם (Aram), Syria - אֶפְרַיִם (Efrayim), the northern kingdom
translationNotes.note: Isaiah 7 sits inside a specific crisis. Rezin, king of Aram at Damascus, and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of the northern kingdom of Israel, joined against Assyria and marched on Jerusalem to force Judah into their alliance and put their own man, the son of Tabeal, on David's throne (7:1-6). Ahaz instead bought Assyrian help; 2 Kings 16:7-9 records the payment and the result, with Tiglath-Pileser taking Damascus and killing Rezin. This is the war behind everything Isaiah says to Ahaz here.

translationNotes.term: the road to the Launderer's Field
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׂדֵה כוֹבֵס (sedeh khoves), the field of the fuller
translationNotes.note: A fuller cleaned and finished newly woven wool by treading it in tubs, using stale urine for its ammonia and alkaline earth as a scouring agent, then bleaching and stretching it out to dry. The work needed running water and a large open drying field, and it stank, so the fuller worked outside the city walls. This spot by the upper pool's channel was the obvious place to meet a king inspecting his water supply before a siege, and Isaiah 36:2 has the Assyrian envoy stand on the same ground a generation later.

stories.keyTakeaway: King Rezin of Aram and King Pekah of Israel attack Jerusalem; Isaiah tells King Ahaz not to fear them and promises a sign - a virgin will conceive and bear a son called Immanuel - but warns that the king of Assyria will devastate the land before that child matures.

stories.title: 👶 Isaiah 8
summaryBullets: Then the LORD said to me, “Take a large scroll and write on it with an ordinary stylus: Maher-shalal-hash-baz. (8:1).
And I will appoint for Myself trustworthy witnesses— Uriah the priest and Zechariah son of Jeberekiah.” (8:2).
And I had relations with the prophetess, and she conceived and gave birth to a son. The LORD said to me, “Name him Maher-shalal-hash-baz. (8:3).
For before the boy knows how to cry ‘Father’ or ‘Mother,’ the wealth of Damascus and the plunder of Samaria will be carried off by the king of Assyria.” (8:4).
And the LORD spoke to me further: (8:5).
“Because this people has rejected the gently flowing waters of Shiloah and rejoiced in Rezin and the son of Remaliah, (8:6).
the Lord will surely bring against them the mighty floodwaters of the Euphrates— the king of Assyria and all his pomp. It will overflow its channels and overrun its banks. (8:7).
It will pour into Judah, swirling and sweeping over it, reaching up to the neck; its spreading streams will cover your entire land, O Immanuel! (8:8).
Huddle together, O peoples, and be shattered; pay attention, all you distant lands; prepare for battle, and be shattered; prepare for battle, and be shattered! (8:9).
Devise a plan, but it will be thwarted; state a proposal, but it will not happen. For God is with us.” (8:10).
For this is what the LORD has spoken to me with a strong hand, instructing me not to walk in the way of this people: (8:11).
“Do not call conspiracy everything these people regard as conspiracy. Do not fear what they fear; do not live in dread. (8:12).
The LORD of Hosts is the One you shall regard as holy. Only He should be feared; only He should be dreaded. (8:13).
And He will be a sanctuary — but to both houses of Israel a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense, to the dwellers of Jerusalem a trap and a snare. (8:14).
Many will stumble over these; they will fall and be broken; they will be ensnared and captured.” (8:15).
Bind up the testimony and seal the law among my disciples. (8:16).
I will wait for the LORD, who is hiding His face from the house of Jacob. I will put my trust in Him. (8:17).
Here am I, and the children the LORD has given me as signs and symbols in Israel from the LORD of Hosts, who dwells on Mount Zion. (8:18).
When men tell you to consult mediums and spiritists who whisper and mutter, shouldn’t a people consult their God instead? Why consult the dead on behalf of the living? (8:19).
To the law and to the testimony! If they do not speak according to this word, they have no light of dawn. (8:20).
They will roam the land, dejected and hungry. When they are famished, they will become enraged; and looking upward, they will curse their king and their God. (8:21).
Then they will look to the earth and see only distress and darkness and the gloom of anguish. And they will be driven into utter darkness. (8:22).
crossRefs: 1 Peter 2:6-8: Peter joins the cornerstone in Zion to the stone of stumbling and rock of offense, the phrase drawn from Isaiah 8:14.
Romans 9:33: Paul quotes the same pairing, a stone of stumbling and rock of offense laid in Zion, and adds that the one who believes will not be put to shame.
Hebrews 2:13: The writer quotes Isaiah 8:17-18, 'I will put My trust in Him' and 'Here am I, and the children God has given Me.'
Deuteronomy 18:10-11: Divination, sorcery, spell-casting, consulting mediums, and inquiring of the dead are all forbidden in Israel.
2 Kings 17:5-6: Assyria besieges Samaria for three years, captures it, and deports Israel to Halah and to Gozan by the Habor River.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עִמָּנוּ אֵל (‘Immanu-El, ‘God with us’), Greek (LXX): Ἐμμανουήλ, Aramaic: עמנואל
translationNotes.note: Name announced as the sign in 7:14 and echoed in 8:8-10.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַהֵר שָׁלָל חָשׁ בַּז (Maher-shalal-ḥash-baz, ‘swift to the spoil, speedy to the prey’)
translationNotes.note: Name given as a sign in 8:1-4.

translationNotes.term: Stone of stumbling / rock of offense
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֶבֶן נֶגֶף / צוּר מִכְשׁוֹל (’even negef / tsur mikshol); Greek (LXX): λίθος προσκόμματος / πέτρα σκανδάλου
translationNotes.note: Metaphors in 8:14.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֹׁמְרוֹן (Shomron)
translationNotes.note: The central highland region between Judea and Galilee; capital of the northern kingdom of Israel from 880 BC until Assyrian deportation in 722 BC. The mixed-population descendants who remained ('Samaritans') were despised by Judeans as ethnically and religiously impure. Jesus' choice to travel through Samaria (John 4) and to make a Samaritan the hero of His parable (Luke 10) deliberately upends that prejudice.

translationNotes.term: the waters of Shiloah that flow gently
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מֵי הַשִּׁלֹחַ (mei ha-Shiloach)
translationNotes.note: Jerusalem's water came from the Gihon spring in the valley below the city, carried along the slope by an open channel to a pool. It was a shallow, quiet, unimpressive trickle, and Isaiah 8:6-8 sets it against the River, meaning the Euphrates, in flood, which is his picture of Assyria. Hezekiah later cut a tunnel 1,750 feet through solid rock to bring that same water inside the walls (2 Kings 20:20, 2 Chronicles 32:30); the tunnel is still walkable, and an inscription found in it in 1880 describes the two digging crews meeting in the middle.

translationNotes.term: A large tablet and a common stylus
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גִּלָּיוֹן גָּדוֹל (gillayon gadol) - חֶרֶט אֱנוֹשׁ (chereth enosh)
translationNotes.note: 8:1 orders the message written big, with an ordinary man's engraving tool rather than a scribe's fine reed, so anyone in the street can read it. 8:2 then has it attested by two named witnesses, Uriah the priest and Zechariah, which is how a legal document was made to stand; the law requires two or three witnesses at Deuteronomy 19:15, and Jeremiah 32:10-12 shows a deed signed, witnessed and stored.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֹבוֹת (ovoth) - יִדְּעֹנִים (yidde'onim)
translationNotes.note: 8:19 describes the sound the practitioners made, tsaphaph, to chirp like a bird, and hagah, to mutter or growl, which is how the voice of the dead was produced for a paying client. Leviticus 19:31 and 20:6 forbid consulting them and Deuteronomy 18:10-11 lists the whole trade. 1 Samuel 28 is the worked example, Saul going by night to the woman at En-dor. 8:20 gives the alternative in four words, to the teaching and to the testimony.

stories.keyTakeaway: Isaiah writes "Maher-Shalal-Hash-Baz" on a scroll with witnesses and names his newborn son the same, signaling that Damascus and Samaria will be plundered before the boy can speak. The LORD warns that Judah will face the Assyrian floodwaters for rejecting him, but declares his purposes cannot be thwarted; Isaiah calls people to trust God's instruction rather than mediums and spiritists, and warns that those who reject his word will face darkness and despair.

stories.title: 🌅 Isaiah 9
summaryBullets: Nevertheless, there will be no more gloom for those in distress. In the past He humbled the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, but in the future He will honor the Way of the Sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations: (9:1).
The people walking in darkness have seen a great light; on those living in the land of the shadow of death, a light has dawned. (9:2).
You have enlarged the nation and increased its joy. The people rejoice before You as they rejoice at harvest time, as men rejoice in dividing the plunder. (9:3).
For as in the day of Midian You have shattered the yoke of their burden, the bar across their shoulders, and the rod of their oppressor. (9:4).
For every trampling boot of battle and every garment rolled in blood will be burned as fuel for the fire. (9:5).
For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given, and the government will be upon His shoulders. And He will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. (9:6).

Of the increase of His government and peace there will be no end. He will reign on the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish and sustain it with justice and righteousness from that time and forevermore. The zeal of the LORD of Hosts will accomplish this. (9:7).
The Lord has sent a message against Jacob, and it has fallen upon Israel. (9:8).
All the people will know it — Ephraim and the dwellers of Samaria. With pride and arrogance of heart they will say: (9:9).
“The bricks have fallen, but we will rebuild with finished stone; the sycamores have been felled, but we will replace them with cedars.” (9:10).
The LORD has raised up the foes of Rezin against him and joined his enemies together. (9:11).
Aram from the east and Philistia from the west have devoured Israel with open mouths. Despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised. (9:12).
But the people did not return to Him who struck them; they did not seek the LORD of Hosts. (9:13).
So the LORD will cut off Israel’s head and tail, both palm branch and reed in a single day. (9:14).
The head is the elder and honorable man, and the tail is the prophet who teaches lies. (9:15).
For those who guide this people mislead them, and those they mislead are swallowed up. (9:16).

Therefore the Lord takes no pleasure in their young men; He has no compassion on their fatherless and widows. For every one of them is godless and wicked, and every mouth speaks folly. Despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised. (9:17).
For wickedness burns like a fire that consumes the thorns and briers and kindles the forest thickets, which roll upward in billows of smoke. (9:18).
By the wrath of the LORD of Hosts the land is scorched, and the people are fuel for the fire. No man even spares his brother. (9:19).
They carve out what is on the right, but they are still hungry; they eat what is on the left, but they are still not satisfied. Each one devours the flesh of his own offspring. (9:20).
Manasseh devours Ephraim, and Ephraim Manasseh; together they turn against Judah. Despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised. (9:21).
crossRefs: Judges 7:19-25: The day of Midian (Gideon) as a precedent for a decisive victory (cf. 9:4).
Matthew 4:14-16: Later citation of Isaiah 9:1-2 regarding Galilee.
2 Samuel 7:12-16: Promise concerning David’s throne and kingdom.
Luke 1:32-33: Promise of throne of David (later announcement).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גְּלִיל הַגּוֹיִם (Gelil ha-goyim), Greek (LXX): Γαλιλαία τῶν ἐθνῶν, Aramaic: גליל דעממיא
translationNotes.note: Regional designation in 9:1.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֹל (ʿol) / מַטֶּה (matteh) / שֵׁבֶט (shevet); Greek (LXX): ζυγός / ῥάβδος / ῥάβδος
translationNotes.note: Instruments of oppression named in 9:4.

translationNotes.term: Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פֶּלֶא יוֹעֵץ (pele yoʿetz), אֵל גִּבּוֹר (El gibbor), אֲבִי־עַד (’Avi-ʿad), שַׂר־שָׁלוֹם (Sar-shalom); Greek (LXX): Μεγάλης Βουλῆς ἄγγελος (var.), Θεὸς ἰσχυρός, Πατὴρ τοῦ μέλλοντος αἰῶνος, Ἄρχων εἰρήνης
translationNotes.note: Royal titles in (9:6); LXX shows variant rendering for the first phrase.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַמִּשְׂרָה עַל־שִׁכְמוֹ (ha-misrah ʿal shikhmo); Greek (LXX): ἡ ἀρχὴ ἐπὶ τοῦ ὤμου αὐτοῦ
translationNotes.note: Rule symbolically carried on the shoulder (9:6).

The central highland region between Judea and Galilee; capital of the northern kingdom of Israel from 880 BC until Assyrian deportation in 722 BC. The mixed-population descendants who remained ('Samaritans') were despised by Judeans as ethnically and religiously impure. Jesus' choice to travel through Samaria (John 4) and to make a Samaritan the hero of His parable (Luke 10) deliberately upends that prejudice.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֹׁמְרוֹן (Shomron)

stories.keyTakeaway: A great light is promised for Galilee; the oppressor’s yoke is broken, and a child with royal names is announced to rule on David’s throne with unending peace and justice.

headings.text: Unto Us a Child Is Born

stories.title: ⚔️ Isaiah 10
summaryBullets: Woe to those who enact unjust statutes and issue oppressive decrees, (10:1).
to deprive the poor of fair treatment and withhold justice from the oppressed of My people, to make widows their prey and orphans their plunder. (10:2).
What will you do on the day of reckoning when devastation comes from afar? To whom will you flee for help? Where will you leave your wealth? (10:3).
Nothing will remain but to crouch among the captives or fall among the slain. Despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised. (10:4).
Woe to Assyria, the rod of My anger; the staff in their hands is My wrath. (10:5).
I will send him against a godless nation; I will dispatch him against a people destined for My rage, to take spoils and seize plunder, and to trample them down like clay in the streets. (10:6).
But this is not his intention; this is not his plan. For it is in his heart to destroy and cut off many nations. (10:7).
“Are not all my commanders kings?” he says. (10:8).
“Is not Calno like Carchemish? Is not Hamath like Arpad? Is not Samaria like Damascus? (10:9).
As my hand seized the idolatrous kingdoms whose images surpassed those of Jerusalem and Samaria, (10:10).
and as I have done to Samaria and its idols, will I not also do to Jerusalem and her idols?” (10:11).

So when the Lord has completed all His work against Mount Zion and Jerusalem, He will say, “I will punish the king of Assyria for the fruit of his arrogant heart and the proud look in his eyes. (10:12).

For he says: ‘By the strength of my hand I have done this, and by my wisdom, for I am clever. I have removed the boundaries of nations and plundered their treasures; like a mighty one I subdued their rulers. (10:13).
My hand reached as into a nest to seize the wealth of the nations. Like one gathering abandoned eggs, I gathered all the earth. No wing fluttered, no beak opened or chirped.’” (10:14).
Does an axe raise itself above the one who swings it? Does a saw boast over him who saws with it? It would be like a rod waving the one who lifts it, or a staff lifting him who is not wood! (10:15).
Therefore the Lord GOD of Hosts will send a wasting disease among Assyria’s stout warriors, and under his pomp will be kindled a fire like a burning flame. (10:16).
And the Light of Israel will become a fire, and its Holy One a flame. In a single day it will burn and devour Assyria’s thorns and thistles. (10:17).
The splendor of its forests and orchards, both soul and body, it will completely destroy, as a sickness consumes a man. (10:18).
The remaining trees of its forests will be so few that a child could count them. (10:19).
On that day the remnant of Israel and the survivors of the house of Jacob will no longer depend on him who struck them, but they will truly rely on the LORD, the Holy One of Israel. (10:20).
A remnant will return — a remnant of Jacob — to the Mighty God. (10:21).
Though your people, O Israel, be like the sand of the sea, only a remnant will return. Destruction has been decreed, overflowing with righteousness. (10:22).
For the Lord GOD of Hosts will carry out the destruction decreed upon the whole land. (10:23).
Therefore this is what the Lord GOD of Hosts says: “O My people who dwell in Zion, do not fear Assyria, who strikes you with a rod and lifts his staff against you as the Egyptians did. (10:24).
For in just a little while My fury against you will subside, and My anger will turn to their destruction.” (10:25).
And the LORD of Hosts will brandish a whip against them, as when He struck Midian at the rock of Oreb. He will raise His staff over the sea, as He did in Egypt. (10:26).
On that day the burden will be lifted from your shoulders, and the yoke from your neck. The yoke will be broken because your neck will be too large. (10:27).
Assyria has entered Aiath and passed through Migron, storing their supplies at Michmash. (10:28).
They have crossed at the ford: “We will spend the night at Geba.” Ramah trembles; Gibeah of Saul flees. (10:29).
Cry aloud, O Daughter of Gallim! Listen, O Laishah! O wretched Anathoth! (10:30).
Madmenah flees; the people of Gebim take refuge. (10:31).
Yet today they will halt at Nob, shaking a fist at the mount of Daughter Zion, at the hill of Jerusalem. (10:32).
Behold, the Lord GOD of Hosts will lop off the branches with terrifying power. The tall trees will be cut down, the lofty ones will be felled. (10:33).
He will clear the forest thickets with an axe, and Lebanon will fall before the Mighty One. (10:34).
crossRefs: Romans 9:27-28: Paul quotes Isaiah 10:22-23, that though the Israelites are like the sand of the sea, only the remnant will be saved.
2 Kings 18:13: In the fourteenth year of Hezekiah, Sennacherib attacks and captures all the fortified cities of Judah.
Judges 7:25: Gideon's men capture Oreb and Zeeb and kill Oreb at the rock of Oreb, the defeat Isaiah 10:26 recalls.
Deuteronomy 27:19: A curse is pronounced on anyone who withholds justice from the foreigner, the fatherless, or the widow.
Exodus 14:26-28: Moses stretches out his hand over the sea and the water flows back and covers Pharaoh's chariots and horsemen.

translationNotes.term: For all this His anger… His hand is stretched out still
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּכָל־זֹאת לֹא־שָׁב אַפּוֹ וְעוֹד יָדוֹ נְטוּיָה; Greek (LXX): ἐν πᾶσι τούτοις οὐκ ἀπεστράφη ὁ θυμός, ἔτι δὲ ἡ χείρ ὑψηλή
translationNotes.note: Refrain repeated at (9:12-21) (10:4).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֵׁבֶט / מַטֶּה (shevet / matteh); Greek (LXX): ῥάβδος
translationNotes.note: Assyria as the rod of the LORD’s anger (10:5).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֹׁמְרוֹן (Shomron)
translationNotes.note: The central highland region between Judea and Galilee; capital of the northern kingdom of Israel from 880 BC until Assyrian deportation in 722 BC. The mixed-population descendants who remained ('Samaritans') were despised by Judeans as ethnically and religiously impure. Jesus' choice to travel through Samaria (John 4) and to make a Samaritan the hero of His parable (Luke 10) deliberately upends that prejudice.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַשּׁוּר (Ashshur)
translationNotes.note: Assyria's method was to break a conquered people by moving it. Tiglath-Pileser III made the practice systematic in the eighth century BC: uproot the population, march it hundreds of miles, and settle other deportees on its land so no one could rebuild a nation. That is what the Assyrian king is boasting of in Isaiah 10:13 when he says he removed the boundaries of peoples. 2 Kings 17:6 records where the northern kingdom went, to Halah, to Gozan on the Habor river, and to the cities of the Medes; Sargon II's own annals, carved on his palace walls at Khorsabad, claim 27,290 people taken out of Samaria.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִכְמָשׂ (Mikhmas), Michmash - נֹב (Nov), Nob
translationNotes.note: Isaiah 10:28-32 is not a list of poetic names; it is a route, and every stop is a real town on the ridge north of Jerusalem. The army comes down through Aiath and Migron, dumps its baggage at Michmash to cross the steep pass there, camps at Geba, and panics Ramah, Gibeah, Anathoth, and the rest in turn. It halts at Nob, the last rise, and can see the city. Michmash is the same pass Jonathan climbed at 1 Samuel 14:4-13, and Anathoth is Jeremiah's home town (Jeremiah 1:1).

translationNotes.term: Decrees against the widow and the fatherless
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֹקְקֵי־אָוֶן (choqeqe aven, those who inscribe iniquity)
translationNotes.note: 10:1-2 indicts the men who write the law, not the men who break it: they enact rulings that strip the poor of their case and make widows their plunder. Widows and orphans are the law's named protected class, with no man to speak for them at the gate; Exodus 22:22-24 attaches a direct threat to harming them, and Deuteronomy 24:17 and 27:19 forbid bending their cases.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כַּרְכְּמִישׁ (Karkemish) - אַרְפָּד (Arpad) - חֲמָת (Chamath)
translationNotes.note: 10:9 is an Assyrian boast made of real conquests, listed in the order they fell as the empire came south. Carchemish sat on the Euphrates crossing, Arpad and Hamath in Syria, then Damascus in 732 BC and Samaria in 722 BC. Every name on the list was a capital that had said it could hold. The point of reciting them is the next one down the road.

stories.keyTakeaway: Isaiah pronounces woe on unjust lawmakers, then declares that God will use Assyria as his instrument of judgment before punishing Assyria itself for its arrogant pride; he assures Judah that only a remnant will survive and that God will break Assyria's oppression as he once defeated Egypt and Midian.

stories.title: ⚔️ Isaiah 11
summaryBullets: Then a shoot will spring up from the stump of Jesse, and a Branch from his roots will bear fruit. (11:1).
The Spirit of the LORD will rest on Him— the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and fear of the LORD. (11:2).
And He will delight in the fear of the LORD. He will not judge by what His eyes see, and He will not decide by what His ears hear, (11:3).

but with righteousness He will judge the poor, and with equity He will decide for the lowly of the earth. He will strike the earth with the rod of His mouth and slay the wicked with the breath of His lips. (11:4).
Righteousness will be the belt around His hips, and faithfulness the sash around His waist. (11:5).
The wolf will live with the lamb, and the leopard will lie down with the goat; the calf and young lion and fatling will be together, and a little child will lead them. (11:6).
The cow will graze with the bear, their young will lie down together, and the lion will eat straw like the ox. (11:7).
The infant will play by the cobra’s den, and the toddler will reach into the viper’s nest. (11:8).
They will neither harm nor destroy on all My holy mountain, for the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the sea is full of water. (11:9).
On that day the Root of Jesse will stand as a banner for the peoples. The nations will seek Him, and His place of rest will be glorious. (11:10).

On that day the Lord will extend His hand a second time to recover the remnant of His people from Assyria, from Egypt, from Pathros, from Cush, from Elam, from Shinar, from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea. (11:11).
He will raise a banner for the nations and gather the exiles of Israel; He will collect the scattered of Judah from the four corners of the earth. (11:12).
Then the jealousy of Ephraim will depart, and the adversaries of Judah will be cut off. Ephraim will no longer envy Judah, nor will Judah harass Ephraim. (11:13).

They will swoop down on the slopes of the Philistines to the west; together they will plunder the sons of the east. They will lay their hands on Edom and Moab, and the Ammonites will be subject to them. (11:14).

The LORD will devote to destruction the gulf of the Sea of Egypt; with a scorching wind He will sweep His hand over the Euphrates. He will split it into seven streams for men to cross with dry sandals. (11:15).
There will be a highway for the remnant of His people who remain from Assyria, as there was for Israel when they came up from the land of Egypt. (11:16).
crossRefs: Romans 15:12: Paul quotes Isaiah 11:10, 'The Root of Jesse will appear, One who will arise to rule over the Gentiles.'
1 Samuel 16:11-13: Samuel anoints Jesse's youngest son David, and the Spirit of the LORD rushes upon him from that day forward.
Isaiah 65:25: The same picture returns at the end of the book, the wolf and the lamb feeding together and the lion eating straw like the ox.
Revelation 5:5: An elder names the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, as the one who has triumphed and can open the scroll.
Exodus 14:21-22: The LORD drives back the sea and Israel walks through on dry ground, the crossing Isaiah 11:15-16 says will be repeated.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֹטֶר (ḥoter, ‘shoot’) / נֵצֶר (netser, ‘branch’); Greek (LXX): ῥάβδος / ἄνθος
translationNotes.note: Terms in 11:1 for growth from Jesse’s stump.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נֵס (nes); Greek (LXX): σημεῖον/σημαία
translationNotes.note: Raised for peoples and nations (11:10-12).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רוּחַ יְהוָה (ruach YHWH)
translationNotes.note: 11:2 names the Spirit once and then in three pairs: wisdom and understanding, counsel and might, knowledge and the fear of the LORD. Chokhmah is skill in handling a thing, the word used of the craftsmen who built the tabernacle (Exodus 31:3). Etsah is the counsel a ruler gives and gevurah is the strength to carry it out, so the pairs run mind, rule, and knowing God.

translationNotes.term: Not by what his eyes see
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֹא־לְמַרְאֵה עֵינָיו (lo le-mar'eh enav)
translationNotes.note: 11:3-4 is a judicial standard. A judge in Israel was forbidden to decide by appearance, by report or by who had paid: Deuteronomy 1:16-17 says hear the small and the great alike and do not be intimidated, and Deuteronomy 16:19 forbids a bribe because it blinds the eyes of the wise. 11:4 gives the result the law aimed at and never got, judging the poor with righteousness.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פַּתְרוֹס (Pathros) - כּוּשׁ (Kush) - עֵילָם (Elam) - שִׁנְעָר (Shin'ar)
translationNotes.note: 11:11 lists where the scattered are to be brought back from, and each is a real country. Pathros is Upper Egypt, the southern Nile valley. Cush is Nubia, above the first cataract in what is now Sudan. Elam lay east of the Tigris in southwestern Iran with its capital at Susa. Shinar is Babylonia, the name used at Genesis 11:2. Hamath is on the Orontes in Syria, and the coastlands are the Mediterranean shores.

translationNotes.term: The tongue of the sea and the River
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לְשׁוֹן יָם־מִצְרַיִם (leshon yam Mitsrayim, the tongue of the sea of Egypt)
translationNotes.note: 11:15-16 uses the exodus as the pattern for the return: the water is split, the river is struck into channels a man can walk across, and there is a highway out of Assyria as there was one out of Egypt. The River without a name is the Euphrates, as at Genesis 15:18. A tongue of sea is a narrow gulf, the shape of the northern end of the Red Sea.

stories.keyTakeaway: A righteous Branch from Jesse's line will judge with justice and be filled with God's Spirit; in that future day, predator and prey will live together peacefully, the nations will gather to him as a banner, and God will reclaim his scattered people from exile across the earth.

stories.title: ⚔️ Isaiah 12
summaryBullets: In that day you will say: “O LORD, I will praise You. Although You were angry with me, Your anger has turned away, and You have comforted me. (12:1).
Surely God is my salvation; I will trust and not be afraid. For the LORD GOD is my strength and my song, and He also has become my salvation.” (12:2).
With joy you will draw water from the springs of salvation, (12:3).
and on that day you will say: “Give praise to the LORD; proclaim His name! Make His works known among the peoples; declare that His name is exalted. (12:4).
Sing to the LORD, for He has done glorious things. Let this be known in all the earth. (12:5).
Cry out and sing, O citizen of Zion, for great among you is the Holy One of Israel.” (12:6).
crossRefs: Exodus 15:1-2: Israel sings at the sea, 'The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation.'
Psalm 118:14: The same line is sung again in a psalm of thanksgiving for deliverance.
Psalm 105:1: 'Give thanks to the LORD, call upon His name; make known His deeds among the nations.'
Zephaniah 3:14-17: Zion is told to sing aloud and stop fearing, because the LORD her King is in her midst and rejoices over her with singing.
John 7:37-38: On the last and greatest day of the feast Jesus stands and calls anyone who is thirsty to come to Him and drink.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עָזִּי וְזִמְרָת יָהּ (ozzi ve-zimrat Yah)
translationNotes.note: Verse 2 is quoting the Song of the Sea. Exodus 15:2, sung after Israel crossed and Pharaoh's chariots did not, reads the LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation. Psalm 118:14 repeats the same line. The reader is meant to hear the exodus under this chapter.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יָהּ יְהוָה (Yah YHWH)
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew here stacks the short form of the divine name in front of the full one, Yah YHWH. Yah is the form that survives in English inside the word hallelujah, which is halelu-Yah, praise Yah, and inside names like Isaiah, Yeshayahu, meaning the LORD saves.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַעַיְנֵי הַיְשׁוּעָה (mayney ha-yeshuah)
translationNotes.note: Yeshuah is the ordinary noun for rescue and deliverance, and it is the word behind the names Joshua and Jesus. Drawing water was daily labor done by hand at a spring or cistern. The Mishnah, tractate Sukkah 4:9, describes a temple ceremony at the Feast of Tabernacles in which water was carried up from the pool of Siloam in a golden pitcher and poured out at the altar; John 7:37 places Jesus' cry about living water on the last and greatest day of that feast.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קִרְאוּ בִשְׁמוֹ (qiru vishmo)
translationNotes.note: In Hebrew usage a name is not a label but the person himself, so calling on the name means appealing to the one who bears it. The phrase begins in Genesis 4:26 and follows Abram from altar to altar (Genesis 12:8; 13:4). Verses 4 and 5 run almost word for word with Psalm 105:1-2 and 1 Chronicles 16:8-9.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קְדוֹשׁ יִשְׂרָאֵל (qedosh Yisrael)
translationNotes.note: This is Isaiah's signature title for God. It appears about twenty-five times in this book, spread across both halves, and only a handful of times in all the rest of the Old Testament (Psalm 71:22; 78:41; 89:18; Jeremiah 50:29; 51:5). Qadosh means set apart, cut off from the common, not simply morally good.

stories.keyTakeaway: A restored people praise the LORD for turning away his anger and providing salvation; they are called to proclaim his deeds to all nations and sing for joy at his greatness.

stories.title: 🏛️ Isaiah 13
summaryBullets: This is the burden against Babylon that Isaiah son of Amoz received: (13:1).
Raise a banner on a barren hilltop; call aloud to them. Wave your hand, that they may enter the gates of the nobles. (13:2).
I have commanded My sanctified ones; I have even summoned My warriors to execute My wrath and exult in My triumph. (13:3).
Listen, a tumult on the mountains, like that of a great multitude! Listen, an uproar among the kingdoms, like nations gathered together! The LORD of Hosts is mobilizing an army for war. (13:4).
They are coming from faraway lands, from the ends of the heavens— the LORD and the weapons of His wrath— to destroy the whole country. (13:5).
Wail, for the Day of the LORD is near; it will come as destruction from the Almighty. (13:6).
Therefore all hands will fall limp, and every man’s heart will melt. (13:7).
Terror, pain, and anguish will seize them; they will writhe like a woman in labor. They will look at one another, their faces flushed with fear. (13:8).
Behold, the Day of the LORD is coming— cruel, with fury and burning anger— to make the earth a desolation and to destroy the sinners within it. (13:9).
For the stars of heaven and their constellations will not give their light. The rising sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light. (13:10).
I will punish the world for its evil and the wicked for their iniquity. I will end the haughtiness of the arrogant and lay low the pride of the ruthless. (13:11).
I will make man scarcer than pure gold, and mankind rarer than the gold of Ophir. (13:12).
Therefore I will make the heavens tremble, and the earth will be shaken from its place at the wrath of the LORD of Hosts on the day of His burning anger. (13:13).
Like a hunted gazelle, like a sheep without a shepherd, each will return to his own people, each will flee to his native land. (13:14).
Whoever is caught will be stabbed, and whoever is captured will die by the sword. (13:15).
Their infants will be dashed to pieces before their eyes, their houses will be looted, and their wives will be ravished. (13:16).
Behold, I will stir up against them the Medes, who have no regard for silver and no desire for gold. (13:17).
Their bows will dash young men to pieces; they will have no mercy on the fruit of the womb; they will not look with pity on the children. (13:18).
And Babylon, the jewel of the kingdoms, the glory of the pride of the Chaldeans, will be overthrown by God like Sodom and Gomorrah. (13:19).
She will never be inhabited or settled from generation to generation; no nomad will pitch his tent there, no shepherd will rest his flock there. (13:20).
But desert creatures will lie down there, and howling creatures will fill her houses. Ostriches will dwell there, and wild goats will leap about. (13:21).
Hyenas will howl in her fortresses and jackals in her luxurious palaces. Babylon’s time is at hand, and her days will not be prolonged. (13:22).
crossRefs: Daniel 5:30-31: Belshazzar king of the Chaldeans is killed that very night and Darius the Mede receives the kingdom.
Jeremiah 51:11: The LORD arouses the spirit of the kings of the Medes because His plan is aimed at destroying Babylon.
Genesis 19:24-25: The LORD rains sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah and destroys the cities, the plain, and everything growing on the ground.
Joel 2:31: The sun is turned to darkness and the moon to blood before the great and awesome Day of the LORD.
Revelation 18:2: An angel cries that Babylon the great has fallen and become a lair for demons and a haunt for every unclean bird.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַשָּׂא (massaʾ), Greek (LXX): ὅρασις/ἄρσις (var.), Aramaic: מטלא
translationNotes.note: Heading term for prophetic pronouncement (13:1) (14:28).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מָדָי (Madai); Greek (LXX): Μῆδοι
translationNotes.note: People named as instruments against Babylon (13:17).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בָּבֶל (Bavel)
translationNotes.note: Babylon stood on the Euphrates about fifty miles south of modern Baghdad, and by the sixth century BC it was the largest city in the world. Its patron god was Marduk, its great processional gate was faced in glazed blue brick and dedicated to the goddess Ishtar, and at its center stood a stepped temple tower called Etemenanki. Isaiah 13:19 calls it the jewel of the kingdoms and the glory of the pride of the Chaldeans, and 13:20-22 says it will never be settled again. Cyrus of Persia took it in 539 BC.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כְּשֹׁד מִשַּׁדַּי (ke-shod mi-Shaddai)
translationNotes.note: 13:6 is two words that chime in Hebrew and cannot in English: shod, violent ruin, coming mi-Shaddai, from the Almighty. Joel 1:15 uses the identical phrase. The sound-match is the point, the name and the ruin built from the same letters, and every English rendering has to drop it.

translationNotes.term: The animals left in the ruins
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צִיִּים (tsiyyim) - בְּנוֹת יַעֲנָה (benoth ya'anah) - שְׂעִירִים (se'irim)
translationNotes.note: 13:21-22 lists what lives in a city after the people are gone, and the exact species behind several of the words are not settled. Tsiyyim are desert creatures, benoth ya'anah are rendered ostriches or owls, iyyim hyenas or jackals. Se'irim means hairy ones and is used for wild goats and, at Leviticus 17:7 and 2 Chronicles 11:15, for goat idols that Israel sacrificed to. The list is a picture of a site nobody will camp on again, which 13:20 says outright about Arabs and shepherds.

stories.keyTakeaway: Isaiah announces God's judgment against Babylon; a mustered army will destroy the land, the heavens and earth will convulse in darkness, and the Medes will overthrow Babylon so completely that it becomes a desolate ruin inhabited only by wild animals.

stories.title: 🏛️ Isaiah 14
summaryBullets: For the LORD will have compassion on Jacob; once again He will choose Israel and settle them in their own land. The foreigner will join them and unite with the house of Jacob. (14:1).

The nations will escort Israel and bring it to its homeland. Then the house of Israel will possess the nations as menservants and maidservants in the LORD’s land. They will make captives of their captors and rule over their oppressors. (14:2).
On the day that the LORD gives you rest from your pain and torment, and from the hard labor into which you were forced, (14:3).
you will sing this song of contempt against the king of Babylon: How the oppressor has ceased, and how his fury has ended! (14:4).
The LORD has broken the staff of the wicked, the scepter of the rulers. (14:5).
It struck the peoples in anger with unceasing blows; it subdued the nations in rage with relentless persecution. (14:6).
All the earth is at peace and at rest; they break out in song. (14:7).
Even the cypresses and cedars of Lebanon exult over you: “Since you have been laid low, no woodcutter comes against us.” (14:8).

Sheol beneath is eager to meet you upon your arrival. It stirs the spirits of the dead to greet you— all the rulers of the earth. It makes all the kings of the nations rise from their thrones. (14:9).
They will all respond to you, saying, “You too have become weak, as we are; you have become like us!” (14:10).
Your pomp has been brought down to Sheol, along with the music of your harps. Maggots are your bed and worms your blanket. (14:11).
How you have fallen from heaven, O day star, son of the dawn! You have been cut down to the ground, O destroyer of nations. (14:12).
You said in your heart: “I will ascend to the heavens; I will raise my throne above the stars of God. I will sit on the mount of assembly, in the far reaches of the north. (14:13).
I will ascend above the tops of the clouds; I will make myself like the Most High.” (14:14).
But you will be brought down to Sheol, to the lowest depths of the Pit. (14:15).
Those who see you will stare; they will ponder your fate: “Is this the man who shook the earth and made the kingdoms tremble, (14:16).
who turned the world into a desert and destroyed its cities, who refused to let the captives return to their homes?” (14:17).
All the kings of the nations lie in state, each in his own tomb. (14:18).
But you are cast out of your grave like a rejected branch, covered by those slain with the sword, and dumped into a rocky pit like a carcass trampled underfoot. (14:19).
