You will not join them in burial, since you have destroyed your land and slaughtered your own people. The offspring of the wicked will never again be mentioned. (14:20).
Prepare a place to slaughter his sons for the iniquities of their forefathers. They will never rise up to possess a land or cover the earth with their cities. (14:21).
“I will rise up against them,” declares the LORD of Hosts. “I will cut off from Babylon her name and her remnant, her offspring and her posterity,” declares the LORD. (14:22).
“I will make her a place for owls and for swamplands; I will sweep her away with the broom of destruction,” declares the LORD of Hosts. (14:23).
The LORD of Hosts has sworn: “Surely, as I have planned, so will it be; as I have purposed, so will it stand. (14:24).
I will break Assyria in My land; I will trample him on My mountain. His yoke will be taken off My people, and his burden removed from their shoulders.” (14:25).
This is the plan devised for the whole earth, and this is the hand stretched out over all the nations. (14:26).
The LORD of Hosts has purposed, and who can thwart Him? His hand is outstretched, so who can turn it back? (14:27).
In the year that King Ahaz died, this burden was received: (14:28).
Do not rejoice, all you Philistines, that the rod that struck you is broken. For a viper will spring from the root of the snake, and a flying serpent from its egg. (14:29).
Then the firstborn of the poor will find pasture, and the needy will lie down in safety, but I will kill your root by famine, and your remnant will be slain. (14:30).
Wail, O gate! Cry out, O city! Melt away, all you Philistines! For a cloud of smoke comes from the north, and there are no stragglers in its ranks. (14:31).
What answer will be given to the envoys of that nation? “The LORD has founded Zion, where His afflicted people will find refuge.” (14:32).
crossRefs: Ezekiel 28:12-19: A lament over the king of Tyre pictures him in Eden covered with precious stones, then cast to the ground for his pride.
Luke 10:18: Jesus tells the seventy, 'I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven.'
Jeremiah 50:2: A banner is raised to announce that Babylon is captured, Bel put to shame, and Marduk shattered.
2 Kings 19:35-36: The angel of the LORD strikes down 185,000 in the Assyrian camp and Sennacherib breaks camp and returns to Nineveh.
2 Chronicles 28:18: The Philistines raid the foothills and the Negev of Judah and occupy Beth-shemesh, Aijalon, and Gederoth during the reign of Ahaz.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַשָּׂא (massaʾ), Greek (LXX): ὅρασις/ἄρσις (var.), Aramaic: מטלא
translationNotes.note: Heading term for prophetic pronouncement (13:1) (14:28).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הֵילֵל בֶּן־שָׁחַר (Helel ben Shachar, ‘shining one, son of dawn’), Greek (LXX): Ἑωσφόρος, later Latin: Lucifer
translationNotes.note: Title in the taunt over the king of Babylon (14:12).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁאוֹל (sheol)
translationNotes.note: The Old Testament realm of the dead; a shadowy underworld where both righteous and wicked descend (Genesis 37:35; Psalm 16:10). Not necessarily a place of torment; more a state of cessation and silence. The Septuagint and New Testament render it with the Greek word hades.

translationNotes.term: the king of Babylon on his couch in Sheol
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רְפָאִים (refaim), the shades of the dead
translationNotes.note: Isaiah 14:9-11 uses the ordinary furniture of an ancient royal burial to mock one. Kings were laid out on a bed or couch, with their weapons, and their honor was measured by the tomb they got. Here the dead kings already below stand up from their thrones to greet the newcomer, and his bedding is maggots. Verse 19 delivers the real insult by the standards of the time: cast out without a grave, which is the fate Jeremiah 22:19 also pronounces on Jehoiakim.

translationNotes.term: The shades stirred up to meet him
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רְפָאִים (repha'im)
translationNotes.note: 14:9 has Sheol rouse the repha'im, a word for the dead as they are after death, used again at Job 26:5, Psalm 88:10 and Proverbs 2:18. What 14:9-11 does with them is court ceremony: the dead kings get up off their thrones to receive a new arrival, and every one of them says the same line, you have become weak as we are.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פְּלֶשֶׁת (Pelesheth)
translationNotes.note: 14:28-31 is dated to the year King Ahaz died and addressed to the Philistine cities on the coastal plain, Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron and Gath. They had been under Judah and then under Assyria, and the broken rod they are told not to celebrate is a dead overlord. 1 Samuel 13:19-22 records the edge they held for generations, a monopoly on ironworking that left Israel without a smith and going down to the Philistines to sharpen its tools.

stories.keyTakeaway: Isaiah pronounces judgment on the king of Babylon through a taunt song, describing his fall from heaven to the grave and God's oath to destroy Babylon and crush Assyria; he also warns the Philistines that a worse oppressor will come despite the breaking of their current rod.

headings.text: The Fall of the King of Babylon

stories.title: 🏜️ Isaiah 15
summaryBullets: This is the burden against Moab: Ar in Moab is ruined, destroyed in a night! Kir in Moab is devastated, destroyed in a night! (15:1).
Dibon goes up to its temple to weep at its high places. Moab wails over Nebo, as well as over Medeba. Every head is shaved, every beard is cut off. (15:2).
In its streets they wear sackcloth; on the rooftops and in the public squares they all wail, falling down weeping. (15:3).
Heshbon and Elealeh cry out; their voices are heard as far as Jahaz. Therefore the soldiers of Moab cry out; their souls tremble within. (15:4).

My heart cries out over Moab; her fugitives flee as far as Zoar, as far as Eglath-shelishiyah. With weeping they ascend the slope of Luhith; they lament their destruction on the road to Horonaim. (15:5).
The waters of Nimrim are dried up, and the grass is withered; the vegetation is gone, and the greenery is no more. (15:6).
So they carry their wealth and belongings over the Brook of the Willows. (15:7).
For their outcry echoes to the border of Moab. Their wailing reaches Eglaim; it is heard in Beer-elim. (15:8).
The waters of Dimon are full of blood, but I will bring more upon Dimon — a lion upon the fugitives of Moab and upon the remnant of the land. (15:9).
crossRefs: Numbers 21:27-30: The ballad of Heshbon names Ar of Moab, Dibon, Nophah, and Medeba, the same towns Isaiah lists in ruins.
Jeremiah 48:1-3: Jeremiah's oracle against Moab opens with Nebo devastated, Kiriathaim captured, and a cry from Horonaim.
Genesis 19:36-37: Lot's older daughter bears a son named Moab, the father of the Moabites.
Deuteronomy 2:9: Israel is told not to harass Moab, because the LORD has given Ar to the descendants of Lot as their possession.
Deuteronomy 14:1: Israel is forbidden to cut themselves or shave their foreheads for the dead, the mourning rites Isaiah 15:2 describes in Moab.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מוֹאָב (Moav) - כְּמוֹשׁ (Kemosh)
translationNotes.note: Moab held the high plateau east of the Dead Sea, good sheep country, and it was a relative: Genesis 19:37 traces the nation to Lot. Its god was Chemosh, which is why Numbers 21:29 calls Moabites the people of Chemosh and 1 Kings 11:7 has Solomon building him a high place outside Jerusalem. What that worship could involve is recorded at 2 Kings 3:27, where the king of Moab, losing a siege, offered his own eldest son as a burnt offering on the city wall. The Mesha Stele, a Moabite victory inscription of the ninth century BC found at Dhiban in 1868, has that same king credit Chemosh with his wars against Israel.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דִּימוֹן (Dimon) / דִּיבוֹן (Dibon)
translationNotes.note: Variant forms in (15:9) and (15:2) place associated with bloodshed imagery.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׂק (saq); Greek: σάκκος (sakkos)
translationNotes.note: A coarse, dark goat-hair fabric worn against bare skin as a universal sign of mourning, repentance, or distress (1 Kings 21:27; Jonah 3:5; Matthew 11:21). Wearing it publicly broadcast grief or contrition; the discomfort itself was part of the symbolism.

translationNotes.term: The towns of the Moab oracle
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נְבוֹ (Nevo) - מֵידְבָא (Medeva) - חֶשְׁבּוֹן (Cheshbon) - דִּיבֹן (Divon)
translationNotes.note: 15:1-9 names about a dozen real towns on the plateau east of the Dead Sea and expects the reader to know the map. Several of them appear on a stone found in 1868 at Dhiban, the biblical Dibon: an inscription set up by Mesha king of Moab in the ninth century BC, which names Chemosh over and over, names Omri king of Israel, and names Nebo and Medeba as towns Mesha took back. The names in this chapter are places that were still standing when it was written.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קָרְחָה (qorchah, baldness) - גְּרוּעָה (geru'ah, cut off)
translationNotes.note: 15:2-3 has Moab mourning with every head shaved, every beard cut, sackcloth in the streets and weeping on the housetops. Roofs were flat and were living space, so grief went on in public view. Israel was forbidden this particular form of it: Leviticus 19:27-28 and Deuteronomy 14:1 bar shaving the head and gashing the body for the dead, which is why the description reads as foreign practice.

stories.keyTakeaway: Isaiah prophesies the sudden destruction of Moab's cities, describing widespread mourning, shaved heads, sackcloth, and weeping across the land as people flee and their resources are stripped away. The waters dry up, vegetation withers, and Isaiah declares he will bring additional judgment - a lion - upon Moab's fugitives and those remaining.

stories.title: 🏜️ Isaiah 16
summaryBullets: Send the tribute lambs to the ruler of the land, from Sela in the desert to the mount of Daughter Zion. (16:1).
Like fluttering birds pushed out of the nest, so are the daughters of Moab at the fords of the Arnon: (16:2).
“Give us counsel; render a decision. Shelter us at noonday with shade as dark as night. Hide the refugees; do not betray the one who flees. (16:3).
Let my fugitives stay with you; be a refuge for Moab from the destroyer.” When the oppressor has gone, destruction has ceased, and the oppressors have vanished from the land, (16:4).
in loving devotion a throne will be established in the tent of David. A judge seeking justice and hastening righteousness will sit on it in faithfulness. (16:5).
We have heard of Moab’s pomposity, his exceeding pride and conceit, his overflowing arrogance. But his boasting is empty. (16:6).
Therefore let Moab wail; let them wail together for Moab. Moan for the raisin cakes of Kir-hareseth, you who are utterly stricken. (16:7).

For the fields of Heshbon have withered, along with the grapevines of Sibmah. The rulers of the nations have trampled its choicest vines, which had reached as far as Jazer and spread toward the desert. Their shoots had spread out and passed over the sea. (16:8).
So I weep with Jazer for the vines of Sibmah; I drench Heshbon and Elealeh with my tears. Triumphant shouts have fallen silent over your summer fruit and your harvest. (16:9).
Joy and gladness are removed from the orchard; no one sings or shouts in the vineyards. No one tramples the grapes in the winepresses; I have put an end to the cheering. (16:10).
Therefore my heart laments for Moab like a harp, my inmost being for Kir-heres. (16:11).
When Moab appears on the high place, when he wearies himself and enters his sanctuary to pray, it will do him no good. (16:12).
This is the message that the LORD spoke earlier concerning Moab. (16:13).

And now the LORD says, “In three years, as a hired worker counts the years, Moab’s splendor will become an object of contempt, with all her many people. And those who are left will be few and feeble.” (16:14).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 3:4-5: Mesha king of Moab, a sheep breeder, pays Israel 100,000 lambs and the wool of 100,000 rams, then rebels after Ahab dies.
Jeremiah 48:29-33: Jeremiah repeats the charge of Moab's pride and mourns the vine of Sibmah and the winepresses that no longer run.
Numbers 32:37-38: Reuben rebuilds Heshbon, Nebo, Baal-meon, and Sibmah, towns that later pass into Moabite hands.
Ruth 4:13-17: Ruth the Moabite bears Obed, who becomes the father of Jesse, the father of David, whose tent Isaiah 16:5 names.
Amos 2:1-3: Moab is judged for burning to lime the bones of Edom's king, and fire consumes the citadels of Kerioth.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סֶלַע (Sela, ‘rock’); Greek (LXX): Πέτρα
translationNotes.note: Location in 16:1 on the route mentioned.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כִּשְׁנֵי שָׂכִיר (kishnei sakir); Greek (LXX): ὡς ἔτη μισθωτοῦ
translationNotes.note: Precise time reckoning for three years (16:14).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֶסֶד (ḥesed), Greek (LXX): ἔλεος, Aramaic: חסדא
translationNotes.note: Term in 16:5 describing the established throne; listed without interpretation.

translationNotes.term: Send the lamb to the ruler
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שִׁלְחוּ־כַר (shilchu khar, send a lamb)
translationNotes.note: 16:1 is tribute, paid the way a herding country pays it. 2 Kings 3:4 gives the figures for the same arrangement: Mesha king of Moab was a sheep breeder and delivered a hundred thousand lambs and the wool of a hundred thousand rams to the king of Israel every year, and stopped when Ahab died. Sending the lamb from Sela to Zion is Moab asking for shelter with the payment in front.

translationNotes.term: The vines of Sibmah and the shout in the presses
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הֵידָד (hedad, the treading shout)
translationNotes.note: 16:8-10 is Moab's wine country going silent. Grapes were trodden barefoot in a rock-cut vat with the juice running through a channel into a lower basin, and the treaders sang and called in rhythm to keep time; hedad is the word for that shout. 16:10 says the treader treads out no wine and the shout has been stopped, and Jeremiah 48:32-33 repeats the same lines about the same vineyards.

stories.keyTakeaway: Moab is urged to send tribute and shelter fugitives, but Isaiah laments Moab's pride and her coming destruction - her vineyards will wither, her joy will cease, and within three years her splendor and people will be greatly diminished. A future ruler from David's house will establish a throne of justice and faithfulness.

stories.title: 🌪️ Isaiah 17
summaryBullets: This is the burden against Damascus: “Behold, Damascus is no longer a city; it has become a heap of ruins. (17:1).
The cities of Aroer are forsaken; they will be left to the flocks, which will lie down with no one to fear. (17:2).
The fortress will disappear from Ephraim, and the sovereignty from Damascus. The remnant of Aram will be like the splendor of the Israelites,” declares the LORD of Hosts. (17:3).
“In that day the splendor of Jacob will fade, and the fat of his body will waste away, (17:4).
as the reaper gathers the standing grain and harvests the ears with his arm, as one gleans heads of grain in the Valley of Rephaim. (17:5).
Yet gleanings will remain, like an olive tree that has been beaten— two or three berries atop the tree, four or five on its fruitful branches,” declares the LORD, the God of Israel. (17:6).
In that day men will look to their Maker and turn their eyes to the Holy One of Israel. (17:7).
They will not look to the altars they have fashioned with their hands or to the Asherahs and incense altars they have made with their fingers. (17:8).
In that day their strong cities will be like forsaken thickets and summits, abandoned to the Israelites and to utter desolation. (17:9).
For you have forgotten the God of your salvation and failed to remember the Rock of your refuge. Therefore, though you cultivate delightful plots and set out cuttings from exotic vines — (17:10).
though on the day you plant you make them grow, and on that morning you help your seed sprout — yet the harvest will vanish on the day of disease and incurable pain. (17:11).
Alas, the tumult of many peoples; they rage like the roaring seas and clamoring nations; they rumble like the crashing of mighty waters. (17:12).
The nations rage like the rush of many waters. He rebukes them, and they flee far away, driven before the wind like chaff on the hills, like tumbleweeds before a gale. (17:13).
In the evening, there is sudden terror! Before morning, they are no more! This is the portion of those who loot us and the lot of those who plunder us. (17:14).
crossRefs: Amos 1:3-5: Oracle against Damascus.
2 Kings 16:5-9: Aram and Israel against Judah; Damascus context.
2 Kings 17:1-6: Fall of Samaria (Ephraim).
Psalm 46:6: Nations rage, kingdoms totter.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דַּמֶּשֶׂק (Dammeseq), Greek (LXX): Δαμασκός, Aramaic: דרמשק (Darmesek)
translationNotes.note: Capital of Aram; target of the oracle (17:1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֲרוֹעֵר (‘Aroʿer); Greek (LXX): Αροήρ
translationNotes.note: Place-name noted as forsaken (17:2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֹלֵלוֹת (‘olelot); Greek (LXX): λείψανα θερισμοῦ
translationNotes.note: Leftover fruit/grain after harvest; image for remnant (17:5-6).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קְדוֹשׁ יִשְׂרָאֵל (Qedosh Yisra’el); Greek (LXX): ὁ ἅγιος τοῦ Ἰσραήλ
translationNotes.note: Isaiah’s frequent divine title (17:7).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נְטִיעוֹת נְעִימִים (netiʿot neʿimim) / נֵכָר (nekar); Greek (LXX): φυτεία ἐπιθυμητή / ἀλλοτρία
translationNotes.note: Agricultural image of quick planting that fails (17:10-11).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲרָם (Aram) - דַּמֶּשֶׂק (Dammeseq)
translationNotes.note: Damascus sits in an oasis watered by the Barada river on the east side of the Anti-Lebanon range, where the caravan roads from Mesopotamia, Arabia, and the coast all meet, which is what made it worth fighting over for three centuries. Its kings, Ben-hadad, Hazael, and Rezin, are Israel's constant northern enemy through 1 and 2 Kings. Isaiah 17:1 says it will cease to be a city; 2 Kings 16:9 records Assyria taking it, deporting its people to Kir, and killing Rezin, in 732 BC.

stories.keyTakeaway: Damascus is declared ruined, Ephraim’s strength fades to gleanings, altars are abandoned, and the roaring nations are rebuked and scattered overnight.

stories.title: 🛶 Isaiah 18
summaryBullets: Woe to the land of whirring wings, along the rivers of Cush, (18:1).

which sends couriers by sea, in papyrus vessels on the waters. Go, swift messengers, to a people tall and smooth-skinned, to a people widely feared, to a powerful nation of strange speech, whose land is divided by rivers. (18:2).
All you people of the world and dwellers of the earth, when a banner is raised on the mountains, you will see it; when a ram’s horn sounds, you will hear it. (18:3).
For this is what the LORD has told me: “I will quietly look on from My dwelling place, like shimmering heat in the sunshine, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest.” (18:4).
For before the harvest, when the blossom is gone and the flower becomes a ripening grape, He will cut off the shoots with a pruning knife and remove and discard the branches. (18:5).
They will all be left to the mountain birds of prey, and to the beasts of the land. The birds will feed on them in summer, and all the wild animals in winter. (18:6).

At that time gifts will be brought to the LORD of Hosts— from a people tall and smooth-skinned, from a people widely feared, from a powerful nation of strange speech, whose land is divided by rivers— to Mount Zion, the place of the Name of the LORD of Hosts. (18:7).
crossRefs: Genesis 10:6-8: Cush among the descendants listed.
Zephaniah 3:10: Suppliants from beyond the rivers of Cush.
Psalm 68:31: “Cush will hasten to stretch out hands to God.”
Isaiah 11:10: Signal (banner) raised for peoples.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כּוּשׁ (Kush), Greek (LXX): Χούς, Aramaic: כוש
translationNotes.note: Region south of Egypt (Nubia/Ethiopia area) (18:1-2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צִלְצַל כְּנָפָיִם (tsiltsal kenafayim); Greek (LXX): πτέρυγες ἠχοῦσαι
translationNotes.note: Descriptive phrase in (18:1) Hebrew given without interpretation.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כְּלֵי־גֹמֶא (klei-gome); Greek (LXX): σκάφη βύβλων
translationNotes.note: Light vessels used for river travel (18:2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נֵס (nes) / שׁוֹפָר (shofar); Greek (LXX): σημεῖον / σάλπιγξ
translationNotes.note: Public summons imagery (18:3).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִנְחָה (minḥah); Greek (LXX): δῶρα/θυσία (var.)
translationNotes.note: Gift brought to Zion (18:7).

translationNotes.term: Cush, and its kings over Egypt
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כּוּשׁ (Kush)
translationNotes.note: Cush is the land up the Nile beyond the first cataract, in what is now Sudan, called Nubia by the Greeks; Isaiah 18:1-2 describes envoys coming down the river in papyrus boats from a people tall and smooth-skinned. This was not a backwater in Isaiah's day. A line of Cushite kings had conquered Egypt and ruled the whole of it as its Twenty-Fifth Dynasty, which is why Isaiah 37:9 can call Tirhakah a king of Cush marching out to fight the Assyrians in Egypt's defense.

stories.keyTakeaway: A message is sent to a distant Cushite land with papyrus boats; the LORD quietly observes and cuts off growth before harvest, and tribute is brought to Mount Zion.

stories.title: ☁️ Isaiah 19
summaryBullets: This is the burden against Egypt: Behold, the LORD rides on a swift cloud; He is coming to Egypt. The idols of Egypt will tremble before Him, and the hearts of the Egyptians will melt within them. (19:1).
“So I will incite Egyptian against Egyptian; brother will fight against brother, neighbor against neighbor, city against city, and kingdom against kingdom. (19:2).
Then the spirit of the Egyptians will be emptied out from among them, and I will frustrate their plans, so that they will resort to idols and spirits of the dead, to mediums and spiritists. (19:3).
I will deliver the Egyptians into the hands of a harsh master, and a fierce king will rule over them,” declares the Lord GOD of Hosts. (19:4).
The waters of the Nile will dry up, and the riverbed will be parched and empty. (19:5).
The canals will stink; the streams of Egypt will trickle and dry up; the reeds and rushes will wither. (19:6).
The bulrushes by the Nile, by the mouth of the river, and all the fields sown along the Nile, will wither, blow away, and be no more. (19:7).
Then the fishermen will mourn, all who cast a hook into the Nile will lament, and those who spread nets on the waters will pine away. (19:8).
The workers in flax will be dismayed, and the weavers of fine linen will turn pale. (19:9).
The workers in cloth will be dejected, and all the hired workers will be sick at heart. (19:10).
The princes of Zoan are mere fools; Pharaoh’s wise counselors give senseless advice. How can you say to Pharaoh, “I am one of the wise, a son of eastern kings”? (19:11).
Where are your wise men now? Let them tell you and reveal what the LORD of Hosts has planned against Egypt. (19:12).
The princes of Zoan have become fools; the princes of Memphis are deceived. The cornerstones of her tribes have led Egypt astray. (19:13).
The LORD has poured into her a spirit of confusion. Egypt has been led astray in all she does, as a drunkard staggers through his own vomit. (19:14).
There is nothing Egypt can do — head or tail, palm or reed. (19:15).
In that day the Egyptians will be like women. They will tremble with fear beneath the uplifted hand of the LORD of Hosts, when He brandishes it against them. (19:16).
The land of Judah will bring terror to Egypt; whenever Judah is mentioned, Egypt will tremble over what the LORD of Hosts has planned against it. (19:17).
In that day five cities in the land of Egypt will speak the language of Canaan and swear allegiance to the LORD of Hosts. One of them will be called the City of the Sun. (19:18).
In that day there will be an altar to the LORD in the center of the land of Egypt, and a pillar to the LORD near her border. (19:19).
It will be a sign and a witness to the LORD of Hosts in the land of Egypt. When they cry out to the LORD because of their oppressors, He will send them a savior and defender to rescue them. (19:20).
The LORD will make Himself known to Egypt, and on that day Egypt will acknowledge the LORD. They will worship with sacrifices and offerings; they will make vows to the LORD and fulfill them. (19:21).
And the LORD will strike Egypt with a plague; He will strike them but heal them. They will turn to the LORD, and He will hear their prayers and heal them. (19:22).
In that day there will be a highway from Egypt to Assyria. The Assyrians will go to Egypt, and the Egyptians to Assyria. The Egyptians and Assyrians will worship together. (19:23).
In that day Israel will join a three-party alliance with Egypt and Assyria— a blessing upon the earth. (19:24).
The LORD of Hosts will bless them, saying, “Blessed be Egypt My people, Assyria My handiwork, and Israel My inheritance.” (19:25).
crossRefs: Exodus 7:20-21: Aaron strikes the water of the Nile, it turns to blood, the fish die, and the Egyptians cannot drink from the river.
Exodus 12:12: The LORD declares He will execute judgment on all the gods of Egypt on the night of the Passover.
Psalm 78:43: God performed His signs in Egypt and His wonders in the fields of Zoan, the city whose princes Isaiah calls fools.
Ezekiel 29:1-5: Pharaoh is addressed as the great monster lying among the channels of the Nile, hauled out with hooks in his jaws.
Zephaniah 3:9-10: The LORD purifies the lips of the peoples so they call on His name, and worshipers bring offerings from beyond the rivers of Cush.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צֹעַן (Tsoʿan, Zoan) / נֹף (Noph, Memphis); Greek (LXX): Τάνις / Μέμφις
translationNotes.note: Egyptian cities named in counsel and judgment contexts (19:11-13).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יְאֹר (ye’or, ‘river’), יאורים (ye’orim), סוּף/קָנֶה (sup/qaneh); Greek (LXX): ποταμός, διώρυγες, πάπυρος
translationNotes.note: River system and vegetation imagery for Egypt’s economy (19:5-7).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִזְבֵּחַ (mizbeaḥ) / מַצֵּבָה (matsebah); Greek (LXX): θυσιαστήριον / στήλη
translationNotes.note: Sign and witness to the LORD in Egypt (19:19-20).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְסִלָּה (mesillah); Greek (LXX): ὁδός
translationNotes.note: Road linking Egypt and Assyria in 19:23.

translationNotes.term: The flax workers and the weavers
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פִּשְׁתִּים שְׂרִיקוֹת (pishtim seriqoth, combed flax)
translationNotes.note: 19:9 names the trade Egypt was known for across the ancient world. Flax was grown on the flooded fields, retted in water, combed out and spun into linen so fine that Egyptian linen was a luxury export everywhere, and it was the cloth Egyptian priests were required to wear. The whole industry depended on the Nile rising, which is why 19:5-10 runs from the water failing to the fishermen mourning to the weavers ruined, in that order.

stories.keyTakeaway: Isaiah pronounces judgment on Egypt: the Lord will cause internal strife, dry up the Nile, devastate crops and livelihoods, and confound Egypt's leaders; yet he also promises that future Egyptian cities will speak Canaan's language, build altars to the Lord, and worship alongside Assyria and Israel.

stories.title: ☁️ Isaiah 20
summaryBullets: Before the year that the chief commander, sent by Sargon king of Assyria, came to Ashdod and attacked and captured it, (20:1).

the LORD had already spoken through Isaiah son of Amoz, saying, “Go, remove the sackcloth from your waist and the sandals from your feet.” And Isaiah did so, walking around naked and barefoot. (20:2).
Then the LORD said, “Just as My servant Isaiah has gone naked and barefoot for three years as a sign and omen against Egypt and Cush, (20:3).
so the king of Assyria will lead away the captives of Egypt and the exiles of Cush, young and old alike, naked and barefoot, with bared buttocks— to Egypt’s shame. (20:4).
Those who made Cush their hope and Egypt their boast will be dismayed and ashamed. (20:5).

And on that day the dwellers of this coastland will say, ‘See what has happened to our source of hope, those to whom we fled for help and deliverance from the king of Assyria! How then can we escape?’” (20:6).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 18:17: The king of Assyria sends the Tartan, the Rabsaris, and the Rabshakeh from Lachish to Jerusalem with a great army.
Micah 1:8: Micah says he will walk barefoot and naked and howl like a jackal as a public act of mourning.
Ezekiel 4:4-6: Ezekiel is told to lie on his left side 390 days and on his right side 40 days, a day for each year, as a sign.
2 Kings 17:4: Assyria discovers that Hoshea has sent envoys to King So of Egypt and stopped paying tribute, and imprisons him.
Amos 1:8: The LORD cuts off the ruler of Ashdod and the one who wields the scepter in Ashkelon, and turns His hand against Ekron.

translationNotes.original: Akkadian/Assyrian title; Hebrew: תַּרְתָּן (Tartan); Greek (LXX): θαρτάν
translationNotes.note: Assyrian commander title in 20:1.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׂק (saq); Greek: σάκκος (sakkos)
translationNotes.note: A coarse, dark goat-hair fabric worn against bare skin as a universal sign of mourning, repentance, or distress (1 Kings 21:27; Jonah 3:5; Matthew 11:21). Wearing it publicly broadcast grief or contrition; the discomfort itself was part of the symbolism.

translationNotes.term: the year the Tartan took Ashdod
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תַּרְתָּן (Tartan), the Assyrian commander-in-chief
translationNotes.note: Isaiah 20:1 dates itself by a campaign: Sargon king of Assyria sent his commander-in-chief against Ashdod, one of the five Philistine cities on the coastal plain, and took it. Sargon's own inscriptions record the same campaign, in 711 BC. Ashdod had revolted and had been trying to draw Judah, Edom, and Moab into the revolt with Egyptian promises of help, which is what Isaiah's sign is aimed at.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עָרוֹם וְיָחֵף (arom veyachef)
translationNotes.note: Isaiah walks for three years as a living sign of what happens to a defeated people (20:2-4), and the picture was not invented. Assyrian palace reliefs show captives driven off in long files, stripped, barefoot, and roped, with the goods of their towns carried behind them. The word rendered stripped can mean lightly clad rather than fully naked, but either way the point is the humiliation of a prisoner of war, and the text says Egypt and Cush will be led away exactly so.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כּוּשׁ (Kush) - מִצְרַיִם (Mitsrayim)
translationNotes.note: 20:3-5 names the two as one hope, and in this period they were one power. Cush is Nubia, the kingdom on the upper Nile above the first cataract in what is now northern Sudan, and its kings had taken Egypt and were ruling it as the twenty-fifth dynasty. That is the alliance Judah was being urged to lean on against Assyria, and 20:5-6 says what happens to those who did: they will be dismayed at their hope, and ask how we shall escape.

stories.keyTakeaway: God commands Isaiah to walk around stripped and barefoot for three years as a sign that Assyria will lead Egyptian and Cushite captives away naked, shaming those nations and dismaying the coastal peoples who relied on them for protection.

headings.text: A Sign against Egypt and Cush

stories.title: 🕯️ Isaiah 21
summaryBullets: This is the burden against the Desert by the Sea: Like whirlwinds sweeping through the Negev, an invader comes from the desert, from a land of terror. (21:1).
A dire vision is declared to me: “The traitor still betrays, and the destroyer still destroys. Go up, O Elam! Lay siege, O Media! I will put an end to all her groaning.” (21:2).
Therefore my body is filled with anguish. Pain grips me, like the pains of a woman in labor. I am bewildered to hear, I am dismayed to see. (21:3).
My heart falters; fear makes me tremble. The twilight I desired has turned to horror. (21:4).
They prepare a table, they lay out a carpet, they eat, they drink! Rise up, O princes, oil the shields! (21:5).
For this is what the Lord says to me: “Go, post a lookout and have him report what he sees. (21:6).
When he sees chariots with teams of horsemen, riders on donkeys, riders on camels, he must be alert, fully alert.” (21:7).
Then the lookout shouted: “Day after day, my lord, I stand on the watchtower; night after night I stay at my post. (21:8).
Look, here come the riders, horsemen in pairs.” And one answered, saying: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon! All the images of her gods lie shattered on the ground!” (21:9).
O my people, crushed on the threshing floor, I tell you what I have heard from the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel. (21:10).
This is the burden against Dumah: One calls to me from Seir, “Watchman, what is left of the night? Watchman, what is left of the night?” (21:11).
The watchman replies, “Morning has come, but also the night. If you would inquire, then inquire. Come back yet again.” (21:12).
This is the burden against Arabia: In the thickets of Arabia you must lodge, O caravans of Dedanites. (21:13).
Bring water for the thirsty, O dwellers of Tema; meet the refugees with food. (21:14).
For they flee from the sword— the sword that is drawn— from the bow that is bent, and from the stress of battle. (21:15).
For this is what the Lord says to me: “Within one year, as a hired worker would count it, all the glory of Kedar will be gone. (21:16).
The remaining archers, the warriors of Kedar, will be few.” For the LORD, the God of Israel, has spoken. (21:17).
crossRefs: Jeremiah 51:8: “Babylon suddenly fallen and broken.”
Revelation 18:2: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great.”
Genesis 25:13: Kedar listed among Ishmael’s sons.
Ezekiel 27:21: Kedar in trade with Tyre.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִדְבַּר־יָם (midbar-yam); Greek (LXX): ἔρημος τῆς θαλάσσης
translationNotes.note: Superscription phrase for the Babylon oracle (21:1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֹׁמֵר (shomer); Greek (LXX): φυλάσσω/σκοπός
translationNotes.note: Sentinel role to report what he sees (21:6-12).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דּוּמָה (Dumah, ‘silence’/place-name) / שֵׂעִיר (Seʿir, Edom region); Greek (LXX): Δουμα / Σηείρ
translationNotes.note: Oracle framed as a call from Seir to the watchman (21:11-12).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קֵדָר (Qedār); Greek (LXX): Κηδάρ
translationNotes.note: Nomadic Ishmaelite group known for archers and tents (21:16-17).

A flat, hard, outdoor surface, usually a leveled rock or beaten-earth circle at the edge of town, where harvested grain was separated from chaff. Oxen pulled a wooden sledge over the stalks; the mixed kernels and chaff were then winnowed in the wind. Threshing floors doubled as public civic spaces (Ruth 3; 2 Samuel 24:18; Solomon's temple site).
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גֹּרֶן (goren)

stories.keyTakeaway: Isaiah reports watchman messages: Babylon falls, a brief answer is given to Dumah, and Arabia’s fugitives are aided as Kedar’s strength is cut within a year.

stories.title: 🏙️ Isaiah 22
summaryBullets: This is the burden against the Valley of Vision: What ails you now, that you have all gone up to the rooftops, (22:1).
O city of commotion, O town of revelry? Your slain did not die by the sword, nor were they killed in battle. (22:2).
All your rulers have fled together, captured without a bow. All your fugitives were captured together, having fled to a distant place. (22:3).
Therefore I said, “Turn away from me, let me weep bitterly! Do not try to console me over the destruction of the daughter of my people.” (22:4).
For the Lord GOD of Hosts has set a day of tumult and trampling and confusion in the Valley of Vision— of breaking down the walls and crying to the mountains. (22:5).
Elam takes up a quiver, with chariots and horsemen, and Kir uncovers the shield. (22:6).
Your choicest valleys are full of chariots, and horsemen are posted at the gates. (22:7).
He has uncovered the defenses of Judah. On that day you looked to the weapons in the House of the Forest. (22:8).
You saw that there were many breaches in the walls of the City of David. You collected water from the lower pool. (22:9).
You counted the houses of Jerusalem and tore them down to strengthen the wall. (22:10).
You built a reservoir between the walls for the waters of the ancient pool, but you did not look to the One who made it, or consider Him who planned it long ago. (22:11).
On that day the Lord GOD of Hosts called for weeping and wailing, for shaven heads and the wearing of sackcloth. (22:12).
But look, there is joy and gladness, butchering of cattle and slaughtering of sheep, eating of meat and drinking of wine: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die!” (22:13).
The LORD of Hosts has revealed in my hearing: “Until your dying day, this sin of yours will never be atoned for,” says the Lord GOD of Hosts. (22:14).
This is what the Lord GOD of Hosts says: “Go, say to Shebna, the steward in charge of the palace: (22:15).
What are you doing here, and who authorized you to carve out a tomb for yourself here — to chisel your tomb in the height and cut your resting place in the rock? (22:16).
Look, O mighty man! The LORD is about to shake you violently. He will take hold of you, (22:17).
roll you into a ball, and sling you into a wide land. There you will die, and there your glorious chariots will remain— a disgrace to the house of your master. (22:18).
I will remove you from office, and you will be ousted from your position. (22:19).
On that day I will summon My servant, Eliakim son of Hilkiah. (22:20).
I will clothe him with your robe and tie your sash around him. I will put your authority in his hand, and he will be a father to the dwellers of Jerusalem and to the house of Judah. (22:21).
I will place on his shoulder the key to the house of David. What he opens no one can shut, and what he shuts no one can open. (22:22).
I will drive him like a peg into a firm place, and he will be a throne of glory for the house of his father. (22:23).
So they will hang on him all the glory of his father’s house: the descendants and the offshoots— all the lesser vessels, from bowls to every kind of jar. (22:24).
In that day, declares the LORD of Hosts, the peg driven into a firm place will give way; it will be sheared off and fall, and the load upon it will be cut down.” Indeed, the LORD has spoken. (22:25).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 18:18; 2 Kings 18:26-37: Shebna and Eliakim named in Hezekiah’s court.
2 Chronicles 32:2-5: Hezekiah’s waterworks and fortifications.
Isaiah 7:3: Upper pool location noted earlier.
Revelation 3:7: “Key of David” wording echoed.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גֵּיא חִזָּיוֹן (Gei Ḥizzāyōn); Greek (LXX): φάραγξ Σιών (var.)
translationNotes.note: Title for Jerusalem in this oracle (22:1-5).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲשֶׁר עַל־הַבַּיִת (asher ʿal ha-bayit); Greek (LXX): ὁ ἐπὶ τοῦ οἴκου
translationNotes.note: Chief palace administrator (22:15).

translationNotes.term: Key of the house of David
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַפְתֵּחַ בֵּית־דָּוִד (maphteaḥ beit David); Greek (LXX): κλεὶς οἴκου Δαυίδ
translationNotes.note: Symbol of authority placed on Eliakim’s shoulder (22:22).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יָתֵד נֶאֱמָנָה (yated ne’emanah); Greek (LXX): πάσσαλος πιστός
translationNotes.note: Metaphor for secure support later said to give way (22:23-25).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַבְּרֵכָה הַתַּחְתּוֹנָה (ha-brekhah ha-taḥtonah)
translationNotes.note: Reservoir referenced within the city’s defenses (22:9-11).

A coarse, dark goat-hair fabric worn against bare skin as a universal sign of mourning, repentance, or distress (1 Kings 21:27; Jonah 3:5; Matthew 11:21). Wearing it publicly broadcast grief or contrition; the discomfort itself was part of the symbolism.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׂק (saq); Greek: σάκκος (sakkos)

translationNotes.term: the tomb Shebna cut for himself
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲשֶׁר עַל־הַבַּיִת (asher al-habayit), the one over the house
translationNotes.note: Isaiah 22:15-19 attacks a palace official for carving himself a monument tomb high on the rock. Jerusalem's wealthy were buried in chambers cut into the cliffs of the Kidron valley, and one such tomb in the village of Silwan carries a Hebrew lintel inscription, found in 1870 and bought by the British Museum in 1871. Nahman Avigad deciphered it in 1953: it names a man whose title is the one over the house, the same office Shebna holds here, whose name survives only as the ending -yahu, and it curses anyone who opens the tomb.

translationNotes.term: the water works and the counted houses
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַבְּרֵכָה הַתַּחְתּוֹנָה (ha-berekhah ha-tachtonah), the lower pool
translationNotes.note: Isaiah 22:8-11 describes a city preparing for siege, item by item: checking the armory in the House of the Forest, counting the houses of Jerusalem and pulling some down for stone, building a reservoir between the two walls, and collecting the water of the lower pool. Every one of those is a real siege measure. Cutting off an attacker's access to the springs outside while storing water inside was the difference between holding out and surrendering, and 2 Chronicles 32:2-5 records Hezekiah doing exactly this.

stories.keyTakeaway: The Valley of Vision oracle describes the city’s panic and self-reliance, condemns feasting instead of mourning, removes Shebna from office, and appoints Eliakim with the key of the house of David.

stories.title: 🚢 Isaiah 23
summaryBullets: This is the burden against Tyre: Wail, O ships of Tarshish, for Tyre is laid waste, without house or harbor. Word has reached them from the land of Cyprus. (23:1).
Be silent, O dwellers of the coastland, you merchants of Sidon, whose traders have crossed the sea. (23:2).
On the great waters came the grain of Shihor; the harvest of the Nile was the revenue of Tyre; she was the merchant of the nations. (23:3).
Be ashamed, O Sidon, the stronghold of the sea, for the sea has spoken: “I have not been in labor or given birth. I have not raised young men or brought up young women.” (23:4).
When the report reaches Egypt, they will writhe in agony over the news of Tyre. (23:5).
Cross over to Tarshish; wail, O inhabitants of the coastland! (23:6).
Is this your jubilant city, whose origin is from antiquity, whose feet have taken her to settle far away? (23:7).
Who planned this against Tyre, the bestower of crowns, whose traders are princes, whose merchants are renowned on the earth? (23:8).
The LORD of Hosts planned it, to defile all its glorious beauty, to disgrace all the renowned of the earth. (23:9).
Cultivate your land like the Nile, O Daughter of Tarshish; there is no longer a harbor. (23:10).
The LORD has stretched out His hand over the sea; He has made kingdoms tremble. He has given a command that the strongholds of Canaan be destroyed. (23:11).
He said, “You shall rejoice no more, O oppressed Virgin Daughter of Sidon. Get up and cross over to Cyprus— even there you will find no rest.” (23:12).

Look at the land of the Chaldeans— a people now of no account. The Assyrians destined it for the desert creatures; they set up their siege towers and stripped its palaces. They brought it to ruin. (23:13).
Wail, O ships of Tarshish, for your harbor has been destroyed! (23:14).
At that time Tyre will be forgotten for seventy years— the span of a king’s life. But at the end of seventy years, it will happen to Tyre as in the song of the harlot: (23:15).
“Take up your harp, stroll through the city, O forgotten harlot. Make sweet melody, sing many a song, so you will be remembered.” (23:16).
And at the end of seventy years, the LORD will restore Tyre. Then she will return to hire as a prostitute and sell herself to all the kingdoms on the face of the earth. (23:17).
Yet her profits and wages will be set apart to the LORD; they will not be stored or saved, for her profit will go to those who live before the LORD, for abundant food and fine clothing. (23:18).
crossRefs: Ezekiel 26-28: Oracles against Tyre’s city, prince, and king.
1 Kings 5:1-12: Tyre’s earlier trade with Israel through Hiram.
Joel 3:4-6: Tyre and Sidon addressed in judgment.
Revelation 18:11-19: Merchants weep over a fallen trading power (later depiction).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֳנִיּוֹת תַּרְשִׁישׁ (’oniyot Tarshish); Greek (LXX): ναῦς Θαρσείς
translationNotes.note: Large sea-going vessels tied to long-distance trade (23:1-14).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שִׁיחוֹר (Shihor); Greek (LXX): Σιώρ
translationNotes.note: Term linked with Nile/its branch; source of grain revenue (23:3).

translationNotes.term: Seventy years… as the days of one king
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שִׁבְעִים שָׁנָה כִּימֵי מֶלֶךְ אֶחָד (shivʿim shanah kiymei melekh eḥad)
translationNotes.note: Fixed period for Tyre’s forgetting (23:15).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קֹדֶשׁ לַיהוָה (qodesh la-YHWH); Greek (LXX): ἅγιον τῷ Κυρίῳ
translationNotes.note: Dedicated use of trade profits for those who dwell before the LORD (23:18).
The distance between thumb-tip and little-finger-tip with the fingers spread; half a cubit, about 9 inches (23 cm). The breastpiece of the high priest was a span square (Exodus 28:16).
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: זֶרֶת (zeret)
Hebrew: צֹר (Tsor), meaning rock
translationNotes.note: Tyre was a Phoenician city built on an island just off the Lebanese coast, which is why it could hold out when everything on the mainland fell. Its wealth came from shipping cedar, from a dye industry that crushed murex sea snails to make the purple that only kings could afford, and from colonies planted right across the Mediterranean, Carthage among them. Nebuchadnezzar besieged it so long that his army's heads were rubbed bare by their helmets and he got nothing for it (Ezekiel 29:18); Alexander finally took it in 332 BC by building a causeway out to the island.

stories.keyTakeaway: The Tyre oracle announces the collapse of the port’s glory, wailing of Tarshish ships, a seventy-year forgetting, and a later period when her merchandise is set apart for those who dwell before the LORD.

stories.title: 🌍 Isaiah 24
summaryBullets: Behold, the LORD lays waste the earth and leaves it in ruins. He will twist its surface and scatter its inhabitants— (24:1).
people and priest alike, servant and master, maid and mistress, buyer and seller, lender and borrower, creditor and debtor. (24:2).
The earth will be utterly laid waste and thoroughly plundered. For the LORD has spoken this word. (24:3).
The earth mourns and withers; the world languishes and fades; the exalted of the earth waste away. (24:4).
The earth is defiled by its people; they have transgressed the laws; they have overstepped the decrees and broken the everlasting covenant. (24:5).
Therefore a curse has consumed the earth, and its inhabitants must bear the guilt; the earth’s dwellers have been burned, and only a few survive. (24:6).
The new wine dries up, the vine withers. All the merrymakers now groan. (24:7).
The joyful tambourines have ceased; the noise of revelers has stopped; the joyful harp is silent. (24:8).
They no longer sing and drink wine; strong drink is bitter to those who consume it. (24:9).
The city of chaos is shattered; every house is closed to entry. (24:10).
In the streets they cry out for wine. All joy turns to gloom; rejoicing is exiled from the land. (24:11).
The city is left in ruins; its gate is reduced to rubble. (24:12).
So will it be on the earth and among the nations, like a harvested olive tree, like a gleaning after a grape harvest. (24:13).
They raise their voices, they shout for joy; from the west they proclaim the majesty of the LORD. (24:14).
Therefore glorify the LORD in the east. Extol the name of the LORD, the God of Israel in the islands of the sea. (24:15).

From the ends of the earth we hear singing: “Glory to the Righteous One.” But I said, “I am wasting away! I am wasting away! Woe is me.” The treacherous betray; the treacherous deal in treachery. (24:16).
Terror and pit and snare await you, O dweller of the earth. (24:17).

Whoever flees the sound of panic will fall into the pit, and whoever climbs from the pit will be caught in the snare. For the windows of heaven are open, and the foundations of the earth are shaken. (24:18).
The earth is utterly broken apart, the earth is split open, the earth is shaken violently. (24:19).
The earth staggers like a drunkard and sways like a shack. Earth’s rebellion weighs it down, and it falls, never to rise again. (24:20).
In that day the LORD will punish the host of heaven above and the kings of the earth below. (24:21).
They will be gathered together like prisoners in a pit. They will be confined to a dungeon and punished after many days. (24:22).
The moon will be confounded and the sun will be ashamed; for the LORD of Hosts will reign on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and before His elders with great glory. (24:23).
crossRefs: Joel 2:10: Sun and moon go dark when the land shakes.
Revelation 6:12-14: Earthquake and celestial disturbances.
Psalm 46:2-3: Earth gives way and mountains fall.
Isaiah 13:10: Lights in the heavens darkened (parallel imagery).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תֹּהוּ (tohu) / שַׁמָּה (shammah)
translationNotes.note: Terms used for desolate, disorderly city (24:10-12).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צְבָא מָרוֹם (tsevāʾ marom); Greek (LXX): τὸ στράτευμα τοῦ οὐρανοῦ
translationNotes.note: “Army of the heights” punished with earthly kings (24:21).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בּוֹר (bor); Greek (LXX): λάκκος
translationNotes.note: Holding place for captives before punishment (24:22).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נוֹעַ תְּנוּעַ (noaʿ tenuaʿ)
translationNotes.note: Image of the earth reeling from guilt (24:20).

stories.keyTakeaway: God empties and shakes the whole earth, a small remnant sings, and the LORD is shown reigning in Zion while rulers are imprisoned and punished.

stories.title: 🍷 Isaiah 25
summaryBullets: O LORD, You are my God! I will exalt You; I will praise Your name. For You have worked wonders — plans formed long ago — in perfect faithfulness. (25:1).
Indeed, You have made the city a heap of rubble, the fortified town a ruin. The fortress of strangers is a city no more; it will never be rebuilt. (25:2).
Therefore, a strong people will honor You. The cities of ruthless nations will revere You. (25:3).
For You have been a refuge for the poor, a stronghold for the needy in distress, a refuge from the storm, a shade from the heat. For the breath of the ruthless is like rain against a wall, (25:4).
like heat in a dry land. You subdue the uproar of foreigners. As the shade of a cloud cools the heat, so the song of the ruthless is silenced. (25:5).
On this mountain the LORD of Hosts will prepare a lavish banquet for all the peoples, a feast of aged wine, of choice meat, of finely aged wine. (25:6).
On this mountain He will swallow up the shroud that enfolds all peoples, the sheet that covers all nations; (25:7).
He will swallow up death forever. The Lord GOD will wipe away the tears from every face and remove the disgrace of His people from the whole earth. For the LORD has spoken. (25:8).
And in that day it will be said, “Surely this is our God; we have waited for Him, and He has saved us. This is the LORD for whom we have waited. Let us rejoice and be glad in His salvation.” (25:9).
For the hand of the LORD will rest on this mountain. But Moab will be trampled in his place as straw is trodden into the dung pile. (25:10).
He will spread out his hands within it, as a swimmer spreads his arms to swim. His pride will be brought low, despite the skill of his hands. (25:11).
The high-walled fortress will be brought down, cast to the ground, into the dust. (25:12).
crossRefs: Hosea 13:14: Death swallowed up (death/Sheol language).
1 Corinthians 15:54: “Death is swallowed up” cited later.
Psalm 9:9: The LORD a stronghold for the oppressed.
Isaiah 2:2-3: Mountain of the LORD theme.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁמָרִים (shemarim); Greek (LXX): οἶνος πεπαλαιωμένος
translationNotes.note: Wine kept on the lees, considered high quality (25:6).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בִּלַּע הַמָּוֶת (billaʿ ha-mavet)
translationNotes.note: Direct statement that death is ended (25:8).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַדְמֵנָה (madmenāh, ‘dunghill’); Greek (LXX): κοπρία
translationNotes.note: Place where straw is trampled; image for Moab’s humiliation (25:10).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מָעוֹז (maʿoz) / מִשְׂגָּב (misgav)
translationNotes.note: Protection terms for the poor and needy (25:4).

stories.keyTakeaway: God is praised as the defender of the poor, He prepares a feast for all peoples, ends death, wipes away tears, and brings down arrogant Moab.

stories.title: 🛡️ Isaiah 26
summaryBullets: In that day this song will be sung in the land of Judah: We have a strong city; salvation is established as its walls and ramparts. (26:1).
Open the gates so a righteous nation may enter— one that remains faithful. (26:2).
You will keep in perfect peace the steadfast of mind, because he trusts in You. (26:3).
Trust in the LORD forever, because GOD the LORD is the Rock eternal. (26:4).
For He has humbled those who dwell on high; He lays the lofty city low. He brings it down to the ground; He casts it into the dust. (26:5).
Feet trample it down — the feet of the oppressed, the steps of the poor. (26:6).
The path of the righteous is level; You clear a straight path for the upright. (26:7).
Yes, we wait for You, O LORD; we walk in the path of Your judgments. Your name and renown are the desire of our souls. (26:8).
My soul longs for You in the night; indeed, my spirit seeks You at dawn. For when Your judgments come upon the earth, the people of the world learn righteousness. (26:9).
Though grace is shown to the wicked man, he does not learn righteousness. In the land of righteousness he acts unjustly and fails to see the majesty of the LORD. (26:10).
O LORD, Your hand is upraised, but they do not see it. They will see Your zeal for Your people and be put to shame. The fire set for Your enemies will consume them! (26:11).
O LORD, You will establish peace for us. For all that we have accomplished, You have done for us. (26:12).
O LORD our God, other lords besides You have ruled over us, but Your name alone do we confess. (26:13).
The dead will not live; the departed spirits will not rise. Therefore You have punished and destroyed them; You have wiped out all memory of them. (26:14).
You have enlarged the nation, O LORD; You have enlarged the nation. You have gained glory for Yourself; You have extended all the borders of the land. (26:15).
O LORD, they sought You in their distress; when You disciplined them, they poured out a quiet prayer. (26:16).
As a woman with child about to give birth writhes and cries out in pain, so were we in Your presence, O LORD. (26:17).
We were with child; we writhed in pain; but we gave birth to wind. We have given no salvation to the earth, nor brought any life into the world. (26:18).
Your dead will live; their bodies will rise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust! For your dew is like the dew of the morning, and the earth will bring forth her dead. (26:19).
Go, my people, enter your rooms and shut your doors behind you. Hide yourselves a little while until the wrath has passed. (26:20).
For behold, the LORD is coming out of His dwelling to punish the inhabitants of the earth for their iniquity. The earth will reveal her bloodshed and will no longer conceal her slain. (26:21).
crossRefs: Psalm 112:7-8: Steady heart trusting the LORD.
Daniel 12:2: Many who sleep in the dust shall awake.
Isaiah 2:10: Hide in the rock from the LORD’s terror (parallel command to hide).
Genesis 4:10: Blood cries out from the ground (exposed bloodshed).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שָׁלוֹם שָׁלוֹם (shalom shalom); Greek (LXX): εἰρήνην εἰρήνης
translationNotes.note: Repetition for emphasis (26:3).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲדֹנִים (adonim)
translationNotes.note: Human powers that ruled them (26:13).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יִחְיוּ מֵתֶיךָ (yichyū metekha)
translationNotes.note: Resurrection wording in 26:19.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דָּמִים (damim)
translationNotes.note: Plural form often used for bloodguilt, including murders (26:21).

stories.keyTakeaway: A song celebrates God’s protection and peace, promises the dead will live, and tells people to hide briefly while God punishes the earth and exposes bloodshed and murders.

stories.title: 🐍 Isaiah 27
summaryBullets: In that day the LORD will take His sharp, great, and mighty sword, and bring judgment on Leviathan the fleeing serpent— Leviathan the coiling serpent— and He will slay the dragon of the sea. (27:1).
In that day: “Sing about a fruitful vineyard. (27:2).
I, the LORD, am its keeper; I water it continually. I guard it night and day so no one can disturb it; (27:3).
I am not angry. If only thorns and briers confronted Me, I would march and trample them, I would burn them to the ground. (27:4).
Or let them lay claim to My protection; let them make peace with Me— yes, let them make peace with Me.” (27:5).
In the days to come, Jacob will take root. Israel will bud and blossom and fill the whole world with fruit. (27:6).
Has the LORD struck Israel as He struck her oppressors? Was she killed like those who slayed her? (27:7).
By warfare and exile You contended with her and removed her with a fierce wind, as on the day the east wind blows. (27:8).

Therefore Jacob’s guilt will be atoned for, and the full fruit of the removal of his sin will be this: When he makes all the altar stones like crushed bits of chalk, no Asherah poles or incense altars will remain standing. (27:9).
For the fortified city lies deserted — a homestead abandoned, a wilderness forsaken. There the calves graze, and there they lie down; they strip its branches bare. (27:10).

When its limbs are dry, they are broken off. Women come and use them for kindling; for this is a people without understanding. Therefore their Maker has no compassion on them, and their Creator shows them no favor. (27:11).
In that day the LORD will thresh from the flowing Euphrates to the Wadi of Egypt, and you, O Israelites, will be gathered one by one. (27:12).

And in that day a great ram’s horn will sound, and those who were perishing in Assyria will come forth with those who were exiles in Egypt. And they will worship the LORD on the holy mountain in Jerusalem. (27:13).
crossRefs: Job 41:1: Leviathan referenced.
Psalm 74:14: God crushes sea monsters’ heads.
Hosea 8:11: Many altars for sin become places of sin (altar theme).
Zechariah 9:14: Trumpet imagery for gathering/deliverance.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לִוְיָתָן נָחָשׁ בָּרִחַ / נָחָשׁ עֲקַלָּתוֹן (livyatan nachash bariakh / nachash ʿaqallaton)
translationNotes.note: Titles for the chaos creature (27:1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כֶּרֶם… אֶשְׁמְרֶנָּה (kerem… eshmrennah)
translationNotes.note: Kept vineyard contrasts with Isaiah 5 (27:2-3).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַבְנֵי־גִּיר (avnei-gir)
translationNotes.note: Crumbled sacred stones (27:9).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נַחַל מִצְרַיִם (nachal Mitsrayim)
translationNotes.note: Southern/western boundary stream (27:12).

A sea or river creature described in Job 41 and Psalm 74:14; most likely the Nile crocodile, depicted with mythic embellishment as the embodiment of primordial chaos. Only God can subdue it, which is the point of Job 41.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לִוְיָתָן (livyatan)

stories.keyTakeaway: God strikes Leviathan, tends His vineyard, removes carved altars, and gathers people one by one from Assyria and Egypt to worship in Jerusalem.

stories.title: 🏰 Isaiah 28
summaryBullets: Woe to the majestic crown of Ephraim’s drunkards, to the fading flower of his glorious splendor, set on the summit above the fertile valley, the pride of those overcome by wine. (28:1).
Behold, the Lord has one who is strong and mighty. Like a hailstorm or destructive tempest, like a driving rain or flooding downpour, he will smash that crown to the ground. (28:2).
The majestic crown of Ephraim’s drunkards will be trampled underfoot. (28:3).

The fading flower of his beautiful splendor, set on the summit above the fertile valley, will be like a ripe fig before the summer harvest: Whoever sees it will take it in his hand and swallow it. (28:4).
On that day the LORD of Hosts will be a crown of glory, a diadem of splendor to the remnant of His people, (28:5).
a spirit of justice to him who sits in judgment, and a strength to those who repel the onslaught at the gate. (28:6).

These also stagger from wine and stumble from strong drink: Priests and prophets reel from strong drink and are befuddled by wine. They stumble because of strong drink, muddled in their visions and stumbling in their judgments. (28:7).
For all their tables are covered with vomit; there is not a place without filth. (28:8).
Whom is He trying to teach? To whom is He explaining His message? To infants just weaned from milk? To babies removed from the breast? (28:9).
For they hear: “Order on order, order on order, line on line, line on line; a little here, a little there.” (28:10).
Indeed, with mocking lips and foreign tongues, He will speak to this people (28:11).
to whom He has said: “This is the place of rest, let the weary rest; this is the place of repose.” But they would not listen. (28:12).

Then the word of the LORD to them will become: “Order on order, order on order, line on line, line on line; a little here, a little there,” so that they will go stumbling backward and will be injured, ensnared, and captured. (28:13).
Therefore hear the word of the LORD, O scoffers who rule this people in Jerusalem. (28:14).

For you said, “We have made a covenant with death; we have fashioned an agreement with Sheol. When the overwhelming scourge passes through it will not touch us, because we have made lies our refuge and falsehood our hiding place.” (28:15).
So this is what the Lord GOD says: “See, I lay a stone in Zion, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation; the one who believes will never be shaken. (28:16).
I will make justice the measuring line and righteousness the level. Hail will sweep away your refuge of lies, and water will flood your hiding place. (28:17).
Your covenant with death will be dissolved, and your agreement with Sheol will not stand. When the overwhelming scourge passes through, you will be trampled by it. (28:18).
As often as it passes through, it will carry you away; it will sweep through morning after morning, by day and by night.” The understanding of this message will bring sheer terror. (28:19).
Indeed, the bed is too short to stretch out on, and the blanket too small to wrap around you. (28:20).
For the LORD will rise up as at Mount Perazim. He will rouse Himself as in the Valley of Gibeon, to do His work, His strange work, and to perform His task, His disturbing task. (28:21).
So now, do not mock, or your shackles will become heavier. Indeed, I have heard from the Lord GOD of Hosts a decree of destruction against the whole land. (28:22).
Listen and hear my voice. Pay attention and hear what I say. (28:23).
Does the plowman plow for planting every day? Does he continuously loosen and harrow the soil? (28:24).
When he has leveled its surface, does he not sow caraway and scatter cumin? He plants wheat in rows and barley in plots, and rye within its border. (28:25).
For his God instructs and teaches him properly. (28:26).
Surely caraway is not threshed with a sledge, and the wheel of a cart is not rolled over the cumin. But caraway is beaten out with a stick, and cumin with a rod. (28:27).
Grain for bread must be ground, but it is not endlessly threshed. Though the wheels of the cart roll over it, the horses do not crush it. (28:28).
This also comes from the LORD of Hosts, who is wonderful in counsel and excellent in wisdom. (28:29).
crossRefs: 1 Peter 2:6-8: Peter quotes the stone laid in Zion, a chosen and precious cornerstone, and says the one who believes will never be put to shame.
1 Corinthians 14:21: Paul quotes Isaiah 28:11-12, that God will speak to this people by strange tongues and foreign lips and still they will not listen.
Psalm 118:22: The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.
2 Kings 17:5-6: Samaria, the proud crown of Ephraim, is besieged three years, captured, and its people deported to Assyria.
Isaiah 5:11-12: An earlier woe falls on those who rise early chasing strong drink and linger into the evening inflamed by wine.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּרִית אֶת־מָוֶת (berit et-mavet); Greek (LXX): διαθήκη πρὸς θάνατον
translationNotes.note: Boast that their pact will protect them (28:15).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֶבֶן פִּנָּה (even pinnah); Greek (LXX): λίθον ἀκρογωνιαῖον
translationNotes.note: Tested, precious foundation stone in Zion (28:16).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁאוֹל (sheol)
translationNotes.note: The Old Testament realm of the dead; a shadowy underworld where both righteous and wicked descend (Genesis 37:35; Psalm 16:10). Not necessarily a place of torment; more a state of cessation and silence. The Septuagint and New Testament render it with the Greek word hades.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צַו לָצָו קַו לָקָו (tsav la-tsav qav la-qav)
translationNotes.note: English prints precept upon precept, line upon line, and the Hebrew is not sentences. They are clipped repeated syllables, the sound of somebody mimicking a drunk or mocking a teacher for talking to grown men as if to a weaned child, which is the complaint 28:9 makes. 28:11 answers that with stammering lips and a foreign tongue God will speak to this people, meaning the language of an invading army. Paul quotes that verse at 1 Corinthians 14:21.

translationNotes.term: The line and the plumb line
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קָו (qav, measuring line) - מִשְׁקֶלֶת (mishqoleth, plumb line)
translationNotes.note: Two builder's tools. The qav is a knotted cord stretched to lay a wall straight, and the mishqoleth is a weight on a string, hung to check that the wall is vertical. Neither one argues; it either matches or it does not. 28:17 hands both to justice and righteousness, and Amos 7:7-8 has the LORD standing on a wall with a plumb line in his hand for the same purpose.

translationNotes.term: Dill, cumin and the cart wheel
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קֶצַח (qetsach, dill or black cumin) - כַּמֹּן (kammon, cumin)
translationNotes.note: 28:24-29 is a lesson in farming procedure. A man does not plow forever, he plows and then sows. Dill and cumin are small soft seeds beaten out with a light stick, because running a threshing sledge or a cart wheel over them would destroy them, while bread grain is crushed harder but not crushed endlessly. Each crop gets the handling it can take, and 28:26 says the farmer was taught this.

stories.keyTakeaway: Isaiah denounces Ephraim's drunken leaders as a fading crown that will be trampled, and warns Jerusalem's scoffing rulers that their covenant with death is false; God will lay a tested stone in Zion as a true foundation and sweep away those who reject it. He closes with a parable about farming, showing that God orchestrates all things with wisdom, bringing both judgment and proper order.

stories.title: 🏰 Isaiah 29
summaryBullets: Woe to you, O Ariel, the city of Ariel where David camped! Year upon year let your festivals recur. (29:1).
And I will constrain Ariel, and there will be mourning and lamentation; she will be like an altar hearth before Me. (29:2).
I will camp in a circle around you; I will besiege you with towers and set up siege works against you. (29:3).

You will be brought low, you will speak from the ground, and out of the dust your words will be muffled. Your voice will be like a spirit from the ground; your speech will whisper out of the dust. (29:4).
But your many foes will be like fine dust, the multitude of the ruthless like blowing chaff. Then suddenly, in an instant, (29:5).
you will be visited by the LORD of Hosts with thunder and earthquake and loud noise, with windstorm and tempest and consuming flame of fire. (29:6).
All the many nations going out to battle against Ariel— even all who war against her, laying siege and attacking her— will be like a dream, like a vision in the night, (29:7).

as when a hungry man dreams he is eating, then awakens still hungry; as when a thirsty man dreams he is drinking, then awakens faint and parched. So will it be for all the many nations who go to battle against Mount Zion. (29:8).
Stop and be astonished; blind yourselves and be sightless; be drunk, but not with wine; stagger, but not from strong drink. (29:9).
For the LORD has poured out on you a spirit of deep sleep. He has shut your eyes, O prophets; He has covered your heads, O seers. (29:10).
And the entire vision will be to you like the words sealed in a scroll. If it is handed to someone to read, he will say, “I cannot, because it is sealed.” (29:11).
Or if the scroll is handed to one unable to read, he will say, “I cannot read.” (29:12).
Therefore the Lord said: “These people draw near to Me with their mouths and honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me. Their worship of Me is but rules taught by men. (29:13).
Therefore I will again confound these people with wonder upon wonder. The wisdom of the wise will vanish, and the intelligence of the intelligent will be hidden.” (29:14).
Woe to those who dig deep to hide their plans from the LORD. In darkness they do their works and say, “Who sees us, and who will know?” (29:15).

You have turned things upside down, as if the potter were regarded as clay. Shall what is formed say to him who formed it, “He did not make me”? Can the pottery say of the potter, “He has no understanding”? (29:16).
In a very short time, will not Lebanon become an orchard, and the orchard seem like a forest? (29:17).
On that day the deaf will hear the words of the scroll, and out of the deep darkness the eyes of the blind will see. (29:18).
The humble will increase their joy in the LORD, and the poor among men will rejoice in the Holy One of Israel. (29:19).
For the ruthless will vanish, the mockers will disappear, and all who look for evil will be cut down— (29:20).
those who indict a man with a word, who ensnare the mediator at the gate, and who with false charges deprive the innocent of justice. (29:21).
Therefore the LORD who redeemed Abraham says of the house of Jacob: “No longer will Jacob be ashamed and no more will his face grow pale. (29:22).
For when he sees his children around him, the work of My hands, they will honor My name, they will sanctify the Holy One of Jacob, and they will stand in awe of the God of Israel. (29:23).
Then the wayward in spirit will come to understanding, and those who grumble will accept instruction.” (29:24).
crossRefs: Matthew 15:8-9: Jesus quotes Isaiah 29:13 against the Pharisees: these people honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me.
1 Corinthians 1:19: Paul quotes Isaiah 29:14, 'I will destroy the wisdom of the wise; the intelligence of the intelligent I will frustrate.'
Romans 11:8: Paul cites a spirit of stupor, eyes that cannot see and ears that cannot hear, the deep sleep of Isaiah 29:10.
2 Samuel 5:6-9: David captures the stronghold of Zion and takes up residence in it, and it is called the City of David.
Revelation 5:1-5: A scroll sealed with seven seals that no one is able to open until the Lion of the tribe of Judah is found worthy.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲרִיאֵל (ʾAriel, ‘altar hearth’/‘lion of God’); Greek (LXX): Αριήλ
translationNotes.note: Poetic name for Jerusalem in siege context (29:1-2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַסֵּפֶר הֶחָתוּם (ha-sefer he-ḥatum)
translationNotes.note: No one can read the message (29:11).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׁעַר (sha'ar)
translationNotes.note: Far more than an entrance; the public square where elders heard legal cases, contracts were witnessed, market business transacted, and news was exchanged. 'Sitting in the gate' (Genesis 19:1; Ruth 4:1-11; Proverbs 31:23) signals civic authority and active community life.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מֻצָּב (mutstsav, siege post) - מְצֻרֹת (metsuroth, siege works)
translationNotes.note: 29:3 describes how a city was actually taken. An army ringed it with a camp, then built an earthen ramp up against the wall so rams and troops could reach the top, since walls were too high and too thick to break at the base. The ramp Sennacherib's engineers raised against Lachish in 701 BC is still standing on the site, and his own palace reliefs show the assault going up it.

translationNotes.term: Their fear of me is a commandment taught by men
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִצְוַת אֲנָשִׁים מְלֻמָּדָה (mitswath anashim melummadah)
translationNotes.note: 29:13 says this people honours God with the mouth while the heart is far off, and that what they hold is a human rule they have been drilled in. Jesus quotes the verse at Matthew 15:8-9 and Mark 7:6-7, naming Isaiah, in the argument over handwashing traditions.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַהֶפְכְּכֶם (ha-hephkekhem, your turning things upside down) - יֹצֵר (yotser, potter)
translationNotes.note: 29:16 opens with a word for inversion and then asks whether the clay may be counted equal to the man shaping it. A potter worked a lump on a wheel he turned with his feet, and could crush and restart it at any moment; Jeremiah 18:1-6 sends the prophet down to the workshop to watch it happen. Isaiah returns to the image at 45:9 and 64:8.

stories.keyTakeaway: Isaiah pronounces woe on Jerusalem, warning of siege and humiliation, but promises God will suddenly destroy her enemies and restore the deaf, blind, and humble while removing the ruthless and those who pervert justice.

stories.title: 🐎 Isaiah 30
summaryBullets: “Woe to the rebellious children,” declares the LORD, “to those who carry out a plan that is not Mine, who form an alliance, but against My will, heaping up sin upon sin. (30:1).
They set out to go down to Egypt without asking My advice, to seek shelter under Pharaoh’s protection and take refuge in Egypt’s shade. (30:2).
But Pharaoh’s protection will become your shame, and the refuge of Egypt’s shade your disgrace. (30:3).
For though their princes are at Zoan and their envoys have arrived in Hanes, (30:4).
everyone will be put to shame because of a people useless to them. They bring neither help nor benefit, but only shame and disgrace.” (30:5).

This is the burden against the beasts of the Negev: Through a land of hardship and distress, of lioness and lion, of viper and flying serpent, they carry their wealth on the backs of donkeys and their treasures on the humps of camels, to a people of no profit to them. (30:6).
Egypt’s help is futile and empty; therefore I have called her Rahab Who Sits Still. (30:7).
Go now, write it on a tablet in their presence and inscribe it on a scroll; it will be for the days to come, a witness forever and ever. (30:8).
These are rebellious people, deceitful children, children unwilling to obey the LORD’s instruction. (30:9).
They say to the seers, “Stop seeing visions!” and to the prophets, “Do not prophesy to us the truth! Speak to us pleasant words; prophesy illusions. (30:10).
Get out of the way; turn off the road. Rid us of the Holy One of Israel!” (30:11).
Therefore this is what the Holy One of Israel says: “Because you have rejected this message, trusting in oppression and relying on deceit, (30:12).
this iniquity of yours is like a breach about to fail, a bulge in a high wall, whose collapse will come suddenly — in an instant! (30:13).

It will break in pieces like a potter’s jar, shattered so that no fragment can be found. Not a shard will be found in the dust large enough to scoop the coals from a hearth or to skim the water from a cistern.” (30:14).
For the Lord GOD, the Holy One of Israel, has said: “By repentance and rest you would be saved; your strength would lie in quiet confidence — but you were not willing.” (30:15).
“No,” you say, “we will flee on horses.” Therefore you will flee! “We will ride swift horses,” but your pursuers will be faster. (30:16).
A thousand will flee at the threat of one; at the threat of five you will all flee, until you are left alone like a pole on a mountaintop, like a banner on a hill. (30:17).
Therefore the LORD longs to be gracious to you; therefore He rises to show you compassion, for the LORD is a just God. Blessed are all who wait for Him. (30:18).
O people in Zion who dwell in Jerusalem, you will weep no more. He will surely be gracious when you cry for help; when He hears, He will answer you. (30:19).
The Lord will give you the bread of adversity and the water of affliction, but your Teacher will no longer hide Himself — with your own eyes you will see Him. (30:20).
And whether you turn to the right or to the left, your ears will hear this command behind you: “This is the way. Walk in it.” (30:21).
So you will desecrate your silver-plated idols and your gold-plated images. You will throw them away like menstrual cloths, saying to them, “Be gone!” (30:22).
Then He will send rain for the seed that you have sown in the ground, and the food that comes from your land will be rich and plentiful. On that day your cattle will graze in open pastures. (30:23).
The oxen and donkeys that work the ground will eat salted fodder, winnowed with shovel and pitchfork. (30:24).
And from every high mountain and every raised hill, streams of water will flow in the day of great slaughter, when the towers fall. (30:25).

The light of the moon will be as bright as the sun, and the light of the sun will be seven times brighter— like the light of seven days— on the day that the LORD binds up the brokenness of His people and heals the wounds He has inflicted. (30:26).
Behold, the Name of the LORD comes from afar, with burning anger and dense smoke. His lips are full of fury, and His tongue is like a consuming fire. (30:27).
His breath is like a rushing torrent that rises to the neck. He comes to sift the nations in a sieve of destruction; He bridles the jaws of the peoples to lead them astray. (30:28).
You will sing as on the night of a holy festival, and your heart will rejoice like one who walks to the music of a flute, going up to the mountain of the LORD, to the Rock of Israel. (30:29).
And the LORD will cause His majestic voice to be heard and His mighty arm to be revealed, striking in angry wrath with a flame of consuming fire, and with cloudburst, storm, and hailstones. (30:30).
For Assyria will be shattered at the voice of the LORD; He will strike them with His scepter. (30:31).
And with every stroke of the rod of punishment that the LORD brings down on them, the tambourines and lyres will sound as He battles with weapons brandished. (30:32).

For Topheth has long been prepared; it has been made ready for the king. Its funeral pyre is deep and wide, with plenty of fire and wood. The breath of the LORD, like a torrent of burning sulfur, sets it ablaze. (30:33).
