crossRefs: 2 Kings 18:21: The Rabshakeh calls Egypt a splintered reed of a staff that pierces the hand of anyone who leans on it.
Deuteronomy 17:16: The king is forbidden to acquire many horses or send the people back to Egypt to get more.
Habakkuk 2:2: The LORD tells the prophet to write the vision down and inscribe it clearly on tablets so a herald can run with it.
2 Kings 23:10: Josiah desecrates Topheth in the Valley of Ben-hinnom so that no one can sacrifice a son or daughter there.
Jeremiah 42:13-19: Judeans determined to go to Egypt are told the sword they fear and the famine they dread will follow them there.

translationNotes.term: Rahab (here: a boastful, powerless symbol for Egypt)
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רַהַב (Rahav), Greek (LXX): Ῥαάβ, Aramaic: רהב
translationNotes.note: Nickname for arrogant power; here meaning Egypt’s ‘big talk, no help’ (30:7).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּשׁוּבָה וָנַחַת… בְּהַשְׁקֵט וּבִטְחָה (b’shuvah va-nachat… b’hashqet u’vitḥah), Greek (LXX): ἐν τῷ ἐπιστρέψαι… ἐν ἡσυχίᾳ καὶ πεποιθήσει, Aramaic: בְּתוּב וּנוּחָא… בְּשַׁקְטָא וּבִטְחָא
translationNotes.note: God’s stated path to rescue (30:15).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תָּפְתֶּה (Tofteh) - גֵּיא בֶן־הִנֹּם (Ge Ben-Hinnom)
translationNotes.note: The image in Isaiah 30:33 is a burning place, deep and wide, with wood piled and fire set. Topheth was a real site in the Valley of Ben Hinnom on the south side of Jerusalem, and it was where children were burned in sacrifice to Molech; Jeremiah 7:31 and 32:35 name it, and 2 Kings 23:10 has Josiah wreck it precisely to stop that. Isaiah turns the place into the sentence, and says the pyre there is now made ready for the king of Assyria. The Greek form of that valley's name is Gehenna, the word translated hell in the New Testament.

translationNotes.term: Through the Negev with the treasure
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּאֶרֶץ צָרָה וְצוּקָה (be-erets tsarah ve-tsuqah, a land of trouble and distress)
translationNotes.note: 30:6 watches the embassy leave: donkeys and camels loaded with wealth, going south through country the verse names for lions, vipers and the flying serpent. That is the desert road from Judah down to Egypt, waterless and preyed on by raiders, and the cargo is the payment for an alliance. The verdict comes in 30:7, Egypt's help is worthless.

translationNotes.term: Write it on a tablet and inscribe it in a book
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לוּחַ (luach, tablet) - סֵפֶר (sepher, scroll)
translationNotes.note: 30:8 names two different media for one message. A luach is a flat board of wood or clay for a public notice, meant to be seen now. A sepher is a scroll, rolled and stored, meant to be read later, which is why the verse gives the reason: that it may be for the time to come, as a witness forever. Habakkuk 2:2 gives the same order about tablets, so a runner can read it.

translationNotes.term: Every stroke to the sound of tambourines
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תֻּפִּים וְכִנֹּרוֹת (tuppim ve-khinnoroth, tambourines and lyres)
translationNotes.note: 30:29 and 30:32 set the sentence on Assyria to festival music, the songs sung on the night a feast is kept and the pipe played on the walk up to the mountain of the LORD. The tuph is a hand drum, a hoop with a skin, played by women leading a procession (Exodus 15:20). The chapter ends with that music over the pyre of 30:33.

stories.keyTakeaway: Isaiah condemns Judah for seeking Egypt's help instead of trusting God, warns that their reliance on deception will collapse like a crumbling wall, yet promises that those who repent and wait on the Lord will find salvation, restoration, and witness his judgment against Assyria and the wicked.

stories.title: 🐎 Isaiah 31
summaryBullets: Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help, who rely on horses, who trust in their abundance of chariots and in their multitude of horsemen. They do not look to the Holy One of Israel; they do not seek the LORD. (31:1).
Yet He too is wise and brings disaster; He does not call back His words. He will rise up against the house of the wicked and against the allies of evildoers. (31:2).

But the Egyptians are men, not God; their horses are flesh, not spirit. When the LORD stretches out His hand, the helper will stumble, and the one he helps will fall; both will perish together. (31:3).

For this is what the LORD has said to me: “Like a lion roaring or a young lion over its prey — and though a band of shepherds is called out against it, it is not terrified by their shouting or subdued by their clamor — so the LORD of Hosts will come down to do battle on Mount Zion and its heights. (31:4).
Like birds hovering overhead, so the LORD of Hosts will protect Jerusalem. He will shield it and deliver it; He will pass over it and preserve it.” (31:5).
Return to the One against whom you have so blatantly rebelled, O children of Israel. (31:6).
For on that day, every one of you will reject the idols of silver and gold that your own hands have sinfully made. (31:7).
“Then Assyria will fall, but not by the sword of man; a sword will devour them, but not one made by mortals. They will flee before the sword, and their young men will be put to forced labor. (31:8).
Their rock will pass away for fear, and their princes will panic at the sight of the battle standard,” declares the LORD, whose fire is in Zion, whose furnace is in Jerusalem. (31:9).
crossRefs: Psalm 20:7: Some trust in chariots and others in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God.
Hosea 14:3: Israel confesses that Assyria will not save them and they will not ride on horses or call their handiwork gods.
Exodus 12:13: The LORD promises that when He sees the blood He will pass over, and no plague will fall on them to destroy them.
2 Kings 19:35: The angel of the LORD strikes down 185,000 men in the Assyrian camp in a single night.
Deuteronomy 32:11-12: The LORD is pictured as an eagle that hovers over its young, spreads its wings to catch them, and carries them.

translationNotes.term: By a sword not of man
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּחֶרֶב לֹא־אִישׁ (b’ḥerev lo-ish), Greek (LXX): μαχαίρᾳ οὐκ ἀνδρός, Aramaic: בְּסַיְפָא דְּלָא דְּאֱנָשׁ
translationNotes.note: Assyria’s fall comes by God’s power, not human armies (31:8).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וְעַל־סוּסִים יִשָּׁעֵנוּ (ve-al susim yishsha'enu, they lean on horses)
translationNotes.note: Egypt was the arms market of the region and chariots were the heavy weapon of the age. 1 Kings 10:28-29 gives the going rate: a chariot imported out of Egypt cost six hundred shekels of silver and a horse a hundred and fifty. Deuteronomy 17:16 forbids a king to build up a stable by sending back to Egypt for them. 31:1 and 31:3 answer the policy in one line, the Egyptians are men and not God, and their horses are flesh and not spirit.

translationNotes.term: As a lion growls over its prey
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כַּאֲשֶׁר יֶהְגֶּה הָאַרְיֵה (ka'asher yehgeh ha-aryeh)
translationNotes.note: 31:4 describes shepherds doing what shepherds did: when a lion took a sheep the whole band was called out to shout it off the carcass. The point of the image is that this one does not let go and is not frightened by the noise. Lions lived in the Jordan thickets into the biblical period; 1 Samuel 17:34-35 has David going after one that took a lamb.

translationNotes.term: His fire is in Zion, his furnace in Jerusalem
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תַּנּוּר (tannur, furnace or oven)
translationNotes.note: 31:9 ends the chapter on the altar. Fire on the altar of burnt offering was ordered never to go out (Leviticus 6:12-13), so a permanent fire burning in Jerusalem was a fact anyone could see. The verse takes that standing fire and makes it the thing the Assyrian officers are running from.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כְּצִפֳּרִים עָפוֹת (ke-tsipporim aphoth)
translationNotes.note: 31:5 uses a bird holding position over the nest, wings beating, between the nest and whatever is coming. The same verb of hovering is used of the Spirit over the water at Genesis 1:2 and of an eagle over its young at Deuteronomy 32:11. The verse stacks four verbs on it: protect, deliver, spare and rescue.

stories.keyTakeaway: Isaiah condemns those seeking help from Egypt instead of the LORD, promising that Egypt's horses and soldiers are merely mortal and will fall; the LORD will defend Jerusalem like a lion and shield it like birds overhead, and Assyria will fall by a divine sword rather than human strength.

headings.text: Woe to Those Who Rely on Egypt

stories.title: 👑 Isaiah 32
summaryBullets: Behold, a king will reign in righteousness, and princes will rule with justice. (32:1).
Each will be like a shelter from the wind, a refuge from the storm, like streams of water in a dry land, like the shadow of a great rock in an arid land. (32:2).
Then the eyes of those who see will no longer be closed, and the ears of those who hear will listen. (32:3).
The mind of the rash will know and understand, and the stammering tongue will speak clearly and fluently. (32:4).
No longer will a fool be called noble, nor a scoundrel be respected. (32:5).
For a fool speaks foolishness; his mind plots iniquity. He practices ungodliness and speaks falsely about the LORD; he leaves the hungry empty and deprives the thirsty of drink. (32:6).
The weapons of the scoundrel are destructive; he hatches plots to destroy the poor with lies, even when the plea of the needy is just. (32:7).
But a noble man makes honorable plans; he stands up for worthy causes. (32:8).
Stand up, you complacent women; listen to me. Give ear to my word, you overconfident daughters. (32:9).
In a little more than a year you will tremble, O secure ones. For the grape harvest will fail and the fruit harvest will not arrive. (32:10).
Shudder, you ladies of leisure; tremble, you daughters of complacency. Strip yourselves bare and put sackcloth around your waists. (32:11).
Beat your breasts for the pleasant fields, for the fruitful vines, (32:12).
and for the land of my people, overgrown with thorns and briers — even for every house of merriment in this city of revelry. (32:13).
For the palace will be forsaken, the busy city abandoned. The hill and the watchtower will become caves forever — the delight of wild donkeys and a pasture for flocks — (32:14).
until the Spirit is poured out upon us from on high. Then the desert will be an orchard, and the orchard will seem like a forest. (32:15).
Then justice will inhabit the wilderness, and righteousness will dwell in the fertile field. (32:16).
The work of righteousness will be peace; the service of righteousness will be quiet confidence forever. (32:17).
Then my people will dwell in a peaceful place, in safe and secure places of rest. (32:18).
But hail will level the forest, and the city will sink to the depths. (32:19).
Blessed are those who sow beside abundant waters, who let the ox and donkey range freely. (32:20).
crossRefs: Isaiah 11:1-5: Righteous ruler from Jesse.
Joel 2:28-29: Spirit poured out on all flesh.
Psalm 72:1-4: Justice for the poor under the king.
Isaiah 30:15: Quietness and trust theme.

translationNotes.term: Spirit poured out from on high
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עַד יֵעָרֶה עָלֵינוּ רוּחַ מִמָּרוֹם, Greek (LXX): ἕως ἂν ἐκχυθῇ ἐφ’ ἡμᾶς πνεῦμα ἄνωθεν, Aramaic: עַד דְּיִתְאֶשְׁדֵּא עֲלַנָא רוּחָא מִלְעֵיל
translationNotes.note: Turning point of renewal (32:15).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׁאֲנַנּוֹת / בֹּטְחוֹת, Greek (LXX): πεποιθυῖαι, Aramaic: שַׁאֲנָן / מִתְרַחֵיץ
translationNotes.note: Targets of a wake-up warning (32:9-11).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שָׁלוֹם… שַׁקֵּט וָבֶטַח, Greek (LXX): εἰρήνη… ἡσυχία καὶ πεποίθησις, Aramaic: שְׁלָם… שַׁקְטָא וּבִטְחָא
translationNotes.note: Results of righteousness dwelling in the land (32:17-18).

A coarse, dark goat-hair fabric worn against bare skin as a universal sign of mourning, repentance, or distress (1 Kings 21:27; Jonah 3:5; Matthew 11:21). Wearing it publicly broadcast grief or contrition; the discomfort itself was part of the symbolism.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׂק (saq); Greek: σάκκος (sakkos)

stories.keyTakeaway: God promises just rule and lasting peace after a hard season; when His Spirit is poured out, society changes at the root.

stories.title: 🛡️ Isaiah 33
summaryBullets: Woe to you, O destroyer never destroyed, O traitor never betrayed! When you have finished destroying, you will be destroyed. When you have finished betraying, you will be betrayed. (33:1).
O LORD, be gracious to us! We wait for You. Be our strength every morning and our salvation in time of trouble. (33:2).
The peoples flee the thunder of Your voice; the nations scatter when You rise. (33:3).
Your spoil, O nations, is gathered as by locusts; like a swarm of locusts men sweep over it. (33:4).
The LORD is exalted, for He dwells on high; He has filled Zion with justice and righteousness. (33:5).
He will be the sure foundation for your times, a storehouse of salvation, wisdom, and knowledge. The fear of the LORD is Zion’s treasure. (33:6).
Behold, their valiant ones cry aloud in the streets; the envoys of peace weep bitterly. (33:7).
The highways are deserted; travel has ceased. The treaty has been broken, the witnesses are despised, and human life is disregarded. (33:8).
The land mourns and languishes; Lebanon is ashamed and decayed. Sharon is like a desert; Bashan and Carmel shake off their leaves. (33:9).
“Now I will arise,” says the LORD. “Now I will lift Myself up. Now I will be exalted. (33:10).
You conceive chaff; you give birth to stubble. Your breath is a fire that will consume you. (33:11).
The peoples will be burned to ashes, like thorns cut down and set ablaze. (33:12).
You who are far off, hear what I have done; you who are near, acknowledge My might.” (33:13).
The sinners in Zion are afraid; trembling grips the ungodly: “Who of us can dwell with a consuming fire? Who of us can dwell with everlasting flames?” (33:14).

He who walks righteously and speaks with sincerity, who refuses gain from extortion, whose hand never takes a bribe, who stops his ears against murderous plots and shuts his eyes tightly against evil— (33:15).
he will dwell on the heights; the mountain fortress will be his refuge; his food will be provided and his water assured. (33:16).
Your eyes will see the King in His beauty and behold a land that stretches afar. (33:17).
Your mind will ponder the former terror: “Where is he who tallies? Where is he who weighs? Where is he who counts the towers?” (33:18).
You will no longer see the insolent, a people whose speech is unintelligible, who stammer in a language you cannot understand. (33:19).

Look upon Zion, the city of our appointed feasts. Your eyes will see Jerusalem, a peaceful pasture, a tent that does not wander; its tent pegs will not be pulled up, nor will any of its cords be broken. (33:20).
But there the Majestic One, our LORD, will be for us a place of rivers and wide canals, where no galley with oars will row, and no majestic vessel will pass. (33:21).
For the LORD is our Judge, the LORD is our lawgiver, the LORD is our King. It is He who will save us. (33:22).
Your ropes are slack; they cannot secure the mast or spread the sail. Then an abundance of spoils will be divided, and even the lame will carry off plunder. (33:23).
And no resident of Zion will say, “I am sick.” The people who dwell there will be forgiven of iniquity. (33:24).
crossRefs: Psalm 46:6-11: God rises and the nations melt.
Isaiah 2:3-4: Zion filled with instruction and justice.
2 Kings 19:35: God destroys the Assyrian force.
Psalm 15:1-5: Who may dwell on God’s holy hill?

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֹׁדֵד / בּוֹגֵד, Greek (LXX): ὁ διαφθείρων / ὁ ἀθετῶν, Aramaic: מַחְבַּל / בּוֹגֵד
translationNotes.note: The one who plunders and betrays will be repaid (33:1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֵשׁ אֹכְלָה, Greek (LXX): πῦρ καταναλίσκον, Aramaic: נוּרָא אָכְלָא
translationNotes.note: Image for God’s holiness that burns away evil (33:14).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֹׁפְטֵנוּ… מְחֹקְקֵנוּ… מַכְּלְכֵנוּ/מַלְכֵּנוּ, Greek (LXX): κριτὴς… νομοθέτης… βασιλεύς, Aramaic: דַּיָּנָא… מְחַקֵּקָא… מַלְכָּא
translationNotes.note: Threefold role of the LORD who saves (33:22).

stories.keyTakeaway: God rises to defend Zion. Those who live uprightly will dwell secure, and the city will be forgiven and healed.

stories.title: 🌋 Isaiah 34
summaryBullets: Come near, O nations, to listen; pay attention, O peoples. Let the earth hear, and all that fills it, the world and all that springs from it. (34:1).
The LORD is angry with all the nations and furious with all their armies. He will devote them to destruction; He will give them over to slaughter. (34:2).
Their slain will be left unburied, and the stench of their corpses will rise; the mountains will flow with their blood. (34:3).
All the stars of heaven will be dissolved. The skies will be rolled up like a scroll, and all their stars will fall like withered leaves from the vine, like foliage from the fig tree. (34:4).
When My sword has drunk its fill in the heavens, then it will come down upon Edom, upon the people I have devoted to destruction. (34:5).

The sword of the LORD is bathed in blood. It drips with fat — with the blood of lambs and goats, with the fat of the kidneys of rams. For the LORD has a sacrifice in Bozrah, a great slaughter in the land of Edom. (34:6).
And the wild oxen will fall with them, the young bulls with the strong ones. Their land will be drenched with blood, and their soil will be soaked with fat. (34:7).
For the LORD has a day of vengeance, a year of recompense for the cause of Zion. (34:8).
Edom’s streams will be turned to tar, and her soil to sulfur; her land will become a blazing pitch. (34:9).
It will not be quenched— day or night. Its smoke will ascend forever. From generation to generation it will lie desolate; no one will ever again pass through it. (34:10).
The desert owl and screech owl will possess it, and the great owl and raven will dwell in it. The LORD will stretch out over Edom a measuring line of chaos and a plumb line of destruction. (34:11).
No nobles will be left to proclaim a king, and all her princes will come to nothing. (34:12).
Her towers will be overgrown with thorns, her fortresses with thistles and briers. She will become a haunt for jackals, an abode for ostriches. (34:13).
The desert creatures will meet with hyenas, and one wild goat will call to another. There the night creature will settle and find her place of repose. (34:14).
There the owl will make her nest; she will lay and hatch her eggs and gather her brood under her shadow. Even there the birds of prey will gather, each with its mate. (34:15).
Search and read the scroll of the LORD: Not one of these will go missing, not one will lack her mate, because He has ordered it by His mouth, and He will gather them by His Spirit. (34:16).
He has allotted their portion; His hand has distributed it by measure. They will possess it forever; they will dwell in it from generation to generation. (34:17).
crossRefs: Jeremiah 49:7-8: Jeremiah's oracle against Edom asks whether wisdom has perished from Teman and tells the dwellers of Dedan to run.
Obadiah 1:1-10: Obadiah's whole word against Edom charges pride in the clefts of the rock and violence against his brother Jacob.
Amos 1:11-12: Edom is judged for pursuing his brother with the sword, and fire is sent on Teman to consume the citadels of Bozrah.
Revelation 6:13-14: The stars fall like unripe figs and the sky recedes like a scroll being rolled up.
Malachi 1:2-4: The LORD says He has made Esau's mountains a wasteland, and whatever Edom rebuilds He will demolish.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֵרֶם (ḥerem), Greek (LXX): ἀνάθεμα, Aramaic: חֵרֶם
translationNotes.note: Ban of total judgment applied here to Edom (34:5).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לִילִית (lilit), Greek (LXX): Λάμια/Λιλίθ (var.), Aramaic: ליליתא (lilita)
translationNotes.note: A rare word in Isaiah 34:14 within a ruin-oracle that lists wild/unclean night creatures. Many translations render it 'night creature' or 'night bird.' The later folklore about 'Lilith' as Adam’s first wife is post-biblical (e.g., the Alphabet of Ben Sira) and is not part of Genesis; Isaiah is not referencing that story.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֱדוֹם (Edom), red - בָּצְרָה (Botsrah)
translationNotes.note: Edom held the broken red sandstone country south of the Dead Sea, and it was Esau's line (Genesis 36:1), so every clash with it is a family quarrel. The grudge is old: Edom refused Israel passage on the way out of Egypt (Numbers 20:14-21), and Obadiah's whole short book charges Edom with standing by and looting while Jerusalem fell. Bozrah was its chief city. The people lived in strongholds cut into cliffs, which is what Obadiah 1:3 means by dwelling in the clefts of the rock.

translationNotes.term: The skies rolled up like a scroll
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וְנָגֹלּוּ כַּסֵּפֶר (ve-nagollu ka-sepher)
translationNotes.note: A scroll left open on a table is rolled shut in one movement when the reading is over, and that is the picture at 34:4. A book with pages will not do it; the image needs a scroll. Revelation 6:14 uses the same line, and 34:4 pairs it with leaves dropping off a vine and figs falling off a tree.

translationNotes.term: The line of confusion and the stones of emptiness
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קַו־תֹהוּ (qav tohu) - אַבְנֵי־בֹהוּ (avne vohu)
translationNotes.note: 34:11 measures Edom for ruin with a builder's cord and a plumb weight, the same tools 28:17 hands to justice. What makes the line land is the two nouns: tohu and bohu, the pair used at Genesis 1:2 for the earth before anything was made of it. The surveyor is marking the ground out back to formless and empty.

stories.keyTakeaway: Isaiah announces God's vengeance against the nations and specifically Edom, describing total destruction, cosmic upheaval, and the land becoming a desolate wasteland inhabited only by wild animals. The destruction will be complete and permanent, fulfilling God's purposes to uphold Zion's cause.

stories.title: 🌋 Isaiah 35
summaryBullets: The wilderness and the dry land will be glad; the desert will rejoice and blossom like a rose. (35:1).

It will bloom profusely and rejoice with joy and singing. The glory of Lebanon will be given to it, the splendor of Carmel and Sharon. They will see the glory of the LORD, the splendor of our God. (35:2).
Strengthen the limp hands and steady the feeble knees! (35:3).
Say to those with anxious hearts: “Be strong, do not fear! Behold, your God will come with vengeance. With divine retribution He will come to save you.” (35:4).
Then the eyes of the blind will be opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped. (35:5).
Then the lame will leap like a deer and the mute tongue will shout for joy. For waters will gush forth in the wilderness, and streams in the desert. (35:6).
The parched ground will become a pool, the thirsty land springs of water. In the haunt where jackals once lay, there will be grass and reeds and papyrus. (35:7).
And there will be a highway called the Way of Holiness. The unclean will not travel it — only those who walk in the Way — and fools will not stray onto it. (35:8).
No lion will be there, and no vicious beast will go up on it. Such will not be found there, but the redeemed will walk upon it. (35:9).
So the redeemed of the LORD will return and enter Zion with singing, crowned with everlasting joy. Gladness and joy will overtake them, and sorrow and sighing will flee. (35:10).
crossRefs: Matthew 11:4-6: Jesus tells John's disciples what they hear and see: the blind receive sight, the lame walk, the deaf hear, and the poor hear good news.
Hebrews 12:12-13: The readers are told to strengthen their limp hands and weak knees and make straight paths for their feet.
Isaiah 51:11: The redeemed of the LORD return to Zion with singing, crowned with everlasting joy, and sorrow and sighing flee away.
Isaiah 40:3-4: A voice calls to prepare the way for the LORD in the wilderness and make a straight highway for God in the desert.
Revelation 21:4: God wipes away every tear, and there is no more death or mourning or crying or pain.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַסְלוּל… דֶּרֶךְ הַקֹּדֶשׁ, Greek (LXX): ὁδὸς ἁγία, Aramaic: אָרְחָא דְּקֳדָשָׁא
translationNotes.note: Safe road reserved for the redeemed (35:8).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֲרָבָה (Arabah) - חֲבַצָּלֶת (chavatstsaleth, crocus)
translationNotes.note: The Arabah is the rift valley floor running south from the Sea of Galilee past the Dead Sea to the Gulf of Aqaba, the lowest and driest ground in the region, salt flats and bare rock. 35:1-2 has that specific country flowering, and gives it the glory of Lebanon, which is cedar forest, and the fertility of Carmel and Sharon. Chavatstsaleth is a bulb flower of open ground, named only here and at Song of Songs 2:1.

translationNotes.term: The mirage shall become a pool
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שָׁרָב (sharav)
translationNotes.note: Sharav is the shimmer of superheated air over baked ground, the thing that looks like standing water to a traveller and is not. 35:7 says the sharav will become a pool: the illusion that has killed people in that country turns into the real thing. The second half of the verse puts reeds and rushes, which need permanent water, where the jackals lay.

translationNotes.term: The blind, the deaf, the lame and the mute
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אָז תִּפָּקַחְנָה עֵינֵי עִוְרִים (az tippaqachnah ene ivrim)
translationNotes.note: 35:5-6 lists four conditions in a fixed order, eyes opened, ears unstopped, the lame man leaping, the tongue of the mute singing. When John's disciples come asking, Jesus answers by listing what they are seeing, and the list is this one: the blind see, the lame walk, the deaf hear, at Matthew 11:4-5 and Luke 7:22.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פְּדוּיֵי יְהוָה (peduye YHWH, the ransomed of the LORD) - גְּאוּלִים (ge'ulim, the redeemed)
translationNotes.note: Both words come from the marketplace. Padah is to buy someone out by paying the price, the verb used for redeeming a firstborn son with five shekels (Numbers 18:16). Ga'al is what a kinsman does when he buys back a relative sold into slavery or a field the family lost (Leviticus 25:25, 25:47-49). 35:9-10 puts the redeemed on the road and the ransomed coming into Zion, and 51:11 repeats the closing line almost word for word.

translationNotes.term: Sorrow and sighing shall flee away
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וְנָסוּ יָגוֹן וַאֲנָחָה (ve-nasu yagon va-anachah)
translationNotes.note: The verb is nus, to run away, the word used of an army breaking and of a man fleeing a pursuer. 35:10 does not say grief is comforted or explained; it says grief runs, and joy is what overtakes the travellers on the road. The line closes the chapter and is quoted back at 51:11 to close another one.

stories.keyTakeaway: The desert will flourish with water and vegetation, and God will heal the blind, deaf, lame, and mute; a holy highway will be established for the redeemed to travel to Zion in joy, where sorrow and sighing disappear.

stories.title: 🏹 Isaiah 36
summaryBullets: In the fourteenth year of Hezekiah’s reign, Sennacherib king of Assyria attacked and captured all the fortified cities of Judah. (36:1).

And the king of Assyria sent the Rabshakeh, with a great army, from Lachish to King Hezekiah at Jerusalem. And he stopped by the aqueduct of the upper pool, on the road to the Launderer’s Field. (36:2).
Then Eliakim son of Hilkiah the palace administrator, Shebna the scribe, and Joah son of Asaph the recorder, went out to him. (36:3).
The Rabshakeh said to them, “Tell Hezekiah that this is what the great king, the king of Assyria, says: What is the basis of this confidence of yours? (36:4).
You claim to have a strategy and strength for war, but these are empty words. In whom are you now trusting, that you have rebelled against me? (36:5).
Look now, you are trusting in Egypt, that splintered reed of a staff that will pierce the hand of anyone who leans on it. Such is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who trust in him. (36:6).
But if you say to me, ‘We trust in the LORD our God,’ is He not the One whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed, saying to Judah and Jerusalem, ‘You must worship before this altar’? (36:7).
Now, therefore, make a bargain with my master, the king of Assyria. I will give you two thousand horses — if you can put riders on them! (36:8).
For how can you repel a single officer among the least of my master’s servants when you depend on Egypt for chariots and horsemen? (36:9).
So now, was it apart from the LORD that I have come up against this land to destroy it? The LORD Himself said to me, ‘Go up against this land and destroy it.’” (36:10).

Then Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah said to the Rabshakeh, “Please speak to your servants in Aramaic, since we understand it. Do not speak to us in Hebrew in the hearing of the people on the wall.” (36:11).

But the Rabshakeh replied, “Has my master sent me to speak these words only to you and your master, and not to the men sitting on the wall, who are destined with you to eat their own dung and drink their own urine?” (36:12).
Then the Rabshakeh stood and called out loudly in Hebrew: “Hear the words of the great king, the king of Assyria! (36:13).
This is what the king says: Do not let Hezekiah deceive you, for he cannot deliver you. (36:14).
Do not let Hezekiah persuade you to trust in the LORD when he says, ‘The LORD will surely deliver us; this city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria.’ (36:15).

Do not listen to Hezekiah, for this is what the king of Assyria says: Make peace with me and come out to me. Then every one of you will eat from his own vine and his own fig tree, and drink water from his own cistern, (36:16).
until I come and take you away to a land like your own— a land of grain and new wine, a land of bread and vineyards. (36:17).
Do not let Hezekiah mislead you when he says, ‘The LORD will deliver us.’ Has the god of any nation ever delivered his land from the hand of the king of Assyria? (36:18).
Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim? Have they delivered Samaria from my hand? (36:19).
Who among all the gods of these lands has delivered his land from my hand? How then can the LORD deliver Jerusalem from my hand?” (36:20).
But the people remained silent and did not answer a word, for Hezekiah had commanded, “Do not answer him.” (36:21).

Then Hilkiah’s son Eliakim the palace administrator, Shebna the scribe, and Asaph’s son Joah the recorder came to Hezekiah with their clothes torn, and they relayed to him the words of the Rabshakeh. (36:22).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 18:13-37: The parallel account of Sennacherib's campaign, the tribute Hezekiah strips from the temple, and the Rabshakeh's speech at the wall.
2 Chronicles 32:1-19: The parallel account, including Hezekiah stopping up the springs outside the city and rebuilding the broken wall.
Isaiah 7:3: Isaiah met Ahaz at the very same spot, the end of the aqueduct of the upper pool on the road to the Launderer's Field.
Isaiah 22:20-21: Eliakim son of Hilkiah, the palace administrator who answers the Rabshakeh, is given Shebna's robe, sash, and authority.
2 Kings 20:20: The annals record how Hezekiah constructed the pool and the tunnel that brought water into the city.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רַבְשָׁקֵה (Rav-shaqeh), Greek (LXX): Ῥαψάκης, Aramaic: רַבְשָׁקֵא
translationNotes.note: Assyrian chief officer/spokesman (36:2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲרָמִית (Aramit) - יְהוּדִית (Yehudit), Judean
translationNotes.note: The officials ask the Assyrian to negotiate in Aramaic, the language of international diplomacy across the whole Near East, so the men on the wall will not understand (36:11). He refuses and keeps shouting in Judean, the Hebrew of the street, because the point of the speech is to break the defenders' nerve, not to reach the king. This is psychological warfare conducted in public, and 36:13-20 is the content: your allies are useless, your god is no better than the gods of the cities we already took.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סוֹפֵר (sopher); Greek: γραμματεύς (grammateus)
translationNotes.note: Originally professional copyists of Scripture. By the New Testament era, scholar-teachers of the Law; often, though not exclusively, aligned with the Pharisees. They formed the educated religious class that adjudicated everyday halakhic questions.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֹׁמְרוֹן (Shomron)
translationNotes.note: The central highland region between Judea and Galilee; capital of the northern kingdom of Israel from 880 BC until Assyrian deportation in 722 BC. The mixed-population descendants who remained ('Samaritans') were despised by Judeans as ethnically and religiously impure. Jesus' choice to travel through Samaria (John 4) and to make a Samaritan the hero of His parable (Luke 10) deliberately upends that prejudice.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לָכִישׁ (Lakhish)
translationNotes.note: Isaiah 36:2 mentions in passing that Sennacherib sent his envoy from Lachish, and that one word carries a great deal. Lachish was Judah's second city, the fortress guarding the western approach from the coastal plain into the hills, and Sennacherib took it in 701 BC. He thought so much of it that he covered a whole room of his palace at Nineveh with a carved stone picture of the siege: the ramp built against the wall, the battering engines pushed up it, archers, defenders throwing down torches, prisoners impaled, and the population marched out with their bundles. Austen Henry Layard dug the panels out in 1845-1847 and they are in the British Museum. The siege ramp itself has been excavated at the site.

translationNotes.term: A broken reed of a staff
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִשְׁעֶנֶת הַקָּנֶה הָרָצוּץ (mish'eneth ha-qaneh ha-ratsuts)
translationNotes.note: The taunt at 36:6 is chosen for the country it is aimed at. Egypt's emblem was the Nile reed, and a reed is hollow: lean your weight on a cracked one and it does not simply fail, it splinters lengthwise and the shaft goes into your hand. The Assyrian is telling the men on the wall exactly what their ally is, in a picture they can see from where they are standing.

stories.keyTakeaway: Sennacherib's field commander arrives at Jerusalem's walls with an ultimatum, mocking Hezekiah's confidence and calling him to surrender while declaring that God himself sent the Assyrians to destroy Judah. Hezekiah's officials remain silent as commanded while the commander addresses the people directly in Hebrew.

stories.title: 🏹 Isaiah 37
summaryBullets: On hearing this report, King Hezekiah tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and entered the house of the LORD. (37:1).
And he sent Eliakim the palace administrator, Shebna the scribe, and the leading priests, all wearing sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz (37:2).
to tell him, “This is what Hezekiah says: Today is a day of distress, rebuke, and disgrace; for children have come to the point of birth, but there is no strength to deliver them. (37:3).

Perhaps the LORD your God will hear the words of the Rabshakeh, whom his master the king of Assyria has sent to defy the living God, and He will rebuke him for the words that the LORD your God has heard. Therefore lift up a prayer for the remnant that still survives.” (37:4).
So the servants of King Hezekiah went to Isaiah, (37:5).
who replied, “Tell your master that this is what the LORD says: ‘Do not be afraid of the words you have heard, with which the servants of the king of Assyria have blasphemed Me. (37:6).
Behold, I will put a spirit in him so that he will hear a rumor and return to his own land, where I will cause him to fall by the sword.’” (37:7).
When the Rabshakeh heard that the king of Assyria had left Lachish, he withdrew and found the king fighting against Libnah. (37:8).
Now Sennacherib had been warned about Tirhakah king of Cush: “He has set out to fight against you.” On hearing this, Sennacherib sent messengers to Hezekiah, saying, (37:9).
“Give this message to Hezekiah king of Judah: ‘Do not let your God, in whom you trust, deceive you by saying that Jerusalem will not be delivered into the hand of the king of Assyria. (37:10).
Surely you have heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all the other countries, devoting them to destruction. Will you then be spared? (37:11).
Did the gods of the nations destroyed by my fathers rescue those nations— the gods of Gozan, Haran, and Rezeph, and of the people of Eden in Telassar? (37:12).
Where are the kings of Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah?’” (37:13).
So Hezekiah received the letter from the messengers, read it, and went up to the house of the LORD and spread it out before the LORD. (37:14).
And Hezekiah prayed to the LORD: (37:15).
“O LORD of Hosts, God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim, You alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth. You made the heavens and the earth. (37:16).
Incline Your ear, O LORD, and hear; open Your eyes, O LORD, and see. Listen to all the words that Sennacherib has sent to defy the living God. (37:17).
Truly, O LORD, the kings of Assyria have laid waste all these countries and their lands. (37:18).
They have cast their gods into the fire and destroyed them, for they were not gods, but only wood and stone — the work of human hands. (37:19).
And now, O LORD our God, save us from his hand, so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that You alone, O LORD, are God.” (37:20).
Then Isaiah son of Amoz sent a message to Hezekiah: “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: Because you have prayed to Me concerning Sennacherib king of Assyria, (37:21).
this is the word that the LORD has spoken against him: ‘The Virgin Daughter of Zion despises you and mocks you; the Daughter of Jerusalem shakes her head behind you. (37:22).
Whom have you taunted and blasphemed? Against whom have you raised your voice and lifted your eyes in pride? Against the Holy One of Israel! (37:23).

Through your servants you have taunted the Lord, and you have said: “With my many chariots I have ascended to the heights of the mountains, to the remote peaks of Lebanon. I have cut down its tallest cedars, the finest of its cypresses. I have reached its farthest heights, the densest of its forests. (37:24).
I have dug wells and drunk foreign waters. With the soles of my feet I have dried up all the streams of Egypt.” (37:25).
Have you not heard? Long ago I ordained it; in days of old I planned it. Now I have brought it to pass, that you should crush fortified cities into piles of rubble. (37:26).
Therefore their inhabitants, devoid of power, are dismayed and ashamed. They are like plants in the field, tender green shoots, grass on the rooftops, scorched before it is grown. (37:27).
But I know your sitting down, your going out and coming in, and your raging against Me. (37:28).
Because your rage and arrogance against Me have reached My ears, I will put My hook in your nose and My bit in your mouth; I will send you back the way you came.’ (37:29).

And this will be a sign to you, O Hezekiah: This year you will eat what grows on its own, and in the second year what springs from the same. But in the third year you will sow and reap; you will plant vineyards and eat their fruit. (37:30).
And the surviving remnant of the house of Judah will again take root below and bear fruit above. (37:31).
For a remnant will go forth from Jerusalem, and survivors from Mount Zion. The zeal of the LORD of Hosts will accomplish this. (37:32).
So this is what the LORD says about the king of Assyria: ‘He will not enter this city or shoot an arrow into it. He will not come before it with a shield or build up a siege ramp against it. (37:33).
He will go back the way he came, and he will not enter this city,’ declares the LORD. (37:34).
‘I will defend this city and save it for My own sake and for the sake of My servant David.’” (37:35).
Then the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 men in the camp of the Assyrians. When the people got up the next morning, there were all the dead bodies! (37:36).
So Sennacherib king of Assyria broke camp and withdrew. He returned to Nineveh and stayed there. (37:37).

One day, while he was worshiping in the temple of his god Nisroch, his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer put him to the sword and escaped to the land of Ararat. And his son Esar-haddon reigned in his place. (37:38).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 19:1-37: The parallel account of the sackcloth, Isaiah's answer, the letter spread before the LORD, the angel, and Sennacherib's death.
2 Chronicles 32:20-23: Hezekiah and Isaiah pray, the LORD sends an angel who cuts off the Assyrian commanders, and Sennacherib returns home in disgrace.
Isaiah 10:5-19: Assyria is the rod of God's anger who boasts as though the axe were greater than the one who swings it, and is judged for it.
Ezra 4:2: Esarhaddon, the son who succeeds Sennacherib in Isaiah 37:38, is named as the Assyrian king who resettled foreign peoples in the land.
Psalm 46:5-7: God is within the city so it will not be moved; nations rage and kingdoms crumble when He lifts His voice.

translationNotes.term: Hook in your nose / bit in your mouth
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חַח… מֶתֶג, Greek (LXX): ἄγκιστρον… χαλινός, Aramaic: חַחָא… מַתְגָּא
translationNotes.note: Assyrian humiliation image turned back on them (37:29).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַלְאַךְ יְהוָה, Greek (LXX): ἄγγελος Κυρίου, Aramaic: מַלְאָךְ דַּיי
translationNotes.note: God’s messenger who kills 185,000 in one night (37:36).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׂק (saq); Greek: σάκκος (sakkos)
translationNotes.note: A coarse, dark goat-hair fabric worn against bare skin as a universal sign of mourning, repentance, or distress (1 Kings 21:27; Jonah 3:5; Matthew 11:21). Wearing it publicly broadcast grief or contrition; the discomfort itself was part of the symbolism.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סוֹפֵר (sopher); Greek: γραμματεύς (grammateus)
translationNotes.note: Originally professional copyists of Scripture. By the New Testament era, scholar-teachers of the Law; often, though not exclusively, aligned with the Pharisees. They formed the educated religious class that adjudicated everyday halakhic questions.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סַנְחֵרִיב (Sancheriv)
translationNotes.note: This campaign is recorded from both sides. Sennacherib's annals, copied onto six-sided clay prisms and now in London, Chicago, and Jerusalem, claim he took forty-six walled cities of Judah, carried off 200,150 people, and shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem like a bird in a cage; he lists the tribute as thirty talents of gold and eight hundred talents of silver, where 2 Kings 18:14 gives thirty talents of gold and three hundred of silver. What the prism never claims is that he took Jerusalem. Isaiah 37:37 has him break camp and go home to Nineveh.

translationNotes.term: killed by his sons in the temple of Nisroch
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֵסַר־חַדֹּן (Esar-chaddon), Esarhaddon
translationNotes.note: Isaiah 37:38 reports that Sennacherib was murdered by two of his sons while worshiping, that they fled to Ararat, and that another son, Esarhaddon, took the throne. Babylonian records note the same killing, dating it to 681 BC, and Esarhaddon's own inscriptions describe having to fight his brothers for the crown before entering Nineveh. Ararat is the region the Assyrians called Urartu, the mountain kingdom around Lake Van in what is now eastern Turkey.

stories.keyTakeaway: Hezekiah tears his clothes and sends officials to Isaiah for prayer against Sennacherib's threats; Isaiah assures him the Lord will turn the Assyrian king back. An angel of the Lord kills 185,000 soldiers in the Assyrian camp that night, Sennacherib withdraws to Nineveh, and is later assassinated by his own sons.

stories.title: ⏳ Isaiah 38
summaryBullets: In those days Hezekiah became mortally ill. The prophet Isaiah son of Amoz came to him and said, “This is what the LORD says: ‘Put your house in order, for you are about to die; you will not recover.’” (38:1).
Then Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed to the LORD, (38:2).
saying, “Please, O LORD, remember how I have walked before You faithfully and with wholehearted devotion; I have done what is good in Your sight.” And Hezekiah wept bitterly. (38:3).
And the word of the LORD came to Isaiah, saying, (38:4).
“Go and tell Hezekiah that this is what the LORD, the God of your father David, says: ‘I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. Behold, I will add fifteen years to your life. (38:5).
And I will deliver you and this city from the hand of the king of Assyria. I will defend this city. (38:6).
This will be a sign to you from the LORD that He will do what He has promised: (38:7).
I will make the sun’s shadow that falls on the stairway of Ahaz go back ten steps.’” So the sunlight went back the ten steps it had descended. (38:8).
This is a writing by Hezekiah king of Judah after his illness and recovery: (38:9).
I said, “In the prime of my life I must go through the gates of Sheol and be deprived of the remainder of my years.” (38:10).
I said, “I will never again see the LORD, even the LORD, in the land of the living; I will no longer look on mankind with those who dwell in this world. (38:11).
My dwelling has been picked up and removed from me like a shepherd’s tent. I have rolled up my life like a weaver; He cuts me off from the loom; from day until night You make an end of me. (38:12).
I composed myself until the morning. Like a lion He breaks all my bones; from day until night You make an end of me. (38:13).
I chirp like a swallow or crane; I moan like a dove. My eyes grow weak as I look upward. O Lord, I am oppressed; be my security.” (38:14).
What can I say? He has spoken to me, and He Himself has done this. I will walk slowly all my years because of the anguish of my soul. (38:15).
O Lord, by such things men live, and in all of them my spirit finds life. You have restored me to health and have let me live. (38:16).
Surely for my own welfare I had such great anguish; but Your love has delivered me from the pit of oblivion, for You have cast all my sins behind Your back. (38:17).
For Sheol cannot thank You; Death cannot praise You. Those who descend to the Pit cannot hope for Your faithfulness. (38:18).
The living, only the living, can thank You, as I do today; fathers will tell their children about Your faithfulness. (38:19).
The LORD will save me; we will play songs on stringed instruments all the days of our lives in the house of the LORD. (38:20).
Now Isaiah had said, “Prepare a lump of pressed figs and apply it to the boil, and he will recover.” (38:21).
And Hezekiah had asked, “What will be the sign that I will go up to the house of the LORD?” (38:22).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 20:1-11: The parallel account of the illness, the prayer, the fifteen added years, and the shadow going back ten steps on the stairway of Ahaz.
2 Chronicles 32:24-26: Hezekiah is mortally ill and given a sign, but his heart grows proud until he humbles himself along with Jerusalem.
2 Kings 20:7: Isaiah calls for a poultice of figs, they apply it to the boil, and Hezekiah recovers.
Joshua 10:12-13: At Joshua's word the sun stands still over Gibeon and the moon over the Valley of Aijalon.
Psalm 88:10-11: A psalm asks whether the dead rise to praise God and whether His faithfulness is proclaimed in the grave.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַעֲלוֹת אָחָז, Greek (LXX): ἀναβαθμοὶ Ἄχαζ, Aramaic: מַעְלַיָּא דְאַחָז
translationNotes.note: A stair/step device that marked the sun’s shadow; the sign reversed it (38:8).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דְּבֶלֶת תְּאֵנִים, Greek (LXX): πλακοῦς σύκων, Aramaic: דְּבָל דְּתֵאִנִין
translationNotes.note: Applied to the boil as part of Hezekiah’s healing (38:21).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁאוֹל (sheol)
translationNotes.note: The Old Testament realm of the dead; a shadowy underworld where both righteous and wicked descend (Genesis 37:35; Psalm 16:10). Not necessarily a place of torment; more a state of cessation and silence. The Septuagint and New Testament render it with the Greek word hades.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צַו לְבֵיתֶךָ (tsav le-vethekha)
translationNotes.note: The words at 38:1 are a legal instruction, not a suggestion to tidy up. Tsav is to give a binding command, and giving it to your house means settling the succession and the estate while you still can. 2 Samuel 17:23 uses the same phrase of Ahithophel, who set his house in order and then hanged himself. Hezekiah at this point has no recorded son, and Manasseh is born in the fifteen years he is given.

translationNotes.term: Rolled up like a weaver's cloth
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קִפַּדְתִּי כָאֹרֵג חַיַּי (qippadti kha-oreg chayyai)
translationNotes.note: 38:12 gives two pictures of a life ending suddenly. The first is a shepherd's tent pulled up and carried off, which took minutes. The second is a weaver finishing a piece on an upright loom and cutting it free of the threads that held it to the frame, and the verse says he cuts me off from the loom, from day to night you bring me to an end.

stories.keyTakeaway: Isaiah tells the dying Hezekiah to prepare for death, but after Hezekiah prays, the LORD extends his life by fifteen years and makes the sun's shadow move backward as a sign. Hezekiah then records his experience of illness and recovery, reflecting on his suffering and gratitude for being spared from death.

stories.title: ⏳ Isaiah 39
summaryBullets: At that time Merodach-baladan son of Baladan king of Babylon sent letters and a gift to Hezekiah, for he had heard about Hezekiah’s illness and recovery. (39:1).

And Hezekiah welcomed the envoys gladly and showed them what was in his treasure house — the silver, the gold, the spices, and the precious oil, as well as his entire armory — all that was found in his storehouses. There was nothing in his palace or in all his dominion that Hezekiah did not show them. (39:2).

Then the prophet Isaiah went to King Hezekiah and asked, “Where did those men come from, and what did they say to you?” “They came to me from a distant land,” Hezekiah replied, “from Babylon.” (39:3).
“What have they seen in your palace?” Isaiah asked. “They have seen everything in my palace,” answered Hezekiah. “There is nothing among my treasures that I did not show them.” (39:4).
Then Isaiah said to Hezekiah, “Hear the word of the LORD of Hosts: (39:5).
The time will surely come when everything in your palace and all that your fathers have stored up until this day will be carried off to Babylon. Nothing will be left, says the LORD. (39:6).
And some of your descendants, your own flesh and blood, will be taken away to be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.” (39:7).
But Hezekiah said to Isaiah, “The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good.” For he thought, “At least there will be peace and security in my lifetime.” (39:8).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 20:12-19: The parallel account of Merodach-baladan's letters and gift, the tour of the treasure house, and Isaiah's word about Babylon.
2 Chronicles 32:31: When the envoys of Babylon came to ask about the sign, God left Hezekiah alone to test him and know what was in his heart.
2 Kings 24:13: Nebuchadnezzar carries off all the treasures of the house of the LORD and the royal palace and cuts up the gold articles.
Daniel 1:3-7: Young men of Judah's royal family are taken to Babylon, placed under the chief of the court officials, and given Babylonian names.
2 Kings 25:13-17: The Chaldeans break up the bronze pillars, the stands, and the Sea of the temple and carry the bronze to Babylon.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סָרִיסִים (sarisim), Greek (LXX): εὐνοῦχοι, Aramaic: סְרִיסִין
translationNotes.note: Court officials often castrated; Isaiah warns some of Hezekiah’s sons will serve this way (39:7).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְרֹדַךְ בַּלְאֲדָן, Greek (LXX): Μαρωδάχ Βαλαδάν, Aramaic: מְרֹדַךְ בַּלְאֲדָן
translationNotes.note: Babylonian ruler sending gifts/letters after Hezekiah’s recovery (39:1).

translationNotes.term: He showed them his treasure house
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֵּית נְכֹתֹה (beth nekhothoh, his house of precious things)
translationNotes.note: 39:2 lists what Hezekiah walked the envoys through: silver, gold, spices, fine oil, the whole armoury, everything in his storehouses. Showing a foreign delegation the treasury was how a king advertised that he was worth allying with. It was also a complete inventory handed to a future enemy, which is what 39:6 says will be carried off, and nothing left.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בָּבֶל (Bavel)
translationNotes.note: In Hezekiah's lifetime Babylon was not yet the power that would take Jerusalem. It was an old city under Assyrian control, and Merodach-baladan held it in revolt against Sargon II before being driven out. An embassy from him to Judah was an approach for a second front against Assyria. 39:6-7 names Babylon as the place everything will end up more than a century before it did.

stories.keyTakeaway: Hezekiah welcomes envoys from Babylon and displays all his treasures to them; Isaiah then prophecies that everything in the palace will be carried to Babylon and some of Hezekiah's descendants will become eunuchs there, which Hezekiah accepts because he expects peace in his own lifetime.

stories.title: 🕊️ Isaiah 40
summaryBullets: “Comfort, comfort My people,” says your God. (40:1).

“Speak tenderly to Jerusalem, and proclaim to her that her forced labor has been completed; her iniquity has been pardoned. For she has received from the hand of the LORD double for all her sins.” (40:2).
A voice of one calling: “Prepare the way for the LORD in the wilderness; make a straight highway for our God in the desert. (40:3).
Every valley shall be lifted up, and every mountain and hill made low; the uneven ground will become smooth, and the rugged land a plain. (40:4).
And the glory of the LORD will be revealed, and all humanity together will see it.” For the mouth of the LORD has spoken. (40:5).
A voice says, “Cry out!” And I asked, “What should I cry out?” “All flesh is like grass, and all its glory like the flowers of the field. (40:6).
The grass withers and the flowers fall when the breath of the LORD blows on them; indeed, the people are grass. (40:7).
The grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of our God stands forever.” (40:8).
Go up on a high mountain, O Zion, herald of good news. Raise your voice loudly, O Jerusalem, herald of good news. Lift it up, do not be afraid! Say to the cities of Judah, “Here is your God!” (40:9).
Behold, the Lord GOD comes with might, and His arm establishes His rule. His reward is with Him, and His recompense accompanies Him. (40:10).
He tends His flock like a shepherd; He gathers the lambs in His arms and carries them close to His heart. He gently leads the nursing ewes. (40:11).

Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, or marked off the heavens with the span of his hand? Who has held the dust of the earth in a basket, or weighed the mountains on a scale and the hills with a balance? (40:12).
Who has directed the Spirit of the LORD, or informed Him as His counselor? (40:13).
Whom did He consult to enlighten Him, and who taught Him the paths of justice? Who imparted knowledge to Him and showed Him the way of understanding? (40:14).
Surely the nations are like a drop in a bucket; they are considered a speck of dust on the scales; He lifts up the islands like fine dust. (40:15).
Lebanon is not sufficient for fuel, nor its animals enough for a burnt offering. (40:16).
All the nations are as nothing before Him; He regards them as nothingness and emptiness. (40:17).
To whom will you liken God? To what image will you compare Him? (40:18).
To an idol that a craftsman casts and a metalworker overlays with gold and fits with silver chains? (40:19).
One lacking such an offering chooses wood that will not rot. He seeks a skilled craftsman to set up an idol that will not topple. (40:20).
Do you not know? Have you not heard? Has it not been declared to you from the beginning? Have you not understood since the foundation of the earth? (40:21).
He sits enthroned above the circle of the earth; its dwellers are like grasshoppers. He stretches out the heavens like a curtain, and spreads them out like a tent to dwell in. (40:22).
He brings the princes to nothing and makes the rulers of the earth meaningless. (40:23).

No sooner are they planted, no sooner are they sown, no sooner have their stems taken root in the ground, than He blows on them and they wither, and a whirlwind sweeps them away like stubble. (40:24).
“To whom will you liken Me, or who is My equal?” asks the Holy One. (40:25).

Lift up your eyes on high: Who created all these? He leads forth the starry host by number; He calls each one by name. Because of His great power and mighty strength, not one of them is missing. (40:26).
Why do you say, O Jacob, and why do you assert, O Israel, “My way is hidden from the LORD, and my claim is ignored by my God”? (40:27).
Do you not know? Have you not heard? The LORD is the everlasting God, the Creator of the ends of the earth. He will not grow tired or weary; His understanding is beyond searching out. (40:28).
He gives power to the faint and increases the strength of the weak. (40:29).
Even youths grow tired and weary, and young men stumble and fall. (40:30).
But those who wait upon the LORD will renew their strength; they will mount up with wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary, they will walk and not faint. (40:31).
crossRefs: Mark 1:3: “Prepare the way of the Lord” applied to John the Baptist.
1 Peter 1:24-25: “Grass withers… word of the Lord remains.”
Psalm 23:1: Shepherd imagery.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נַחֲמוּ (naḥamu), Greek (LXX): παρακαλεῖτε, Aramaic (Targum/Syriac): נַחֲמוּ
translationNotes.note: Command to speak tenderly and announce the end of penalty (40:1-2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְבַשֶּׂרֶת (mevaseret, ‘one who brings news’), Greek (LXX): εὐαγγελιζόμενος, Aramaic: מבשר
translationNotes.note: Herald language for announcing God’s reign (40:9-10).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פֶּסֶל (pesel), Greek (LXX): εἴδωλον, Aramaic: פַּסִיל
translationNotes.note: Carved image contrasted with the living Creator (40:18-20).
The distance between thumb-tip and little-finger-tip with the fingers spread; half a cubit, about 9 inches (23 cm). The breastpiece of the high priest was a span square (Exodus 28:16).
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: זֶרֶת (zeret)

stories.keyTakeaway: God announces comfort and a new arrival; His word stands, idols are nothing, and He strengthens the weary.

headings.text: Prepare the Way for the Lord

stories.title: ⚖️ Isaiah 41
summaryBullets: “Be silent before Me, O islands, and let the peoples renew their strength. Let them come forward and testify; let us together draw near for judgment. (41:1).

Who has aroused one from the east and called him to his feet in righteousness? He hands nations over to him and subdues kings before him. He turns them to dust with his sword, to windblown chaff with his bow. (41:2).
He pursues them, going on safely, hardly touching the path with his feet. (41:3).
Who has performed this and carried it out, calling forth the generations from the beginning? I, the LORD — the first and the last— I am He.” (41:4).
The islands see and fear; the ends of the earth tremble. They approach and come forward. (41:5).
Each one helps the other and says to his brother, “Be strong!” (41:6).
The craftsman encourages the goldsmith, and he who wields the hammer cheers him who strikes the anvil, saying of the welding, “It is good.” He nails it down so it will not be toppled. (41:7).
“But you, O Israel, My servant, Jacob, whom I have chosen, descendant of Abraham My friend— (41:8).
I brought you from the ends of the earth and called you from its farthest corners. I said, ‘You are My servant.’ I have chosen and not rejected you. (41:9).
Do not fear, for I am with you; do not be afraid, for I am your God. I will strengthen you; I will surely help you; I will uphold you with My righteous right hand. (41:10).
Behold, all who rage against you will be ashamed and disgraced; those who contend with you will be reduced to nothing and will perish. (41:11).
You will seek them but will not find them. Those who wage war against you will come to nothing. (41:12).
For I am the LORD your God, who takes hold of your right hand and tells you: Do not fear, I will help you. (41:13).
Do not fear, O Jacob, you worm, O few men of Israel. I will help you,” declares the LORD. “Your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel. (41:14).
Behold, I will make you into a threshing sledge, new and sharp, with many teeth. You will thresh the mountains and crush them, and reduce the hills to chaff. (41:15).
You will winnow them, and a wind will carry them away; a gale will scatter them. But you will rejoice in the LORD; you will glory in the Holy One of Israel. (41:16).
The poor and needy seek water, but there is none; their tongues are parched with thirst. I, the LORD, will answer them; I, the God of Israel, will not forsake them. (41:17).
I will open rivers on the barren heights, and fountains in the middle of the valleys. I will turn the desert into a pool of water, and the dry land into flowing springs. (41:18).
I will plant cedars in the wilderness, acacias, myrtles, and olive trees. I will set cypresses in the desert, elms and boxwood together, (41:19).
so that all may see and know, may consider and understand, that the hand of the LORD has done this and the Holy One of Israel has created it.” (41:20).
“Present your case,” says the LORD. “Submit your arguments,” says the King of Jacob. (41:21).
“Let them come and tell us what will happen. Tell the former things, so that we may reflect on them and know the outcome. Or announce to us what is coming. (41:22).
Tell us the things that are to come, so that we may know that you are gods. Yes, do something good or evil, that we may look on together in dismay. (41:23).
Behold, you are nothing and your work is of no value. Anyone who chooses you is detestable. (41:24).
I have raised up one from the north, and he has come — one from the east who calls on My name. He will march over rulers as if they were mortar, like a potter who treads the clay. (41:25).
Who has declared this from the beginning, so that we may know, and from times past, so that we may say: ‘He was right’? No one announced it, no one foretold it, no one heard your words. (41:26).
I was the first to tell Zion: ‘Look, here they are!’ And I gave to Jerusalem a herald of good news. (41:27).
When I look, there is no one; there is no counselor among them; when I ask them, they have nothing to say. (41:28).
See, they are all a delusion; their works amount to nothing; their images are as empty as the wind. (41:29).
crossRefs: Isaiah 45:1-4: The one stirred up from the east is named outright: Cyrus, whose right hand the LORD grasps to subdue nations before him.
2 Chronicles 20:7: Jehoshaphat prays to the God who gave this land forever to the descendants of Abraham His friend.
James 2:23: Abraham believed God, it was credited to him as righteousness, and he was called a friend of God.
Deuteronomy 7:7-8: The LORD did not choose Israel because they were numerous, since they were the fewest of all peoples, but because He loved them.
Micah 4:13: Zion is told to rise and thresh, given horns of iron and hooves of bronze to break many peoples to pieces.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אִיִּים (iyyim, ‘coastlands/islands’), Greek (LXX): νῆσοι, Aramaic: איי
translationNotes.note: Shorthand for distant peoples summoned to hear (41:1-5).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֶבֶד (ʿeved), Greek (LXX): παῖς/δοῦλος, Aramaic: עַבְדָּא
translationNotes.note: Title used for Israel (41:8-9) and for the figure who brings justice (42:1-7); context decides the referent.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִשְׁפָּט (mishpat), Greek (LXX): κρίσις, Aramaic: דִּינָא
translationNotes.note: Not only verdicts; here the right order God establishes among the nations (42:1-4).

stories.keyTakeaway: God calls the nations to a judgment and asks who stirred up a conqueror from the east; he then assures Israel, his chosen servant, that he will strengthen them, make their enemies vanish, provide water in the desert, and challenges the idols to declare the future as proof of their power, which they cannot do.

stories.title: ⚖️ Isaiah 42
summaryBullets: “Here is My Servant, whom I uphold, My Chosen One, in whom My soul delights. I will put My Spirit on Him, and He will bring justice to the nations. (42:1).
He will not cry out or raise His voice, nor make His voice heard in the streets. (42:2).
A bruised reed He will not break and a smoldering wick He will not extinguish; He will faithfully bring forth justice. (42:3).
He will not grow weak or discouraged before He has established justice on the earth. In His law the islands will put their hope.” (42:4).

This is what God the LORD says— He who created the heavens and stretched them out, who spread out the earth and its offspring, who gives breath to the people on it and life to those who walk in it: (42:5).
“I, the LORD, have called you for a righteous purpose, and I will take hold of your hand. I will keep you and appoint you to be a covenant for the people and a light to the nations, (42:6).
to open the eyes of the blind, to bring prisoners out of the dungeon and those sitting in darkness out from the prison house. (42:7).
I am the LORD; that is My name! I will not yield My glory to another or My praise to idols. (42:8).
Behold, the former things have happened, and now I declare new things. Before they spring forth I proclaim them to you.” (42:9).
Sing to the LORD a new song— His praise from the ends of the earth— you who go down to the sea, and all that is in it, you islands, and all who dwell in them. (42:10).
Let the desert and its cities raise their voices; let the villages of Kedar cry aloud. Let the people of Sela sing for joy; let them cry out from the mountaintops. (42:11).
Let them give glory to the LORD and declare His praise in the islands. (42:12).
The LORD goes forth like a mighty one; He stirs up His zeal like a warrior. He shouts; yes, He roars in triumph over His enemies: (42:13).
“I have kept silent from ages past; I have remained quiet and restrained. But now I will groan like a woman in labor; I will at once gasp and pant. (42:14).
I will lay waste the mountains and hills and dry up all their vegetation. I will turn the rivers into dry land and drain the marshes. (42:15).

I will lead the blind by a way they did not know; I will guide them on unfamiliar paths. I will turn darkness into light before them and rough places into level ground. These things I will do for them, and I will not forsake them. (42:16).
But those who trust in idols and say to molten images, ‘You are our gods!’ will be turned back in utter shame. (42:17).
Listen, you deaf ones; look, you blind ones, that you may see! (42:18).
Who is blind but My servant, or deaf like the messenger I am sending? Who is blind like My covenant partner, or blind like the servant of the LORD? (42:19).
Though seeing many things, you do not keep watch. Though your ears are open, you do not hear.” (42:20).
The LORD was pleased, for the sake of His righteousness, to magnify His law and make it glorious. (42:21).
But this is a people plundered and looted, all trapped in caves or imprisoned in dungeons. They have become plunder with no one to rescue them, and loot with no one to say, “Send them back!” (42:22).
Who among you will pay attention to this? Who will listen and obey hereafter? (42:23).
Who gave Jacob up for spoil, and Israel to the plunderers? Was it not the LORD, against whom we have sinned? They were unwilling to walk in His ways, and they would not obey His law. (42:24).
So He poured out on them His furious anger and the fierceness of battle. It enveloped them in flames, but they did not understand; it consumed them, but they did not take it to heart. (42:25).
crossRefs: Matthew 12:17-21: Matthew quotes Isaiah 42:1-4 in full about Jesus: He will not quarrel or cry out, and a bruised reed He will not break.
Matthew 3:16-17: The Spirit of God descends on Jesus like a dove and a voice says, 'This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.'
Exodus 15:3: 'The LORD is a warrior, the LORD is His name,' the picture Isaiah 42:13 uses of God marching out.
Acts 26:17-18: Paul is sent to open their eyes so they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God.
Isaiah 6:9-10: The commission of ever hearing but never understanding, ever seeing but never perceiving, matches the deaf and blind servant here.

translationNotes.term: A bruised reed and a smoldering wick
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קָנֶה רָצוּץ (qaneh ratsuts) - Hebrew: פִּשְׁתָּה כֵהָה (pishtah kehah)
translationNotes.note: A qaneh is a marsh reed, cut and used as a measuring rod or a pen; once it is cracked it is worthless and gets thrown away. The pishtah is a twist of flax serving as a lamp wick, and a wick that only smokes gets pinched out. Matthew 12:18-21 quotes verses 1 to 4 of this chapter and applies them to Jesus.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אִיִּים (iyyim)
translationNotes.note: The word covers islands and coastlands together, and in Isaiah it means the far shores of the Mediterranean, the outer edge of the known world seen from Jerusalem. It is a way of saying the most distant peoples there are, not a reference to specific islands.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קֵדָר (Qedar) - Hebrew: סֶלַע (Sela)
translationNotes.note: Kedar was a confederation of desert Arab tribes descended from Ishmael's second son (Genesis 25:13), living in black goat-hair tents in northern Arabia; Song of Songs 1:5 compares a woman's darkness to their tents, and Jeremiah 49:28-29 describes their flocks and tent curtains being carried off. Sela means rock and is the Edomite cliff stronghold in the highlands of Seir, captured by Amaziah in 2 Kings 14:7. Verse 11 calls on the desert nomads and the mountain fortress together.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַסֵּכָה (massekhah) - Hebrew: פֶּסֶל (pesel)
translationNotes.note: Two different manufacturing processes. A pesel is carved, usually from wood, and a massekhah is poured, cast metal. Isaiah 40:19-20 and 41:6-7 describe the actual shop work: a smith casts the figure, a goldsmith overlays it with gold and fits silver chains, and someone nails it down so it will not topple over.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֵּית כֶּלֶא (beit kele)
translationNotes.note: Israel had no penal prison system; confinement was for holding a man until his case was decided, and the holding place was often a dry cistern, a bell-shaped pit cut in rock with no exit but the mouth. Joseph was thrown into one and later held in the Egyptian round-house (Genesis 37:24; 40:15), and Jeremiah was let down into a cistern and sank into the mud (Jeremiah 38:6). That is the picture behind verses 7 and 22.

stories.keyTakeaway: God presents his servant who will bring justice to the nations quietly and faithfully, while declaring himself the sole Lord who will guide the blind and make a way through the wilderness; Israel has been plundered and captured because they rejected God's ways, yet he poured out his anger without their understanding.

stories.title: 🎶 Isaiah 43
summaryBullets: But now, this is what the LORD says— He who created you, O Jacob, and He who formed you, O Israel: “Do not fear, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by your name; you are Mine! (43:1).

When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and when you go through the rivers, they will not overwhelm you. When you walk through the fire, you will not be scorched; the flames will not set you ablaze. (43:2).
For I am the LORD your God, the Holy One of Israel, your Savior; I give Egypt for your ransom, Cush and Seba in your place. (43:3).
Because you are precious and honored in My sight, and because I love you, I will give men in exchange for you and nations in place of your life. (43:4).
Do not be afraid, for I am with you; I will bring your offspring from the east and gather you from the west. (43:5).
I will say to the north, ‘Give them up!’ and to the south, ‘Do not hold them back!’ Bring My sons from afar, and My daughters from the ends of the earth— (43:6).
everyone called by My name and created for My glory, whom I have indeed formed and made.” (43:7).
Bring out a people who have eyes but are blind, and who have ears but are deaf. (43:8).

All the nations gather together and the peoples assemble. Who among them can declare this, and proclaim to us the former things? Let them present their witnesses to vindicate them, so that others may hear and say, “It is true.” (43:9).

“You are My witnesses,” declares the LORD, “and My servant whom I have chosen, so that you may consider and believe Me and understand that I am He. Before Me no god was formed, and after Me none will come. (43:10).
I, yes I, am the LORD, and there is no Savior but Me. (43:11).
I alone decreed and saved and proclaimed— I, and not some foreign god among you. So you are My witnesses,” declares the LORD, “that I am God. (43:12).
Even from eternity I am He, and none can deliver out of My hand. When I act, who can reverse it?” (43:13).
Thus says the LORD your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: “For your sake, I will send to Babylon and bring them all as fugitives, even the Chaldeans, in the ships in which they rejoice. (43:14).
I am the LORD, your Holy One, the Creator of Israel, and your King.” (43:15).
Thus says the LORD, who makes a way in the sea and a path through the surging waters, (43:16).
who brings out the chariots and horses, the armies and warriors together, to lie down, never to rise again; to be extinguished, snuffed out like a wick: (43:17).
“Do not call to mind the former things; pay no attention to the things of old. (43:18).
Behold, I am about to do something new; even now it is coming. Do you not see it? Indeed, I will make a way in the wilderness and streams in the desert. (43:19).
The beasts of the field will honor Me, the jackals and the ostriches, because I provide water in the wilderness and rivers in the desert, to give drink to My chosen people. (43:20).
The people I formed for Myself will declare My praise. (43:21).
But you have not called on Me, O Jacob, because you have grown weary of Me, O Israel. (43:22).
You have not brought Me sheep for burnt offerings, nor honored Me with your sacrifices. I have not burdened you with offerings, nor wearied you with frankincense. (43:23).
You have not bought Me sweet cane with your silver, nor satisfied Me with the fat of your sacrifices. But you have burdened Me with your sins; you have wearied Me with your iniquities. (43:24).
I, yes I, am He who blots out your transgressions for My own sake and remembers your sins no more. (43:25).
Remind Me, let us argue the matter together. State your case, so that you may be vindicated. (43:26).
Your first father sinned, and your spokesmen rebelled against Me. (43:27).
So I will disgrace the princes of your sanctuary, and I will devote Jacob to destruction and Israel to reproach.” (43:28).
crossRefs: Revelation 15:3: Song celebrating God’s works (new song motif).
2 Corinthians 1:10: God who delivers (salvation theme).
Exodus 14:21-22: Way through the sea (exodus backdrop).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גָּאַל (gaʾal), Greek (LXX): λυτρόομαι, Aramaic: פָּרַק/גאל
translationNotes.note: Family/legal rescue language; God claims Israel as His (43:1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֵדִים (ʿedim), Greek (LXX): μάρτυρες, Aramaic: סַהֲדִין
translationNotes.note: Israel is appointed to testify that the LORD alone is God (43:10-12).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֲדָשָׁה (ḥadashah), Greek (LXX): καινόν, Aramaic: חדתא
translationNotes.note: Fresh saving act, like a second exodus (43:19).

A milky-white resin from the Boswellia tree of southern Arabia. Burned as incense in the temple (Exodus 30:34); offered with every grain offering. The magi's second gift, traditionally read as signaling priesthood.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לְבוֹנָה (levonah); Greek: λίβανος (libanos)

stories.keyTakeaway: God promises rescue for His blind, plundered people, declares them His witnesses, and announces a new exodus through wilderness and waters.

stories.title: 🪵 Isaiah 44
summaryBullets: But now listen, O Jacob My servant, Israel, whom I have chosen. (44:1).
This is the word of the LORD, your Maker, who formed you from the womb and who will help you: “Do not be afraid, O Jacob My servant, Jeshurun, whom I have chosen. (44:2).
For I will pour water on the thirsty land, and currents on the dry ground. I will pour out My Spirit on your descendants, and My blessing on your offspring. (44:3).
They will sprout among the grass like willows by flowing streams. (44:4).
One will say, ‘I belong to the LORD,’ another will call himself by the name of Jacob, and still another will write on his hand, ‘The LORD’s,’ and will take the name of Israel.” (44:5).
Thus says the LORD, the King and Redeemer of Israel, the LORD of Hosts: “I am the first and I am the last, and there is no God but Me. (44:6).
Who then is like Me? Let him say so! Let him declare his case before Me, since I established an ancient people. Let him foretell the things to come, and what is to take place. (44:7).
Do not tremble or fear. Have I not told you and declared it long ago? You are My witnesses! Is there any God but Me? There is no other Rock; I know not one.” (44:8).
All makers of idols are nothing, and the things they treasure are worthless. Their witnesses fail to see or comprehend, so they are put to shame. (44:9).
Who fashions a god or casts an idol which profits him nothing? (44:10).
Behold, all his companions will be put to shame, for the craftsmen themselves are only human. Let them all assemble and take their stand; they will all be brought to terror and shame. (44:11).

The blacksmith takes a tool and labors over the coals; he fashions an idol with hammers and forges it with his strong arms. Yet he grows hungry and loses his strength; he fails to drink water and grows faint. (44:12).

The woodworker extends a measuring line; he marks it out with a stylus; he shapes it with chisels and outlines it with a compass. He fashions it in the likeness of man, like man in all his glory, that it may dwell in a shrine. (44:13).
He cuts down cedars or retrieves a cypress or oak. He lets it grow strong among the trees of the forest. He plants a laurel, and the rain makes it grow. (44:14).

It serves as fuel for man. He takes some of it to warm himself, and he kindles a fire and bakes his bread. He also fashions it into a god and worships it; he makes an idol and bows down to it. (44:15).
He burns half of it in the fire, and he roasts meat on that half. He eats the roast and is satisfied. Indeed, he warms himself and says, “Ah! I am warm; I see the fire.” (44:16).
From the rest he makes a god, his graven image. He bows down to it and worships; he prays to it and says, “Save me, for you are my god.” (44:17).
